WIND SONGS. A mighty minstrel is the wind, With music every changing; From highest notes of rapturous joy To saddest dirges ranging; It frolics round the waving grain, Running before and after, It warbles through the summer trees, Like rippling waves of laughter. To. night it moans about the house, And holds our eyelids waking, It comes and goes with mournful sighs, As if some heart were breaking; As if some loving mother, bent Above a dear child dying, Were pouring out her anguished soul In long and bitter crying. When the dull summer heats are o'er The north wind comes resounding, To rouse the stagnant soul to life, And set the pulses bounding. It wakes us with its martial stir, Like trumpet voices ringing, And fills the forest with the swell Of its majestic singing. But dire and dreadful is the strain, When from rough fields of ocean, Some drxfting ship draws near the shore, And none can stay its motion. The death•knell pealing through the shrouds, The prayers to heaven ascending, Proclaim how weak the arm of man With Nature's wrath contending. A mighty minstrel is the wind, For now it idly lingers, To touch some soft and gentle string With Its lEolian fingers. And now it sweeps across the world, In its loud-sounding chorus, And pours its swelling tides of song In joy or terror o'er us.

Lady Montague said, "It goes far towards reconciling sue to being a woman when I reflect that I am in no danger of marrying one." Now, that is singular. The very thing which she feared is just what reconciles the rest of us to being men. "John," said a gentleman the other day, "I am going to church, and if, as it now has the appearance, it should rain, T wish you to come with the umbrella for ins. However, you need not come unless it should 'rain downright.'" The gentlemln went—it did rain; but, according to John's con- struction of his orders, it was not necessary, from the appear. ance of the rain, to go with the umbrella. While standing at the door, watching the weather, he was not a little , astonished to see his master approaching the house with drenched clothes and a look of implacable anger. "John, I John," said the good man, "why didn't you bring the um- brella 2" "Because, sir," replied John, "It rained slanting." , MUSHROOM•OROWING no Towxs.—Mushrootn-gro wing is indeed one of those pursuits that those in crowded towns may follow as successfully as the more favoured horticul- turist in the country. The best of horse-droppings abound In towns. Boxes of all kinds are also plentiful, and a few of these properly filled could even be placed on areas, bal. I conies, and house-tops. Carefully covered over, and pro- tented from extremes of drought and of cold, the spawn would run as freely and as strongly among surrounding soot, dust, and dirt, as in the purest air of the country. The portable mushroom-beds, canopied with cocoa-fibre, tissue' I moss, or, if preferred, an old flannel petticoat, will feel none I of the untoward influences around them, and are, when they puela through, smoothly covered with an anti-adhesive skin, that the blacks will glide as harmlessly off from as water from a duck's back. Besides, they need never be exposed to the light at all, as there is no perceptible difference either ' in substance or flavour between mushrooms grown in the dark and in the light. To the mushroom, in fact, as basal- ready been observed, the darkness and the light are both alike. Even the very poor, who live alike in the blinding glare of the garret and the stifling gloom of the cellar, and who in both mostly manage to keep some flowering plants alive in some broken jar or cracked tea pot, may have some of the pleasures and profits of mushroom-growing brought within their reach. The portable culture of the mushroom will prove easy to those who have done so much and so well , with other plants, under difficulties that seem as appalling I as insurniountable.—Cassell's Popular Gardening. FRESH AIR.—WHY WE WANT IT, AND HOW TO GET IT.
To be healthy and enjoy life, nothing is more important than fresh air. Tbe morefresh air we breathe, the less wilt be our doctors' ' •

.„ It is Nature's free and molt valuable gift, and yet it is generally foolishly excluded from our dwellings. Every time we breathe, the blood is affected. Breathing ,fresh air enriches the blo 3d. Breathing impure air poisons the blood.

Impure air in our rooms is produced by our own breath, o and:es, lamps, gas, vegetable matter, dirty linen, and want of cleanliness. As we are constantly breathing and rendering the air im- pure, it is absolutely necessary for health that fresh air should be constantly coming into the room. We must try to get fresh air without draught, and without feeling cold. Although fires are necessary, our bodies will be kept warm by a good circulation of the blood, produced by fresh air, !pod food, and warm clothing, mach cheaper than by a forge amount of fuel. Let as much fresh air into our MOM as possible. Our rooms ,hould imitate our lungs, and constantly breathe in feesh air and breathe out impure air. The Air should Always be Moving. This is cheapest done by having a hole cut say ten inches square over the door, and covered with perforated zinc, and by fastening a piece of perforated zinc to the top of the sash frame the whole width of the window and about four inches deep; the top sash can then be lowered, and in this way the air is being constantly changed above our heads, and we do not feel draughts. Any working-man can do this for a few pence. In bedrooms this is even more important than in Bitting. rooms.

A JOKER CAUGHT.—Dr. M—, an army surgeon during the war, was very fond of a joke (if not perpetrated at his own expense), and had, moreover, a great contempt for citizen officers, who were more renowned for their courage than their scholarship. One day, at mess, after the decanter had performed certain perambulations of the table, Captain S—, a brave and accomplished officer, and a great wag, remarked to the doctor, who had been somewhat severe in his remarks on the literary deficiencies of some of the new offfeers—" Dr. act —, are you acquainted with Capt. G—?" "Yes, I know him well," replied the doctor; "he's one of the new set. Bat what of him ?" "Nothing in particular," replied Capt. B—. "I have just received a letter from him, and I will wager you a dozen of old port that you can- not guess in six guesses how he spells eat" "Done," said the doctor. "It's a wager." "Well, commence guessing," said S. " K, a, double t." "No." "Kate." "No." "Cates." "No." "Catt." "No." "Kat." "No, that's not the way; try again, it's your last guess." " Caght." No," said 8---, "you're wrong again; and you've loot your wager." " Well," said the doctor, with much petulance of manner, "how, then, does he spell it ?" "Why, he spells it C, A, T," replied S— with the utmost gravity. Amid the roar of the mess, and almost choking with rage, the doctor sprang to his feet, exclaiming, " Captain S—, I am too old a man to be trifled with in this manner." It is a curious fact that a large majority of literary men invariably seem anxious at some period or other of their career to test by the medium of anonymous publication the value of public opinion with regard to their own work. "It is not, periwig, generally known," writes a correspondent of the Pall Mall Gazette," that The Lady of Lyons' was brought out quite anonymously, and that on the night of its first production beyond Macready and Balwer Lytton himself, no one in London had been allowed to know the secret of the authorship of the play. Between the acts Dickens, who had been one of a delighted audience, went behind the scenes to talk over the play with Macready and Balwer, congratulating Macready on his wonderful imper- sonation of Claude Melnotte. Dickens was in raptures with the whole thing, and asked Balwer what he thought of it. Balwer affected to find some fault with the plot, and suggested improvements here and there in various situa- tions. Come, no v,' said Dickens, 'it is not like you, Bel- war, to cavil at such small things as those. The man who wrote the play may have imitated your work here and there, perhaps, but he is a deuced clever fellow for all that. To hear you speak so unfairly is almost enough to make one think that you are jealous." The papers next morning lauded the play to the skies, even going so far as to suggest that it would be well for Mr. Bulwer to take pattern by this unknown writer, and try to improve himself in those parti- cular points in which the anonymous author of " The Lady of Lyons" had been so brilliantly successful. About a fortnight later Bulwer'a authorship of the play was made known, to the mingled consternation and amusement of the critics and the general public. MIKE THE CHILDREN SELF•RELIANT.—There can be DO question but that it is natural for some children to be far less daring and self-reliant than others; but that timidity and nervous terrors are much increased by the over•sym- pethy of mothers I have not the slightest doubt. Bid your two.year.old Carrie to bring some article from the next room. "It's dark," she says, shrinkingly. "Oh ! not too dark to get mother what she wants," you answer cheerily; and almost invariably the child will go at once. Be careful not to prelude your request by, "Are you afraid to go in the dark ?" Too of ten the mother says pityingly, "Oh ! she's afraid • I'll go," and the result is that the child never ven- tures alone in a darkened room. Semebody must go up- stairs with it, somebody must get it a drink of water, some- body must put away its hooks or hat, because "it'd dark." We have seen this child-formed habit cling to persons even of mature years, a habit exceedingly uncomfortable to them- selves and others. This unwise sympathy of mothers causes themselves mach unnecessary work, inasmuch as it renders children more independent than they need be. There are mothers too sympathetic to teach infants to sit alone, but weary, back and arms, holding them. This unwise seen- I pathy causes a child to magnify trifling ills into great mis- fortunes, and helps to strengthen as with cords the two ready selfishness of the heart. As an excellent writer said but lately, "a saintly, unselfish woman may have very die- 'agreeable, selfish children, ever putting herself last; but it is her own fault." Expect something of your child, and show him or her that you do expect something, and in nine cases out of ten your child responds to you, even at a much earlier age than soft disciplinarians will admit. As a char- , acter in a late book for girls energetically puts it, "Set I your children on their feet —on their own feet!" They are 'neither angels nor toys, but human beings, with immortal I souls, whose usefulness and happiness in this world, and Ipreparations for another, may be greatly marred, if not lost, by unwise training. REMINISCENCES OF CHARLES Mum—Despite his elabo- rate theories about art, Mr. Reade was in reality only guided by practical results. I have frequently known him take grave exception to an actor's conception of a part at rehearsal, but if the offender struck fire at night, the end justified the means, even if his views were diametrically op- posed to those of the author. If from some adverse cir- cametance—a bad house, an east wind, an unsympathetic audience—the play did not elicit the usual modicum of ap- plause, then the actors were stigmatised as "duffers"— "Differs, sir, who have defiled my composition mixed ditch-water with my champagne, murdered my work." The next night perhaps there was a good house—perhaps the wind was not in the east, perhaps a thousand things—at any rate, if the play was received enthusiastically, then all was condoned and forgiven. The popular applause was music to Mr. Reade ; he would ensconce himself in his box, turn his back to the stage, and as the audience laughed or cried he laughed and cried with them, and their tears or cheers were always his barometers of the actor's ability. I have often heard him say that he thought the great orator or the great actor quaffing the full wine of applause crushed in one moment into a golden cup and drained from the pub • lie heart, was the most enviable of human beings. No man, except himself, ever combined, in one and the same person, such an extraordinary mass of contradictions as I Charles Reade. Of course, it is well known, that if any one assailed him, he dipped his pen in vitriol, and poured I the vials of his wrath upon his luckless adversary. On these occasions nothing could restrain the headstrong rush of his impetuosity, nothing check the torrent of his oblate gationa. Yet, on the other hand, if called upon to advise a friend under similar circumstances, he frequently exercised quite a judicial function, and was the very incarnation of mildness.—John Coleman, in Temple Bar, for August. ORIGIN OF THE POST OFFICE.—The post office was originally the office which arranged the posts or places at which, on the great roads' relays of horses and men could be obtained for the rapid forwarding of Government de. spatches. There was a chief postmaster of England many years before any system of conveyance of private letters by the Crown was established. Such letters were conveyed either by carriers, who used the same horses throughout their whole journey, or by relays of horses maintained by private individuals, that is, by private poet. The scheme of carrying the correspondence of the public by means of Crown messengers originated in connection with foreien trade. A post office for letters to foreign parts was estab- lished, "for the benefit of the Eaglish merchants," in the reign of James 1., but the extension of the system to inland letters was left to the succeeding reign. Charles 1., by a proclamation issued in 1635, may be said to have founded the present post office. By this proclamation he commanded his Postmaster of England for foreign parts to settle a run. fling post or two, to run night and day between Edinburgh and London, to go thither and come back again in six days, and to take with them all such letters as shall be directed to any post town in or near that road. Neighbouring towns, such as Lincoln and Hull, were to be linked on to this main route, and posts on similar principles were directed to be established on other great high roads, such as those to Ches- ter, Holyhead, Exeter, and Plymouth. So far no monopoly was claimed, but two years afterwards a second proclama• tion forbade the carriage of letters by any messengers ex- cept those of the King's Postmaster-General, and thus the present system was inaugurated. The monopoly thus claimed, though no doubt devised by the King to enhance the Royal power, and to bring mosey into the exchequer, was adopted by Cromwell and his Parliament, one main advantage in their eyes being that the ca:riage of corres• pondence by the Government would afford "the beat means to discover and prevent any dangerous and wicked designs against the Commonwealth." The optort inity of an exten- sive violatirn of letters, especially if they proceeded from suspected Royalists, was no doubt an attractive halt; and it is rather amusing to notice how the tables were turned on the monarchical party by means of one of the Sovereign's own acts of aggression. However, from one motive or another, Royalists and Parliamentarians agreed in the es- tablishment of a State post, and the institution has come auee. without a break from the days of Charles I. to our own. Ia Scotland, however, a dense mist enshrouded many of the moors, and the weather generally interfered with the shooting. THE EXPORT OF CATTLE TO THE UNITED ST/ans.—The United States Consul in London announces that prior to the export of neat cattle from Europe the exporter must obtain from the Commissioner of Agriculture at Washington a per- mit to export, and American consuls in the United King- dom are instructed not to authenticate invoices unless upon the production of such permit giving particulars of the I cattle for which it has been granted. A SHORT PEA SEASON.—According to my experience, weather influences and modes of cultivation have a great deal to do with the length or shortness of the pea season, but it is also a question of variety. Some varieties appear to stop podding and become too old and dry for use before , they have well begun to be useful. We have had rows of kinds in Jane and July which were ready for use at the beginning of a week, and almost over before the end of it; I while neighbouring rows of different kinds, under the same conditions, which were more satisfactory. Amongst these latter some new varieties have behaved uncommonly well. Gardeners' Chronicle.

Hoetair.—A Scotch bee keeper writes :—Times are changed now from what they were 20 years ago. We then had no difficulty in getting 2s. 61. per pound for supers, often 3s. 61, and sometimes more; bat now is. 61. is the maximum, except in scarce years such as last one was, when 2s. was readily obtained for heather comb. At no time now have we any diffichlty in getting from is. 31. to Is. 61. per pound for dript honey; so that in reality, taking the wax into consideration, and the extra outlay for sections, dript honey is the least trouble and most profitable to the bee keeper. So much has been written about the advantages of frame hives and non-productiveness of straw ones, that I am sur- prised that bee keepers have not been up in arms long since. All the honey merchants in Glasgow I have conversed with prefer supers to sections; and while in Edinburgh I in- quired which was most in favour, and all of them said supers holding from 3lbs. to 81b3. were preferred. Sections Iwere objectionable more ways than one. Large supers, if divisiele, were also in favour. The foregoing, though brief, ; will, I think, be understood and accepted as reliable from experience. AGRICULTURAL RETURNS F3R 1884.—The Agricultural Department of the Privy Coancil has issued the agricultural returns of Great Britain for 1884. The returns, which were collected cn Jane 4'.11 show that the extent of land in Great Britain under wheat is 2,876,477 acres, barley 2,159,485 acres, oats 2,692,576 acres, potatoes 562,311 acres, and hops 69,258 acres. As compared with 1883 there is an increase in wheat under cultivation of 63,315 acres, or 24 per cent.; ' barley, a decrease of 132,506 acres, or 5 8 per cent.; oats, a decrease of 82,805 acres, or 2 8 per cent.; potatoes, an in- crease of 18,889 acres, or 3•5 per cent.; and in hops an in- crease of 1,242 acres, or 18 per cent. The total number of live stock at the date the returns were collected were as foi- -1 lows :—Cattle, 6,211,127 ; sheep and lambs, 26,037,217; pigs, 2,582,323, showing, as compared with 1883, an increase In cattle of 278,348, or 47 per cent ; sheep and lambs, an increase of 968,917, or 39 per cent.; and pigs a decrease of of 35,434, or 14 per cent., and as compared with 1882 there is an increase in cattle of 433,636, or 7 5 per cent.; sheep land lambs, 1,717,449, or 7 1 per cent.; pigs, an increase of 71,921, or 2 9 per cent. .

JOININGSWARMS.—As the season is now upon us to make the most of our bees, but in which the largest harvest of honey is to be obtained, providing the bees have access to the heather, and fine weather favours the blooming period, the stocks strong and supers well wrapped up, the bee- keeper will assuredly be rewarded with a bountiful harvest. 'There is seldom any difficulty in manipulating straw hives, but too many frame hives are not so easily managed in this respect. To be successful in joining swarms to frame hives, simply uncap some of the cells, disturbing the bees a little until every one is gorged with honey, the swarms to be added having previously been well sprinkled with thinned honey or syrup. Now cast the swarm on to a frame hive, and not a bee will be killed. NVhere there is no ventilation take steps to have all floors provided with this safety valve, not forgetting to make provision for the escape of the vitiated air at the top of the hive. That being attended to, over. heating becomes impossible, and the stocks seated in pairs Instead of equidistant, so as to prevent confusion and fight- ing, all will go well. Then as supers are finished and empty ones added, all will have been done that the bee-master can do. We only hope and wait for a favourable season, which is at the present promising.

A 250 WORDS ESSAY ON BUTTER MAKING —The Wis- consin Dairymens' A.sociation last year offered prizes for the best essays on butter making, the best essays not to ex- ceed 250 words. Competition was active, and many vain. able little treatises was the result. The first prize was won by D. W. Curtis, of Fort Atkinson, and his essay reads as follows:—" Select Cows rich in batter making coslities. Pastures should be dry, free from slough-holes, well.seeded with different kinds of tame grasses, so that good feed is assured. If timothy or clover, cat early and cure properly. Feed corn, stalks, pumpkins,ensilage, and plenty of vegetables in winter. Corn and oats, corn and bran.oll meal in small quantities. Let cows drink only such water as you would yourself. Gentleness and cleanliness should be shown in managing cows. Brush the udder to free it from impurities. Milk in a clean barn, well ventilated, quickly, cheerfully, with clean hands and pails. Seldom change milkers. Strain milk while warm; submerge in water 48 deg. Open setting 60 deg. Skim at 12 hours; at 24 hours. Care must bs exercised to ripen cream by frequent stirrings, keeping at 60 deg. until slightly sour. Better have one cow less than be without a thermometer. Churns without inside fixtures. Lever butter worker. Keep sweet and clean. In churning, stir the cream thoroughly; temper to 60 deg. ; warm or cool with water. Churn immediately when properly soured, slowly at first, with regular motion, in 40 to 60 minutes. When butter is formed in granules the size of wheat kernels, draw off the buttermilk; wash with cold water and brine until no trace of butter is left. In working and salting, let the water drain Out; weigh the butter; salt one ounce to the pound; sift salt on the butter and work with a lever. worker. Set away two to four hours; re work lightly and pack." D:STRICT CROP Norms.—The special correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, writing of the crops in Lanca- shire, says:—" In going north to the Fylde district I find most of the grain in the Irwell valley is cut, and from Los. tock to where the rail crosses the Douglas at Adlington the greater portion of the oat crop is to cut. Reapers are busy' at work, but there is no urgency, as grain is later here and not very heavy. The old meadow hay has been all cleared, off. In the neighbourhood of Eaxton grain was not quite ready for catting, but about Leyland and Farington a fair proportion was cut, though the crops are not heavy. In the valley of the Ribble, where there is some good wheat land, formerly liable to flooding, the wheat crops are scarcely ready for cutting. There is nothing of any moment done in the way of harvesting in the Fylde as far as Kirkham, and taking northward through Greenhalgh, Esprick, and Thistleton. Cutting has not commenced in this district, but there are some very good oats, though not much wheat. At Larbrick grain is ten days or a fortnight earlier, and ma- i ting both of oats and wheat is going on rather briskly. The I crops, however, are not so forward as by the Mersey. On the way from Kirkham to the Wyre across country there is aban- dance of grass on the pastures, and the eddish is well grown. The clover crops are generally heavy, and farmers are straining every point while the sunny weather lasts, as they have fears of a wet spell to follow. A very cheerful nth. fled tone prevails amongst them. On the Singleton and Weeton side grain cutting has commenced, the crops being various. Where the grub has not been mischievous oats are good. The outlook for potatoes is gratifying, and cattle are looking well without exception, and very splendid herds there are to be met with. The general wish is for the weather to hold out, so that the whole of the crops requiring sun and wind drying can be housed with little delay. Over Wyre cutting Is very active. A correspondent from the Fylde district, who has been trained to farming there, writing to me on the 19th inst. from the neighbourhood of Richmond, Yorkshire, says :—"There is a wide difference between the farming in these dales and in the Fylde. It is a novelty to see a field of grain, but in some places you find a few turnips and potatoes which look fairly well. Farmers are just finishing getting in their hay, and are busy getting in the winter store of bedding for cattle, which consists of bracken off the Moors. They very seldom use a cart for housing hay. They generally make a round stack in the meadow and use a sleigh or sweep. The hay crop has been about an average yield. Sheep have done very well, and on the whole farmers seem more prosperous than in the Fylde." Another correspondent, writing from the dairying district between the Fylde and the Fells, says Everyone here agrees that there never has been a finer season for all kinds of farm produce. They are now housing in Whittingham some of the finest second crops of clover that has ever been Cut here."

A SPEARING DOG.—A. gentleman entered a restaurant and asked for the bill of fare. 1' What shall I get you, sir ?" asked the waiter. "I'll take a couple of poached eggs to at ill with." "And so will I," said the dog, who had perched himself on a chair by the side of his master. The waiter looked scared. A few moments later the guest called out, " Waiter, bring me roast beef and potatoes." "And me too," added the dog. Intense stupefaction on the part of the waiter. At the next table eat an Englishman, who now looked up and said, "You must have taken immense trouble to teach your dog to talk." "Yes." " You wouldn't like to part with it ?" " Not for any money." "Pray don't sell me!" excliimed the dog, in suppliant tones. " Will , you take a thousand pounds for it ?" said the Englishman, eagerly. " A thousand pounds is a large sum," was the reply. At length the bargain was struck; the Englishman wrote out a cheque of £I,OOO and took up the dog. "As you have cold me," said the latter, looking back at his master," I'll hive my revenge, and won't speak any more!" Of ceuree it was ventriloquism.

div.head: 11IE EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST 30, 1884 COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: 11IE EXAMINER SATURDAY. AUGUST 30, 1884 COTTAGE GARDENING

Most subjects are new at a standstill in the vegetable garden. Peas and beans have been considerably diminished. The former, in dry, hot weather, Bach as we have expe- rienced, soon become hard and mealy, and the haulm re- fuses to extend itself and produce successional crops. Scarlet runners and the dwarf French beans are setting better than one would expect. Cauliflowers no sooner form their compact heads than they are expanded in all direc- tions. When it is necessary to save these for a certain date much in the way of retarding may be accomplished by placing a shade over them. In the usual way some of their own leaves will answer the purpose, but with such heat as we have experienced lately they soon perish, so it is best to place on them some fabric. If this expedient fails to retard them sufficiently, pull them up, and without trimming any more than a few rough leaves store them away in a dark, cool place, such as a cellar, where they will maintain their freshnen for some days. Celery in various stages requires earthing up, but we have been waiting for rain, because to water some of it now would require a large quantity to be applied to reach all the roots, and to earth up with dry soil, and enclose more equally dry, would only create an addi- tional barrier to the passage of the rain when it comes. The shower of Tuesday was refreshing, but the amount of rain was inadequate for this purpose, and if we do not have more soon we shall water a portion of earth up immediately. Celery receives very rough treatment at the hands of some in their attempt to earth it up, and many of the heads are In consequence crippled. The correct way of proceeding is to grasp the plant with one hand and place earth to it with the other as high as the short leaves which spring up in the middle. Upon no account should soil be allowed to enter between the leaves. Pressing the soil too firmly towards the top prevents the centre from pushing up, and when the heads are dug they are usually found deformed and useless. STRAWBERRTES.—As soon as the ground is softened by rain, take the first opportunity to make a fresh bed, but at the time we write we can neither get them lathe ground nor out of it without water. The plants may be placed in a I single row at distances of 12 inches, and 2 feet between the I rows, and after cropping one year, every alternate plant can Ibe cut away. Another method that may be adopted is to plant two feet apart in the row, and one on each side of the one forming the straight line, so as to form a triangle, and I these two additional ones can be cropped away after the first year's fruiting. The advantage of either of these methods is to increase the produce two or threefold the first year. Numbers who ought to know better make a straw- berry plantation and reap no benefit till the second year ' after planting. The plants that will produce the crop we guarantee are not such as are picked up haphazard, but each as have been prepared according to instructions already given in this column. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The tropical temperature we have experienced seems to have sailed many of the tenants of the front garden. Asters, stocks, and zinnias notably so. I The latter is one of the most delicate of annuals; vet we saw some good flowers in a cottage garden more than a week ago. The various nastartinms are as floriferous as they well can be. The ease with which these can be grown, may be gleaned from the following incident. One of the young members of our family, a few weeks ago, with the assist- ' ance of a table fork, removed the soil from between the sets which formed the pavement of a yard, and planted some nasturtiums about two inches high which had been cast on one side, and such were the hopes entertained of their success, that pieces of string were fixed to the wall for them to cling to and climb two or three feet high. They have sow just reached one-half the maximum height estimated, and are well covered with flowers. Considering that they do not receive the benefit of sunshine till after midday they have done well. It may not be generally known that the seeds of the nasturtium are largely used as a substitute for capers in the preparation of caper sauce. THE WINDOW.—If the pelargoniums have been attended to as previously advised, the wood made the past season will be a brown colour two or three inches from the base, which is a sure indication that it has been properly matured. In pruning the plants from one to two inches of it may be left, and several shoots will be produced by each piece which will form the plant the following year. The plant should be dust dry at pruning time and for a day or two after, when it may receive daily sprinkling in the imitation of a light shower, and in very hot weather twice a day; and the quantity of water may be increased as the growth p rogesses. All the pranings having a portion of well ripened wood at the base make the best of cuttings, which may vary in length from three to six joints' and if inserted round the inside of a small pot and treated as to water for the present, similar to the parent plant, the majority of them will form roots and make nice plants next year. They should have light sandy soil and be pressed moderately firm as each ma- ting is put in, or they will dry and shrivel.
down. For light birds height is of no moment, if the house Is roomy, but for heavy birds, or in small houses, about 18 or 24 inches is sufficiently high.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. A FLOATING ISLAND.—On Lake Derwentwater the float- ing island has again made its appearance. It is now of comparatively small area, though gradually enlarging. Four years ago the island was first seen, and, as it only ap- pears daring exceptionally hot summers, it is locally re- rded as the forerunner of continued fine weather. 13BILLIANT METEOI4—Mr. W. Harding Smith writes to The Times from Christchurch, Hampshire, to describe the extraordinary lustre of an aerolite, which at 10 30 on Saturday night illumined everything around with alight as brilliant as the most vivid lightning. An immense ball of blue fire traversed the sky at a most rapid pace, leaving a train of a luminous kind, which remained in sight for some minutes after the nucleus was extinguished, gradually bend- ing up at the extremity before it disappeared. EDUCATIONAL 0 rEII•PRESSURE.-111rs. Dr. Anderson, sum- ming up the question of educational over-pressure, says "the truth about over-pressure in primary schools appears, then, as far as I am able to judge, to be this—that there is exceedingly little of it; that there is less risk of it now than there was under the last code; that it would not be for the interest either of the children in the schools, or of the taxpayers who provide the school grants, to yield to the demands made by the teachers and based upon the charge of over-pressure."

A—Cnulica LIGHTED BY ELECTRICITY.—The Roman Catholic Church of Sc. John, built by the Marquis of Bate, at Old Cumnock, Ayrshire, has recently been fitted through- out with the electric light, under the personal superintend- ence of Mr. William Massey, of Twyford, electrical engi- neer to the Royal Palaces. There are in all about 70 glow lamps of 20 candles each, and the effect is very perfect, the architectural features of the building having been carefully studied and the lamps arranged with due regard to the reli- gious character of the place. The necessary current is supplied by means of a dynamo and steam engine placed in a small house hidden among the trees of the churchyard, where it is also intended to generate electricity for working the organ bellows. A PLevuo Kumla CartufactE.—The Pall Mall Gazette says :—"Through the courtesy of the South-Eastern offi- cials, our representative has had the opportunity of inspect- ing this latest novelty in carriage building. In appearance it is like an ordinary composite coach, except that the sides and ends are covered with plates of metal, and shine like an electroplated dish cover or the dome of a Russian church. Every experiment is commendable, and the railway world will await the results of experience in this case with the greatest interest. Will the saving in paint and cleaning be such as to cover thetntlay for plates? Will the heat be excessive? Why has Mr. Wainwright lined the guard's van with metal, and will not his berth be a very hot one in August and a very cool one in January? Such are some of the questions that arise. Railway men will like to see this glorified coach after it has been running for a few months. At present it is as bright and beautiful as a new tricycle. PRINTING BY ELECTRICITY.—The Lawrence American of July 9 says:—" For more than ten days past the entire power for running not only the large Hoe press upon which this psper is printed, but for the cylinder and job presses of the entire printing establishment, has been from electricity coming over a single wire from the dynamos, four blocks away; the fires under our steam boiler have now slept nearly two weeks, while the little electrical machine, weigh- ing only 8001 b , gatetly, steadily, unceasingly, without jarr- ing Of difficulty, keeps up its marvellously equal revolu- tions. There is no delay in waiting to get up steam, no loss of time from any of the ordinary uncertainties of boilers, but, whenever the minute comes when the power is required a single movement of the lever and the wheel starts upon its swift unchanging revolutions. We believe the American is the first daily newspaper, if not the first regularly pub- lidied journal of any description, to be printed in this country with electrical power. To what will not this yet but little underatood power be turned?

WOMEN As Drrssrons.—The question has often been raised (says the Academy) whether the higher education of women in science can conduce to anything more than their own intellectual benefit, and whether they are able to con- tribute to its advancement by means of original work. We are glad to have to record one more instance showing that this question mast be answered in the affirmative. The mechanical division of a line into any number of equal parts is a problem that has often taxed the ingenuity of technical men, and which has only just been satisfactorily solved by a former student of Girton College. The " Line Divider," invented by Miss Sarah Marks, consists of a hinged divided rule sliding in a plain rule in such a way that the free limb of the hinged rate indicates successively the divisions re- quired on the line to be divided. This remarkably simple and accurate instrument, which Is an application of the properties of similar triangles, will render good service to architects, engineers, painters, geometricians, and in fact to all those who have to do with the line and rule.

A PAINLI33B DEATH.—Dr. Richardson's experiments for the painless extinction of animal life have been brought to a successf al termination. As the electric shock, which at one time was advocated for this purpose, did not prove sufficiently safe, Dr. Richardson sought for an anaesthetic agent which would make death rapid as well as painless. Be successively experimented with nitrous and carbonic oxides, ether, chloroform, methylene, carbonic acid, bisul- phide of carbon, coal-gas combined with chloroform, all of which more or less fulfilled their end. The results have been very satisfactory, as carried out at thealHome for Lost Dogs, where a chamber was charged with carbonic oxide, the gas having been previously passed over a porous surface, from which it took up vapour containing cloroform. Into this chamber was introduced a cage containing so many dogs, who in a very short time passed from life to death in a pro- found sleep, withoat evincing the slightest pain or con- sciousness. Dr. Richardson has also administered the same narcotising agent to sheep, so as to allow of their being killed in a perfectly painless manner. THE INVENTOR OF THE STEAMBOAT,—A Pads corres- pondent says that at &ninon a statue has been unveiled, with becoming pomp, to the memory of Jouffroy d'Abbans. Jonffroy is held in France to have been the inventor of the steamboe, Fulton being considered an imitator. Be that as it may, his first experiment was made on the Doubs as early as 177 U, and repeated in 1783 on the Saone at Lyons. Jouffroy, however, was poor, his invention was never pro- perly taken up, and his life was the sad one of a man who sew others reap the reputation and success which he thought should have been hia. The statue represents him in a pensive attitude, with one hand on the then primitive steam engine, and the other as if engaged in the un- ravelling of a problem. On the pedestal there are three reliefs. One represents him in the act of instructing his machinist at Baume les Dames, the second reveals his un- couth steamer on the Saone at Lyons, and the third the poor inventor, ruined and in despair, a soldier, dying at the Invalides. In the background books are mingled with his accoutrements. The sculptor is M. Gautier, and the pedestal is the work of St. Ginest, both belonging to the department of Franche-Comte. The festivities were attended by M. de Lesseps and the Minister of Public Works, who made speeches appropriate to the occasion, the latter coupling the names of Jouffroy and De Lessen the one as the inventor of the steamship, the other as the man who has afforded such large scope for its employment.

. - LORD BRABAZON AND EMIC&TION.—Lord Brabazon having recently offered prizes of the value of £2OO to teachers and scholars of the London School Board for pro- ficiency in gymnastics and swimming on the part of men and boys, and for a knowledge of cookery, Swedish gym- naatics, first aid to the wounded and ambulance work on the Dart of the women and girls, received a reply stating "that the Board had entire sympathy with the object which his lordship had in view, but they were bound to point out that the special instruction and arrangements that would in general be necessary to give full effect to his lordship's wishes would involve a great disturbance of the ordinary curriculum of the Board schools as laid down in the Govern- ment code. With reference moreover, to gymnastics and calisthenics, the Board remarked that there was insufficient apparatus in the schools of the Board to enable these sub- jects to be taught to the children in all the schools." Hence for the reasons elven the Board declined to accept his lord- ship's offer. Writing to his secretary, Captain Thompson, from Switzerland, whither he has gone for the benefit of his health, Lord Brabazon says: " When I made the offer I was quite aware that the special instructions and arrangements that would be neoesaary to give full effect to my wishes would involve a great disturbance of the ordinary carrion- -1 am of the Board schools as laid down in the Government code;' and it was in order to effect such a disturbance that I made my offer4for I felt that too mach attention was being paid to the strictly intellectual portion of education and too little to the physical and practical needs of the scholars. Now I should be sorry if no result came from my offer, and I should like you to think over how best the at- tention of the School Board authorities could be attracted to what I believe is a great need in our School Board educa- tion. I want to see our education carried out on some practical and useful lines taking into consideration the class which usually attends public elementary schools." SERICULTURE IN VIE UNITED Sments —An increasing Interest is being manifested throughout America in the im- portant question of silk raising, and the Californian Bureau for the promotion of the object has recently issued a report containing much information on the cultivation of the worm and the adaptability of the industry to the United States. The rapid development of the silk manufacture is quite a sufficient reason why every facility /should be given for the production of the raw material. In 1850 the num- ber of silk factories in the United States was 29, employing 857 workpeople, and a capital of 600,000 dollars; whereas In 1880 these had risen to 383 establishments, employing 30,000 hands, and a capital of 20,000,000 dollars; and at the present time there are 388 works engaged in the silk trade. California, however, is by no means the only State that is interesting itself in the silk culture, the Middle and Southern States being peculiarly suitable to the cultivation, and especially those of Mississippi and Missouri. Mr. Wrotnowski, who resider(rit Baton Rouge, Louisiana, was formerly the proprietor of a large maguaneria in Pay du Dome, and has reported most favourably on the exoellence of the silkworms raised in Louisiana, on the leaves of the Horus multicaulis, which, from his experience, he believes to be the best and most profitable of all mulberries, the healthiest for the worms, and producing the beat cocoons and the finest quality of silk. The Caucasian mulberry tree has been imported into Nebraska from the German colonies in Southern Russia, and is highly spoken of, the trees having attained a growth of eight inches in diameter and 16 feet high in the short space of six years. Silk cul- ture has been promptly taken up by ladies' associations which exist in Alabama, California, and Philadelphia, while

'a considerable trade is being carried on in cocoons at Corinth (Mississippi) and Memphis (Tennessee). A food which ap- pears to be specially useful for silkworms is the Osage orange (maclura aurantia,ca), which grows abundantly in the hedges; and it is said that the very beat silk is procured from the worms reared on this food, the tests showing that a less weight ofcocooas spun by maclura-fed worms was re- quired for a pound of reeled silk than of cocoons from mul- berry-fed worms.

AMERICAN HOSPITALITY. The hospitality of the Yankees is unbounded. They cannot do too much for a man when they take to him. It would perhaps be better for the guest if the host knew how to modify his show of welcome. But he does not know it; and you have to take everything he sets before you or insult him. It would be vain to utter a protest. You might as well bid the spread eagle close its wings, and not look so "darned defiant," as offer to expostulate. If you are at dinner you have a dish of clams to begin with, the finest bivalves in the world according to your friend's notions. But if your stomach does not give a "squirm" when your eyes behold the semblance of a small bedroom candle, with the "snuff" bent at the top, you are fit to do roughing work among any tribe of Indians who stop short of canni- balism. These disposed of you have to face bacon and beans, and drink hot tea, with the thermometer at 90 degrees in the shade, and the cooking-stove at your elbow. If you get through this course you begin to "give out;" and you sigh to be under a tree in Dunham Park, with a tender beef sandwich, and "suthin" grateful to wet your whistle with. But you have not finished yet. There are sweet cakes, dough nuts, green corn, stewed prunes, and the inevitable candy. And if you have not reconciled yourself to drinking alternate draughts of iced water and hot tea, you have got to do it now. Men you have to talk religion; or, what amounts to the same thing with some people, your favourite minister. Godliness may enter into some part of the creed; but it is a puzzle to find it. The "noble art of self- defence" may have its beautiful points; but who is the bast "slogger ?" is the question most to be considered by the lovers of pugilism. On the same principle lam afraid that the glories of real religion are too often observed by the shadow of the beat "devil-mauler." Then you get on poli- tics. What are B.aine's chances? and what do you think of Arthur's last "boom ?" You must have an opinion, so take your cue from your host.

- Politics enter more into the social life of America than they do in England. Their newspaper literature of the pre- sent time is full "right through" of the doings of Repub- licans and Democrats, on account of the coming election of President. The Republican convention at Chicago has been the theme of every tongue, and ended in bad blood. Next we shall have the Democratic convention, daring the sittings of which we are bound to have another deluge of political printers' ink. This excitement will be kept up until November, when the President will be elected. The atmos- phere will be resonant w th " booms " in the meantime; and we shall have piles of sensational headings, and political slang sufficient to stock a dozen burlesques, and as many pantomimes. Whit a pity these things should occur in the hottest weather, when thousands of people are away to the cooler North, "doing" the Alps and the Rhine; and explor- ing the lair of the toothless Saxon lion ! Why not "get through" with them in winter, when a little warmth is re- quired, unless it Is from a fear of the le, crop being damaged by the heat of political controversy, and a good source of income diminished?

I have been reminded of these things by an incident that followed an invitation to supper with a genuine old English- man in one of the cities "down east." Mine host and his wife still cherished the prejudices they had brought with them from the " old country," whilst their daughter, a hot-pressed, gilt-edged, Russian leather copy of the "Yankee gal," who had never scented the hawthorn, nor cooled her face in May dew, to keep down freckles, did not believe there was anything in England worth their remem- bering, except it might be their "sparking" days, and she "guessed" that was the secret of her parents' love for their old home. The mother was inconveniently, but not stone deaf; and as deaf people have an awkward way of telling the truth when it ought to have been concealed, this old lady had the misfortune of disarranging the "Connections" of the domestic telephone to the utter discomfiture of the daughter. On my visit to this family I was an hour late for "supper," which in England means" tea," in Lancashire in particular," baggin'." I bogged to apologise, and hoped I had not kept them waiting, although I was the only guest. "Not a moment," said the daughter; "we didn't expect you until quite this time." That assurance caused me to feel as much at ease as the temperature of the weather would permit. But the mother, putting in her "motty," had the effect of disturbing this serenity; and I felt as if there was thunder ailout. "We'd gan you up," said the honest old dame, who did not believe in telling falsehoods to make things pleasant. "My dowter said Englishmen wur never to be depended on; an' we made it out that yo'd better fish to fry, and war abovo cocain' to spend a net wi' poor folk. Warno' that it, Jennie ? '

The daughter's looks were needles • but she had got to make the best of matters as they stood'. "Mother is kinder deaf," she remarked in an undertone ; "and she gets things Into her head she thinks she has heard. If you listen to her she'll just lose you. Tea or coffee?" Tea I preferred: and the young lady retired. "I'd give a trifle for a quart o' English cockles," said the old dame, her mouth watering at the thought. " We'n nowt here that tastes like 'ern. But yon yer folk say that clams are th' best shell fish that con be f'und anywheere. They wouldno' say so if they'd as mony dollars i their pockets as would carry 'em back to owd England. Give a mon a Rola Island clam, an' a Southport cockle, an' I know which he'd put on th' stove fast. Now I'm straight forrad, an' say what I think."

The daughter here entered with the tea and coffee. " Wheem's thy feyther ?" demanded the mother. I had noticed there was a set chair that no one came to occupy. "Gone to see the telegrams from Chicago," was the reply. "Wheay, what's to do theere ? It's not a fire again, is it ?"

'No ; there's a meeting of Republican delegates to select a man to run for President. Father's a Blaine man." "He is, is he ? Ile'ra not a plain mon when he're thy age, let me tell thee. He'ra better lookin' than thou art, anyway. Thou taks too lurch o' thy mother to be pratty." More needle-pointed glances shot across the table. "Will you take a cake, Mr. Brierley ? "said the daughter, handing me a plate. "They are very nice,—my own making."

" Are yo' troubled with your liver ? " inquired the elder party, when she saw I was offering to take one. "I am," I replied. "That was the cause of bringing me here. But why do you a* ? " "Ay ; but I conno' gether fro' that whether yo' want to be made better, or wurr." "Better, of cour3e."

"Ay, I guess yo dale. But if yo done want to be better dunno ate thoose cakes. Butter's as dear here as it is i' England; an' yo conno' get marjoram at fifteen cents a pound as good as butter at thirty-six. But they'n passed a new law fort' prevent marjoram fro' bein' made. Next time yo come we shall happen be able to offer yo cakes wi' gradely butter in 'em."

The needles in the daughter's eyes had grown to razors; but a smile of incredulousness prevented them being shied across the table; and she begged that I should not take any further notice of her mother. I had dismissed the clams, and felt satisfied when they were not pressed upon rue! and took the cake, so as not to appear prejudiced. "Knock th' cat of yor knee," said the elder dame. "It wants to lake th' milk fro' th' strawberries."

Cats are eats in America; not the puny things we see chasing sparrows in England, or playing with a ball of worsted ; but fine, noble animals, that your first impulse suggests being on friendly terms with, or being armed with a "shot-gun." They rub against your legs without giving the familiar purr, and you begin to suspect that you have a prairie wolf about you, or an Adirondack leopard. This I had been informed, was a " gentleman " cat, and could "play snakes" with rats. After supper he appeared upon the scene with a mouthful of prey that he had tilt brought from the jungle, nor caught in the cellar; but for the possession of which some butcher's shop had been laid under tribute. It was a loin of mutton chop, that caused his tail to erect itself to beyond the perpendicular. The struggle was a fierce one; but the prey continued to have the beet of it. "Is the cat an old one ?" I inquired, thinking the animal's teeth might be getting worse for wear. "No; but I guess the chop is," mine host replied. "Bob wouldno' ha' getten that if it had been fit for a table. That mutton has seen moore than one president." "I have not tasted a tender bit of mutton since I came over." I remarked.

"Guess yo' need no' ha' towd me that," said mine host; "it isn't to be got. Sent to the old country. What we have left here's only fit for dryin', an mak-in into shingles for chicken hutches. Yo' may get a steak sometimes that doesno' mak' yo'r ears wartch wi' chewin' ; but yo can never depend on mutton." But the cat has caused me to jump over a part of my story. Mine host had not yet returned from his news hunt- ing expedition; and in his absence I had a good deal of fencing to do with his deafer half. There was nothing American that pleased her. The love of the mother country was too deeply ingrained in the old woman's system to be removed by anything short of cauterisation. And yet these people had returned to England twice with the intention of settling; but could not rest there. The bright skies they had left beyond the Atlantio shone brighter in their me- mories when they beheld the cheerless atmosphere, made more dreary by the contrast—of their native land. They sold up a third time, and were here again, as dissatisfied as ever.

"i"o'n ha' to sweeten yor tae yorsel," said the old woman, seeing that I was twirling my spoon for nothing. "There's 'o'er little of owt done for folk I' this country. How don yo like yor atin wheere yo'n bin?"

" Not over well," ireplied. "Not accustomed to the style, nor the cooking." " Yo'n had no broth, I guess ? " I shook my head. "Nor potato pie?" " No." "Nor steak dumplin ? " I had not. "Nor steak pie?" "No; but I have had real pie." "Then a Lancashire woman made it?" ‘‘,l believe she was from Lancashire." "No doubt o' that. War there a cup INV middle r, "I don't remember !" " Hoo*d happen be feart o' breakin it, an' havin to buy a new un. Tho' hoo shouldno' ha' bin feart, for cups are mad• so thick you can hardly get yor top lip o'er th' rim."

"What is the reason of there being made so thick and cl ?As,' ?" I inquired. 'So that they wittno' break," was the reply. "We 1132 to pay a heavy duty on pots; an' it we broke 'ern, as `- vants hreaken 'em i England, we should be ruinated in a month. Me an' my tally went three miles one Sandal a-lookin at a set a chancy (china); an' there war others theere beside us. I dust hardly touch it for fear efttib tumblin to pieces. Yo duntio' seem to be gettin on with your supper." • "You don't give the gentleman a chance," put in hi' daughter, who had hitherto kept a dignified silence. I assured my entertainers that I was doing exceedinglY well; but my tardiness gave that statement the lie. " Have yo store teeth that yo'r so slow ?" inqui red the elder party. "Mother, you're insulting the gentleman," said tbe daughter, with a severe protest in her looks. 'snee "Nowt o'th' sort. He's nobbut like other folk. it th' fashin to wear their own, no moore than it is seein out spectacles. But PR say nowt no moore ;" and the ()lc! girl subsided for a time. It was well she did, as her hushauu made his appearance. he "Oh, yo'n come at last," said the head of the house, es ,d brushed into the room. "We'd given yo up. I said Ye very likely gone wi' th' mayor, an' yo'rn havin a good tinn on't. I think by th' appearance o' things BlaMe 'll have, vote. Well Jim has done good work in his time, aa deserves to be th' President." "I've been told that he's disposed to make trouble with England 2" I observed. "No doubt yo'n bin towd that. An' it's as likely 70 Wilt, be towd that he'll tak Egypt, an' India, an' Australy ; he'll ha' th' Prince o' Wales put in a cage, an' shown amen% like a guinea pig. He'll see that justice is done to Irelano,. so that it'll stop emigration, as we're gettin so crowded . one mon has to stood while another sits' W 5 to send to other countries for ' beef. Jiro J3l/ 'll cause o that if yo'n tak any notice 0' what a soreYe says." Not a bad introduction to a tea-table debate, I thong „ The old man warmed with his tea; and was at one tl.e3„;s an' corn, an shall down on all Yankees; and at another pitting them agah.- the "blorsted British snobs." ins " Yo're as slow at yor eatin' as a girl," remarked host, seeing that I was not bolting my food at the speed was. "Don't yo' like it ?" ed " Yes; but I can't get into your ways of eating," "You seem to get through your work as if you it by the piece." „A on "We can't do slow work here. We've got to quick, or be left behind. In England they'd sit an hour - this, they'd relish it so well." "They wouldn't sit long over a slice of melting iue some new potatoes, three on a fork; and a boiling of pion peas about the size of ballets ; and home-brewmake it come-again-able." I had the old man there, found. "I've a good mud to go back with yo'," he exclain!edi throwisg down his spoon as though he meant it for a cpbig lenge. " Yo'n reached a corner o' my stomach that ha' bit shut down mony a year. What is life worth, if we uutiltibat roasted, an' clammed, an' worked to deeath here, while tight little island's brimmin' o'er wi' good things till tlitfei hang off tit' edges? It would be just about wakes time went after th' fourth o' July. That's tit' time for doings !" It is wonderful to me how the Americans can afford as hospitable as they are. It is not because they are earr"ot much just now. Trade is very bad; and the amountt taxes they have to pay would, if transferred to Engiana,.}n. only turn out a Government, but smash the Constitutin No Britisher would stand it in his own country. Nere friend pays as much in various kinds of rates conneetio with two dwelling-houses as his sister in Eagland PaYsses rent for a tolerable good cottage. He growls when °lvo are named; curses the Republic'' and wishes the); „cs under the British Government. The country was ater"t being upset with elections. He would have the Pre' chosen for twelve years instead of four, and behead biOenif lge,. he did not do what was right. He would take awaY salaries of aldermen and councilmen; and make thew for their honour, as they do in England. He would hot then he got into a fury; and I whistled the "St .r-sPunft, Banner," which pumped his patriotic blood hat his and he "Whipped Johnny Bull like an old coon." 101 "There is one thing you ought to be proud of," I rem Ir when my friend's patriotism had cooled a little. "What is that ?" he wished to know. "You have no great national debt to hold you dawn. tho He drew himself to his full height,—the eagle was ou wing. . ride "You are right there, my friend," he said, with sufficient for a battalion. "We pay as we go on, We Won't owe a cent if we can pay it." "The more honourable course," I observed. "No posterity with debts of your contracting. You will leavudy your successors a clean book; so that they can go en or veloping the resources of the country untrammelled thing." 'Here, I say, you git me there. Don't see why we e.ltip fight and pay for a lot of Johnnie s to come over and P1,,,e tter the cake. Wouldn't there be some plundering then? 1,400 have a debt for ballist to keep us steady going, than into another war. lam for posterity paying in advane`ibs am, then they can tight as they darn please. This .15 land of freedom and plenty! I drink to it."

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE PRESERVATION OF EGGS. At various times we have given directions as to the pre- servation of eggs, and recorded several experiments made in this direction. The need for preserving eggs is apparent at once. Eggs are most valuable daring the winter, when few are produced, and whether for domestic or commercial purpose., if they could be kept from the summer season when they are plentiful and consequently cheap to the winter, it would be a very great advantage to the producer. That they can be so kept there is little doubt, but as one of the great requirements of the case is that they shall be kept perfectly fresh, this is not quite so easily attained. To keep them so that they will be fresh enough for cooking purposes is not difficult. But thatis not the same as fresh enough for boiling or poaching. What we could not eat at our breakfast tables would be perfectly good for puddings and sweets. But what is wanted is to preserve eggs so that, after being kept from July to January, they cannot be told from new laid eggs. Whether it is possible to attain this end we are not prepared to say, but efforts are being made in that direction, and, if it is possible, then both producers and consumers will welcome the discovery. Many attempts have been made to solve the problem, and some have had even a ludicrous side to them. Lime water has been spoken of as a good method, but the experience of more than one has been that if just a little too mach lime is put into the water it forms a solid mass, and the eggs have to he broken out with a hatchet. As this is impossi- ble without breaking them, or it is not nice to have a lamp of lime with an egg in it on the breakfast plate, the pre- servation is too complete..

It will be remembered that last December we gave an ac. count of an egg preserving experiment in connection with the Birmingham (Bingley Hall) Show, which was in some respects successful, though the period during which the test took place and its duration were not the best for the pur- pose. We have not heard whether there is to be a farther test this year, but we are happy to announce that one is now being made in connection with the Dairy Show, which takes place early in October. The eggs were sent in on the Bth of July, and will be kept until the Bth of October before being opened—a period of three months. As this will cover the worst months of the year, if any eggs are pre- served satisfactorily, there is little doubt but that they can be kept at any time of the year and for a longer period. Toliere have been, we believe, about thirty lots of eggs sent in for this competition, SO that there will be a sufficient number of systems tried to give it interest. We shall watch the result and record it in due course, so that our readers may be able to learn what is the best method. The systems that won at Birmingham were, first, common salt, and, second, described as follows—Melt one part of white wax to two parts of spermaceti, boil and mix thoroughly; or two parts of clarified suet to one of wax and two of sper- maceti. Take new laid eggs, rub with antiseptic salt or fine rice starch. Wrap each egg in fine tissue paper, putting the broad end downwards; screw the piper at the top, leav- ing an inch to hold it by. Dip each egg rapidly into the fat, heated to 100 deg. Withdraw, and leave to cool. Pack broad end downwards in dry white sand or sawdust.

div.head: TABLE FOWLS.
div.p: TABLE FOWLS.

At both the last Dairy and Birmingham Shows prizes were given for table fowle, which were shown alive first and then killed, so that they could be seen and tested under both conditions. The Birmingham experiment was a very great success. but in both instances there Was not so good a classification as WAS needed. This was et rwn at Birming- ham, where not a singles French fowl was killed, and we then advocated there should be classes for the different varieties, so that they could be compared one with the other in a thorough manner. So long as they are all lumped together the prizes nearly all go to Dorkings, with the result that breeders oi other varieties know that it is useless contending against them, and do not send their birds. We are glad to see that this saggestion has been taken up at both the shows named, and this year there will be classes for both pure and cross bred varieties. At the Dairy Show, we believe, it is intended to have seven classes in all, three for pure breeds, and four for crosses. The pure breeds will be (1) game or Dorkings, (2) French, and (3) any other variety; and the cross breeds (1) Dor- kings with game, (2) Dorkings with Asiatics, (3) any Eng- lish with any French breed, and (4) any other cross. We should have been glad to have seen one or two more classes for the pure breeds, such as the game and Dorking separated, and a class for Asiatics; but this is a very great advance on the past, and we mast be content with it this year. The birds will be shown alive those selected by the judges will be killed and trussed, and then the prizes awarded. The arrangements for the table fowl classes at the Bit- mingham Show are even more complete for pure breeds, but not so good for the crosses. In the former section there will be six classes-0) Dorkings, (2) Brahmas or Cochin,, (3) French, (4) Game, (5) Langsbans or Plymouth Rocks, and (6) any other variety. There will be only two classes for cross breeds, unless these be added to, which we hone the committee will see their way to do. Here the birds will be shows in pairs, consisting of a cockerel and pullet, a better arrangement, we think, than that at the Dilry Show, where, we believe, they are to be shown in couples, con- sisting of two cockerels or two pullets. By the former method a great deal more will be learnt than by The latter, and we wish the Dairy Show had adopted the same plan.

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

Many of the young fowls will now be ready to transfer from the chicken houses to toe used for the larger fowls, and will know for the first tirrte in their life what it is to have a perch to rest upon. A great mistake is often made by having the perches too narrow and too high. The result of the first is crooked breasts, which are so objectionable in a show pen, often throwing out a bird otherwise first rate, and which are equally objectionable upon the table, thus spoiling the appearance of the bird both alive and dead. For a perch, a good fir pole about three inches in diameter is the best, or failing that, a round pole of the same thick- ness, but never less Strips of wood, square or even cor- nered, ought never to be used.
