CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—The military authorities here re- teived a telegram to-day that Lord Wolseley's temporary aPPointment to the command in Egypt is due to declaration of General Stephenson that the present plan of t'anipaign by way of the Nile is impracticable. , Lord Wolseley and Lord Northbrook will travel to Egypt Way of Trieste, where they will embark on board liar 4'iestY's despatch vessel Iris for Alexandria. Major Kitchener telegraphs that a spy from El Hodes reports the arrival of a messenger who states that kteneral Gordon gained a great victory about the 11th inst, la which two of the rebel leaders were killed. No details are given. LORD WOLSELEY TO COMMAND THE FORCES IN EGYPT. General Lord Wolseley, G.C.8., will immediately proceed Egypt to assurne the temporary command of the militarY °tees irs that country. The successful conduct of the Red Itiver expedition by Lord Wolseley has furnished him with ILO experience which is not possessed to the same extent by any other officer, and it has been thought desirable to en- vast to him the supervision on the spot of the measures Which have been to a great extent adopted on his advice. , A. Renter's Cairo telegram states that Lord Wolseley and Ord Northbrook will travel to Egypt by way of Trieste, where they will embark on board her Majesty's d..spatch Vessel Iris for Alexandria.

Lord Wolseley was engaged in London during Wednesday tett, the War Office in concluding the final arrangements for Ins departure for Egypt and in appointing the staff which VII accompany him. Among the latter will be Colonel rove, Deputy Assistant Adjutant-General, whose functions !till be discharged in his absence by Major Stanley Creek. :t Was at first arranged that not more than 5,000 should ne the expedition, but the complexion of affairs has been rtnooterially altered in many respects, and this number is now I_los increased by 2,000 more. Another half regiment has ?cen ordered to prepare to embark for Egypt—the Ist Bat- talion Royal Scots, numbering about 700 men, and now Itallartered in the West Indies, who will leave Btrbadoes in h,e troopship Orontes in time to arrive at tiexandria by October. These, with the two regiments front 'Mire three battalions from Gibraltar, Malta, and Cyprus, and the forces already at Alexandria, and on the Nile, will !cake up a total strength of 14,000 men, from which force 4erd Wolseley will be able to select the expeditionary army " 7,000. Orders are expected for the preparation of trans- torts for the conveyance of 1,000 marines from Suakim to enez, whence, if they should be required, they will proceed .9 rail and road to Asseuan. The flotilla of four hundred ellver boats, for the construction of which contracts had been igned, was found on Tuesday to be numerically insuffi- nlent, and Mr Dann, of the construction department of the kiluiralty, in pursuance of further instructions, accepted Contracts for nearly four hundred more at the stipulated Price of seventy-five pounds from thirteen boat and ship- Sliders at Liverpool, Dundee, Hartlepool, Hull, London, !ad on the Clyde and the Tyne. It is competed that six nsired transports would be sufficient for the conveyance of Ine first 400 boats, the first batch of which will leave Eng- end between September Ist and oth. E ich boat will carry Uvelve to fourteen men. It has not been decided whether tnY extra steamboats shall be sent out to augment the n er of those already hired to tow the boats up the cataracts, as tt is thought a sufficient number can be engaged on the spot. je believed that the expeditionary force will proceed in mats direct to Khartoum, along the Nile, and that no part " the journey will be overland, especially as no very large Purchases of camels have been mode. TIIL REPORTED VICTORY OF GENERAL GORDON. „The Daily News Cairo correspondent says, on the 12th, 'dle enemy endeavoured to capture Khartoum. The attack Was kept up until the 14tb, when they retired, being judi- tously out-flanked at an angle of the earth Works by eneral Gordon. Many of the rebels were shot including tWS chiefs. THE PLAN OF THE CAMPAIGN. ee4 Standard Cairo telegram despatched at midnight on W.ednesday rays :—Lord Wolseley telegraphs that the Sus- 'Z Regiment is to be sent on at once to Dongola, and or- eeers have accordingly been given for a start from Wady ctalfe to-morrow. Lord Wolseley also lays down a plan tit campaign by which he proposes to arrive with the whole expedition at Dongela on the 7th November, one Month after the date fixed ter the arrival of the flotilla Lnf boats at Sarrash. He declares himself confident of 'cling able to accomplish this programme without difficulty. ATTACK ON A DHOW BY OSMAN DIGMA. , Cent.), Tmensnes NIGIIT.—A dhow near Suakim has seen attacked by Osman Digma, who killed several men and took 25 prisoners. BERLIN. THURSDAY NIGHT.—Lord Wolseley's appoint- tnent attracts much attention here. Colonel Swain, military Ittache at the Berlin Embassy, has just received orders to go to Egypt, and leaves shot tly for Brindisi. WAR BETWEEN FRANCE AND CHINA. FOOCHOW BOMBARDED. 'IRE CHINESE FLEET DESTRO ED.—FRENCH SHIP SUNK. ON TUE MIN RIVER,' SATURDAY EVENING.--The bom- ntelirueut was a sickening business. The Chinese fleet, t!tely on the Min has, except two ships, been blotted out. 440 surrender was allowed to the disabled and sinking yes- The guns having been silenced, they were shelled for anurs. Admiral Courbet opened fire at two o'clock, and the vhinese replied almost simulteneously. The dockyard ,eltreenal fired immediately, but with only partial success. he eleven vessels forming the Chinese fleet, mostly light liver and ceast transports, were really toys. The Manch :lad eight heavily-armed ships—the Volta, the Dungnay 4,Fouim, Detaining, Aspic, Vipere, Lynx, and Villars. The 4riomphante ironclad arrived soon after fire had been nePened. Several of the Chinese gunboats maintained "rAvely a desultory fire for about 15 minutes, when the sur- vivors of the crews leapt overboard; but the combat was nraeticelly finished in seve n minutes. The superior artillery nf the French made the contest, after the disabling of the Chinese vessels, no fight. It was a massacre. This was the nninion of every spectator. The 18 ton gunboats fought Well, one sinking near the Champion (English), while the ther above the junks made a good stand. The French Pt up the fire on the arsenal and the neighbouring build- inge, forte, barracks, aed even villages, until five o'clock, although the resistance of the shore lettteries had ceased at about three o'clock, Some of the French and Chinese ships • Were firing close to the Vigilant and Champion. Three .„burning gunboats floated down the stream, one carrying , 'french colours. One pissed close to us, and so also did nurneroue fire-junks. blazing in a dangerous manner; but they were all feuded off. One English barque was saved u 9 the English. Tne French torpedo boats exploded the sterna of the Yangwoo transport and of two sinking gun- The scenes on the river as the dead and wounded %en floated by were terrible. The English saved many of the latter. The forts lower down have not yet been attacked. POoCHOW, MONDAY.—At two this afternoon the French lronclads entered the mouth of the river. The White Fort nPened with Krupp guns at a distance of three miles. They were engaged for a hour, after which the French retired. The Chinese fire was good.—Times. SHANGHAI, Suemay.-Foochow arsenal was destroyed yes- terday, after three hours' bombardment by Admiral Coot- bet's squadron. During the bomberdment seven Chinese Runboats were sunk. Two, however; suceeded in escaping. The European settlement was undisturbed. TIENUSIN, SIINDAY.—The French Charge' d'Affaires and VS Staff have left Tientsin. An Acting-Consul will remain here. It is reported that one French man-of-war was sunk, and that two others sustained damage during the bombard- tnent of Foochow. Chang Peilun is leading the Chineee troops against the French. PARIS, SENDAI/ —A telegram from Shanghai, dated two O'clock this afternoon, states that the French fleet sustained So damage during the bombardment. PARIS, MOEDA:Y.—AII our Chinese news cames &OM Lon- don. In official circles the opinion is freely expressed that the conduct of Admiral Courbet, in refusing quarter to the Chinese sailors after the enemies vessels had atm& their colours, will, unless modified by circumstances not yet cause intense exasperation among the Chinese at the treaty ports. It is feared that the feeling of the natives may COO so high as to get beyond the control of the authorities, and thus render it difficult for the Chinese Government to Rive the Eurooean residents the necessary protection. Appre- hensions are also expressed on behalf of the European pais- eionaries residing in the interior. A considerable business has been done at Lloyd's in war risks, at from 24 01 to 53 per cent above the ordinary pre- mium on vessAs outward bound to Chia se ports. As much 43 10S per cent was paid to-day on zome goods which may be liable to be considered contraband. PARIS, TUESDAY.—The morning papers are unanimous in "complainitig of the partiality of The Vraes, and what they style its odious attack upon Admiral Courbet. Colonel Tsehenkikeng, secretary to the Chinese Embassy, remains Paris. 'Das Republique Francaise expresses admiration of the ability displayed by Admiral Courbet, who only car- ried oat his instructions. The Vo'taire retorts with a refer- ence to the burning of Alexandria. REPORTED FRENCH DEFEAT IN TIIsIQUIN. DESPATCH FROM ADMIRAL COURBET. SHANGHAI, WEDNESDAY, 11-45 A. --TllO French less in the borriblid,nent of Foochow Arsenal was seven killed and fourteen wounded. The Chinese loss is estimated at 1,000 killed and 3,000 wounded. The Chinese war vessel Yang Wu was blown up by a torpedo after she had fired a broad- Side at the French torpedo boat. The boiler of the latter Was exploded by the hand grenades thrown from another Chinese vessel, and that boat was sunk by the Volta in order

to prevent her being captured. The French are expected to occupy the heights commanding the Pagoda anchorage, but 75,000 Chinese troops are reported to be in the vicinity. According to the reports received here from the south a force of 80,000 Chinese has invaded Toiaquin and annihilated the French troops. It is added that several thousands of the Chinese were killed in the engagement. PARIS, WEDNESDAY, 8-25 AM—A despatch from Shan- received here states that there is gill no further offi- cial lhiellfgence rtprElttig the Freildi coritlons. The Chinese loss during the riornoerament of Foochoe is esti- mated at between 2,000 and 3,000. The French lost sue torpedo boat. No particulars have been received regard- ing the engagement with the forts on Monday, and it is considered probable that private telegrams are being delayed by the Chinese. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The Minister of Marine received this morning a telegram from Admiral Courbet, dated Foochow, 24th nest, merning, the text of which is as follows : " A good beginning has been made. We opened Ire on the 23rd inst st two o'clock in the afternoon. At six o'clock nine of the Chinese war vessels and twelve junks bad been sunk. One of our torpedoes sank a large Chinese cruiser. The Krupp battery commending the arsenal was !silenced, Two of the enemy's vessels remaining escaped to the upper part of the river, where none of our gunboats, owing to their large draught ceuld follow them. The vessels of the squad- ron which took part in the action were the Volta, which hoisted my flag, the Duguay-Trouin, the Triomphante, the Villars, the D'Eetaing, and the Aspic, Lynx. and Viare, with the torpedo boats Nos. 45 and 46. We had six killed and 27 wouneed, 14 of whom are only slightly hurt. Our vessels have only sustained damage that can be reptired on the spot with their own re- sources. The torpec:o boat No. 46 had its boiler burst by a cannon ball from the enemy. The Chinese losses were very considerable. During the night from the 23rd to the 24th inst we were constantly beset by burning wreckage carried backwards and forwards by the current running at the rate of four to five knots. We were also harrassed by burning logs launched against us and by tor- pedo cutters. I shall clear away all this to-day and after- wards bombard the arsenal. Da not count upon our leaving the river Min before the 28th or 30-h inst. The officers and men of the squadron are animated by the greatest ar- dour." PARIS, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—Admiral Payron, Minister of Marine. has sent a telegram to Admiral Coacher, expres- ing the entire satisfaction of the French Government at the brilliant beginning of his operations, and wishing him com- plete success. TtiE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR.—FOATS DESTROYED. PARIS, TRIIRSDAY.—A telegram received here from Shan- ghai, of to-day's date, announces that the Mingan Forte were finally silenced on Tuesday evening. Admiral Courbet yesterday attacked the Kintai Forts. Heavy camonading ensued, the result of which, it is added, is not yet known.

The second edition of the Tees contains the following telegram from its Foochow correspondent dated Thursday: "The Kinpsi forts have been destroyed. 1 have just re. turned from Kinpai. All the main defences are gone. The troops bolted. The French fleet can bombard, but an oc- cupation of the mainland is impossible." THE CHOLERA.. . . .

Cholera still rages in France, Cannot be said to be de- creasing its number of victims. From Saturday morning up to five o'clock on Monday there had died from the epi- demic—at Marseilles 29, Toulon 15. and 51 in various southern departments. In Italy the cholera is seriously spreading. An official bulletin issued on Sunday says there were then known 44 cases and 11 deaths. Among patients then under treatment in the province of Cuney 39 persons had succumbed, making a total of 58 from the 21st to the 23rd instant. At Spezia in two days there were 70 cases of cholera, including 48 deaths. It is believed that at that place the spread of the disease was mainly due to the pollu- tion of the water which was used for drinking purposes. In consequence of the cases of cholera that have occurred at Geneva, Dr Costella, the Federal delegate, has recom- mended the sanitary authorities to organise immediately a system of sanitary inspection at La Plaine, the first railway station on the frontier. MARSEILLES, TUESDAY.—Three cholera deaths occurred here last night. TOULON TUESDAY Mommee.—Twe deaths from cholera occurred here last night. GENEVA, TUESDAY.—It is officially announced that no fresh cases of cholera have occurred here. Roma TUESDAY.—The official sanitary bulletin to-day Waters there have been sixdeaths from cholera in the province of Bergammo, twenty in Campobasso, including Busse, three in Massa Carrara, four in Parma, five at Spezia, three in Porto Maurizo, and three in Turin. Tonws, Tuuusnay.—There were two deaths from cholera in Bon Recontre Hospital last night. One instantaneous case occurred at Mourillon, where five serious cases are re- ported owing to a sudden fall in the temperature. THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

MONTREAL, Tatum:ay.—The Sectional Presidents' ad- dresses were all delivered to-day. Papers were read by Sir Thomson Reynolds in section A. by Messrs Gibbs and Har- court in B, by Messrs Gilpin and Eloneyman in C, by Messrs Bates and Carpenter in D, by Mr Lefroy in E, and by Messrs Atkinson: Wegtaarth, and Douglas in E. WRECK OF A FRENCH TRANSPORT. ADEN, SATURDAY.—The French transport Aveyron has been driven and wrecked at Cape Guardafui. Of the offi- cers and crew, 286 have arrived here ; the rest, numbering 300 officers and men, remain on the spot. H.M.S. Briton has been ordered to Cilia Guardafui to assist. The Aveyron left Saigon on July 24th with 345 men, who were returning to France. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Minister of Marine has received a despatch announcing the safe arrival at Aden of all the pas- sengers and crew of the French transport Aveyron. BUGGARIA.—ATROCITIES. . • '

SOPHIA, MONDLY.—According to intelligence received here three Christians have lt,ten flayed alive by Turks in the village of Negilovo, in the district of Kuprulu, Macedonia. In the village of redleo, in the sate district, a Turk named Ahmed Aya is said to have murdered a Christian.

INAHLRECTION IN ARMENIA. BBRLIN, SATORDANZ.—TiIe Tiflis journal Kavkas publishes intelligence from Asia Minor stating that in the large Turk- ish province of Dersirn, Armenia, an insurrection had broken out azainst the Turkish Government which had assumed alarming proportions, and was expected to occasion serious embarrassment to the Porte. Four tribes refused either to pay the taxes or perform military service. The Turkish officials in the valley of Owadshik, the most populous part of the province, have been driven away. The insurgent leaders openly declared to the Governor of the province that they did not acknowledge the Turkish Government, and the Governor was entirely powerless against them. TIIE AFGHAN BOUNDARY COMMISSION.

SATURDAY.—It has been arranged that the Afghan Boundary Commission shall leave Quettah on the let of September. They will travel via alushici, through Northern Beluchistan, and will enter Afghanistan at the Helmand. Thence they will make their way to Herat and Sarrakha. The Ameer Abdur Rahman has expressed himself not very favourably to the passage of the Commission through Afghan territory, but has nevertheless promised every assistance in his power. The Commission and escort will number about 1,000 persons. WRECK OF A BRITISH BARQUE. .
NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY:A despatch from Valparaiso of yesterday's date announces that the British barque Eden has been wrecked. The crew were saved. PERU. _ _

LIMA, TUESDAY.—The troops under General Caceres, who lately proclaimed himself Dictator of Peru, were yesterday repulsed near Lima, as they were advancing on the capital by the forces of General Iglesias, President of the Republic

div.p: DETERMINED ATTEMPTS AT
SUICIDE.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, a respectable-looking young man named Alfred Williamson, a tailor, and a native of Bold, who is living in Edgeworth-street, was charged before Alderman Cnandley and Mr. John Fairclough, with attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a knife the same morn- ing.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that the prisoner was a tailor by trade, working for and living with Mr. John Banner, master tailor, Edgewortb-street. On Tuesday pri• soner had been drinsing, and about mid-night he went up- stairs as if to go to bed. In a few minutes, however, he re- turned and went to a cupboard, thence proceeding towards the door leading out of the house. Mr. Benner followed and noticed him draw something across his throat. Mr. Banner did what he thought was the best method under the circum- stances and knocked the prisoner down, holding him on the ground with the assistance of another man. no two took a large clasp knife from the prisoner and held him in charge until the police arrived. Prisoner was accustomed to drink- ing bouts, and professedly or otherwise, attempted to destroy himself. About four weeks ago he was found suspended by a rope that was fastened round his neck, but was cut down and came round again. Under those circumstances it was thought best to lock him up.—Alderman Chandley : It is a cowardly trick to attempt to rid yourself of life in the way yoa have done, and to be an annoyance to everyone about you. Do not you think that if you were to sign the pledge and be determined to keep it that you could have strength of mind enough to do s.—Prisoner : Yes, sir.—Alderman Chand- ley : Will you promise the Bench that if they will let you go you will sign the pledge, be determined to keep it, and try to earn an honest livlibood.—Mr Hunt: He WAS drink- ing yesterday, and the question is whether all the alcohol is out of him. Three times, lam told, he has done this.—Mr Banner: I would not stand sponkor for him —Mr Hunt : Supposing you were called upon to find a surety of £25 or £5O for your good behaviour, (lo you think you could find such a person 7—Prisoner : Yes.—Mr Banner : As sure as ever he has attempted to do it he will do it again.—Mr Hunt : There has generally been someone there when he has attempted it. Someone not far off 7—Mr Banner : He has no father, and I think he does not know whether his mother is living or not.—lde WAS ordered to be kept in cus- tody for two days to reflect upon his conduct, and then to brought up again to be dealt with.

eeee-e-eeeee-ee-yeeeeee-e-e-e----------- A committee is being formed in Calcutta to promote the candidature of an Indian at the next general election. In an affray between hop pickers at Tonbridge, a man named Bowles has killed his nephew with a blow from his fist. Another death from sunstroke occurred at Canterbury on Saturd a labourer named 4nderson dying efter a Yery painful illness of sOMe days' duration. At Cashel!, on Sunday, a young woman named Crowe was shot dead, her brains being blown out by the discharge of a gun which was being handled by a young brother. DR. CAMERON, M.l'. for Glasgow, has published a premph:. let strongly reflecting on the management of the commis- sariat and transport department during the last Egyptian camp sign. BleurAlaTe IN AN Asyteem.—At Maidstone, on Saturday, James Bun, an attendant at the Kent Lunatic Asylum, Banning, was charged with violently assaulting Frederick Brattle, a patient. While Brettle was sitting astride a stool cleaning old bricks, Hein came in with a rake end struck him on the head, shoulders, and hands with it.—He wee fined .L 4 and 13s costs, or in default a month. He was re- moved be custody, THE Rgaeeeon op a rtASettetE, some ninths ago, annoanced his intention after Christmas of not burying with the rites of the Church any parishioner who was not a communicant. The Bishep of Carlisle having expressed his opinion that the proposed course was unwise in itself and unjustifiable In any officer of the Church, the 1.1 ctor has withdrawn his original announcement, but says he still adheres to the con- viction which prompted it. THE MAAMTRASNA MURDERS.—The Liri-LlSUtenll"3 has forwarded to the Archbishop of Tuam a long letter in which he sets forth his reasons for declining to reopen, by Com- mission or ctherwise, the question of the guilt or innocence of those now in penal servitude for participation in the Maemtrasna tragedy. His Exeellency, consequent upon the recent "confessions" of an approver, has made the strictest inquiry into the affair, and has come to the conclusion that the verdict and sentence were just and right. A PRIEST UNDER POLICE PROTECTION.—A parish priest near Tipperary has had himself paced under special police proteciion in consequence of threatening letters received by him after he had appointed a head schoolmistress from a distant part of the county to the national schools under his patronage, instead of from the immediate locality. This, at least, is stated to have been the cause of the threatening letters, and now he goes to perform his spiritual functions attended-by a police escort, who occupy during the service , the pew immediately in front of the altar, which has hitherto been occupied by his relatives. THE WORTHING SALVATION Rio-vs.—The three men, Reed, Standing, and Eldridge, charged with demolishing the shop and premises of Mr. Head, at Worthing, were brought before the magistrates on Saturday and cemmitted for trial at the assizes, bail being refuted. The prosecutor gave a detailed account of the attack, and said he and his sons first drove the prisoners and others out with shovels, and when they came again he fired a revolver. He stated that Reed tried to set fire to the place, and that Eldridge threw lighted matches amongst his oil measures. He believed the attack was made because he had let the barracks to the Salvation DYEING A Doo.—A gentleman named Oswald Puckridge has been arrested at Sandwich by the Kent county police under peculiar circumstances. At the last general election Mr Puckridge, who occupied a good position in society, took a prominent part In electioneering' matters, and, as an evidence of his enthusiasm, dyed his dog with some yellow dye, with the result that the animal suffered great torture and had to be killed. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals took up the matter, and Mr Puckridge was sentenced to imprisonment for six weeks with hard la- bour, without the option of a fine. He appealed, and was granted bail, and thereupon he escaped to the Continent. On Friday night he was identified at Sandwich Railway Station, having paid a surreptitous visit to some of his friends. He was arrested and removed to prieon to undergo ' his sentence. THE FUNERAL OF A "MIDGET."—An extraordinary scene took place at Birmingham, on Sunday, in connection with the funeral of the midget. In consequence of the mother being anxious to dispose of the body to a showman, the deputy-coroner ordered the corpse to be under police sur- veillance until after the burial. The coffin of the mite was 13i inches long, six inches wide, and four and a half inches. deep. Crowds of persons had beseiged the house since the inquest. Early in the afternoon a mourning coach drove up to the house to convey the remains to the Birmingham Cemetery, a distance of two miles. For nearly half an hour the funeral could not be got away, owing to the pressure of the enormous crowd which filled the street and the adjoin- ing thoroughfares. The mother, who was censured by the deputy.coroner for "performing to death" her child, was hissed and yelled at, and would probably have been lynched but for the police. Ex eRAORDINARV EXPLOSION AND FIRE IN MANCHESTER. —A tare, originating under peculiar circumstances, was re- ported to the Manchester Fire Brigade on Saturday. In- formation was received that tne cottage occupied by Thomas M•Tighe, at 73, Collyhurst-street. was on the. Assistant- Superintendent Savage and the brigade found the lower part of the house considerably damaged by an explosion of ben- fal'Tighe was in the act of cleaning a men's vest on a table with benzoline. He had saturated the garment, and a bottle containing more was standing near. Unaware that a lucifer m etch had been left in one of the packets M' fighe commenced rubbing the vest, and the match ignited. There was a loud explosion, and M`Tighe was severely burnt about the arms and face. When the brigade arrived they found that considerable damage had been done in the house, and the beck window had been blown out. Mcrighe was taken to the Infirmary, where his injuries Were attended to. STRANGE QUARREL OVER e DEATHBED —A summons has been issued against a !latish prieet of Cloone in Con- naught, for an assault on the wife of the Rev J Tresham Cooke, who was attending the deathbed of a Protestant widow, whose husband was a Catholic, her sons being of the same religion. The woman, named O'Connor, when dying, last week signed a will expressing her desire to die as she had lived a Protestant, and asking Mr Cooke, the rector, to direct the funeral arrangements accordingly. The two sons of Mrs O'Connor were opposed to this, and while the rector with his wife and the dying woman's two daughters were standing round the bed the Roman Catholic priest and a large number of his followers forced open the door and took possession of the house. A disgraceful scene was then enacted round the deathbed, and finally, after a stubborn resistance and amid the yells of the crowd, the rector was literally thrown out of the house. The rector retarned in the evening with several constables, read the will to the crowd, and declared his determination to carry out the wiehes of the deceased. ELOPEMENT OF A LANDLADY WITH HER BRF.WER'S DRAYMAN —At Derby Police Court, on Friday, T Yates, brewers' drayman, was charged with stealing £8 103 in money, and a quantity of wearing apparel, the property of S Mitchell, landlord of the Welcome Stranger Inn, near Bury. Prisoner had been for 19 years in the employ of the Crown Brewery Company, Bury, and had been in the habit of delivering ale at Mitchell's Latterly, although he has a wife and eight children of his own, he struck up an ac- quaintance with Mrs Mitchell, who has two children, and on Tuesday last the two eloped together, taking with them the property enumerated. The pair were traced to Derby, where on Friday the man was apprehended. He denied having taken any of Mitchell's property, but as he was leaving the house he was noticed to throw into his para- mour's lap a parse, which on being secured by the police was found to contain the missing money and 4s in addition. Yates, who looked very crestfallen, was ordered to be de- tained until the arrival of the Lancashire police.—On Mon- day Yates and Mrs Mitchell were both sent for trial.

DESPERATE AFFRAY WITH POACHERS.—About one o'clock on Friday morning a desperate struggle between four poachers and four gamekeepers took place at Tandle Hills , Wood, near Oldham. The keepers surprised the poachers, , wno were in possession of nets and three rabbits. A scuffle , ensued, stones and sticks being freely used ; and both ; poachers and keepera were severely injured. The keepers , secured one of the poachers and gave him into custody, but the other three escaped. The preserve belongs to the Roch- dale Hunt. In the afternoon, at Rochdale, Peter Johnson, alias John Jones, the man arrested, was charged with poaching. It was proved that the prisoner and three other men set 160 yards of netting, and that there was a desperate fight. When Andrew Stott and three other keepers endea- voured to take them into custody they were belaboured with sticks and were much disfigured. The prisoner was at ' last captured, but the other three poachers escaped. The magistrates sent Jones to prison for four months, and ordered him to be bound in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each, to be responsible for his good behaviour for two years, or a further imprisonment for two months. INSURANCE SOCIETIES AND THEIR AGENTS the Lord Mayor's Court on Saturday, before Mr Woodthorpe Brae- don (assistant judge) and a common jury, an action was brought by Mr John Napier, of Lewisham, to recover £5O 4a, the balance of salary due to him from the defendants, the Provident Industrial Society, Limited. The action was was brought for 13 week's salary at £5 per week, from De- cember 23rd to March 23rd. Various sums had been paid on account, which left a balance of the amount of the claim. The plaintiff was engaged under an agreement which was very singular. The fourth clause said the plaintiff was to have £220 per annum' and the sixth clause said he was to have £2 per week, but that the rest of the £5 was to ba paid at the discretion of the directors. Further, that the plaintiff was to be paid before the directors received their fees. In the last report issued by the society, however' they had taken £5O. The plaintiff was called and said that he wag engaged by the di- rectors of the society, as manager, and occupied that posi- tion until March last. The agreement under which he was engaged was drawn by the defendant's solicitor. Mr Ayres, one of the directors' after having held tha office for 13 weeks only, moved that £lOO be paid to the directors which was carried by two voting for it and one against. (Laugh- ter.) For the defence it wig urged that the plaintiff was to have .12 per week, and that when the funds. would permit he was to have CI It was contended that the financial position of the society would not allow of the payment. The accountant to the society was called, and showed that the society had been in a position to pay the plaintiff his money. The secretary of the society was called to show that the receipts and expenditure of the society now show a loss of £soo.—The jury found for the amount claimed.— His Lordship certified for costs. Now, during the whole of that period the pub- lic accounts were published with punctuality, and there never was the slightest ground of suspicion as to their truthfulness and accuracy. However, owing to the compli- cated nature of the borough accounts, it was necessary, and he believed legally necessary, that a borough treasurer should be appointed, but the result, so far as that borough was concerned, had been extremely unfortunate. Notwith- standing all the safeguards which the Council devised to prevent errors and frauds, great mistakes had been dis- covered, and embezzlements of serious sums of the rate payers' money had been brought to light. It was now the duty of the Council to devise some other regulations which would prevent the recurrence of offences of that nature. lie did not wish to trench on the Finance Committee, but he was sure they would pardon him if he submitted to the Council for the consideration of the committee a few sugges- tions, which, if worked out and adopted, would, he thought, end in the saving of the money of the ratepayers.—The sug- gestions, which deal with the receiving of loans, the keep- ing of the accounts, the issuing of the annual statements, the auditing of the books, and periodiCal inspection of cash balances, were recommended to the Finance Committee for consideration.

WATEEFOOT-IN-ROSSENDALE.—A meeting was held on a piece of vacant land at Watertoot, on Saturday, in sapport of the Government and the Franchise Bill, and to protest against the power of veto possessed by the House of Lords. Mr Edward Ashworth, of Staghills, presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs H Abraham, W R Shanks, and R Heyworth, Dr Watson, Messrs Win. Loncl, Thomas Pilling. Edward Nuttall, John Mills, and others. The proceedings commenced with the singing of the" Non- Electors' Hymn" to the accompaniment of a brass band.— The Rev R HEYWORTII moved a resolution condemning the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill, and expressing its entire approval of the decision of the Government to hold an autumn session to secure the passing of the bill in its present form ; and moreover assur- ing the Government of its hearty support in such measures as they may think it advisable to adopt to put an end te the power of the House of Lords to resist the will of the people.—The Rev W R SHANHS seconded the resolution.— rite resolution was carried unanimously.—The Cumnarars , afterwards asked those in the audience who passed a vote to raise one hand, and not more than thirty hands were raised. lie then asked those who had not the vote to raise one hand, Ind a perfect forest of hands were then held aloft. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT But:lr.—Bury was on Sat- urday the scene of an enthusiastic Liberal demonstration, the gathering being chiefly composed of persons living in

the district or adjacent towns, and not imported from a long distance by very cheap excursion trains in order to enjoy themselves in lovely grounds The Bury meeting assembled for business and not for the sake of pleasure. The demon- stration was of a twofold character—it consisted of a series or i,;;.octssions awl e !none!? nublm Irom, Prest- vilco, White&ld, 11.1dclide, fottinetall, Eamsbotiom, Eden. field, Shuttleworth, and other localities in the neighbour- hood large contingents of Liberals came—on foot from the nearer and by train from the more distant places—to swell the processions; and for several hours the streets of the town were enlivened by the passing of long lines of men, carrying banners and marching to the s'rains of brass bands. All the forces were joined in one grand array on the fair ground near the public market, whence they marched to the place appointed for the meeting, Unian•square. This is a large open space in the centre of the town, and as it was the site of the old hustings, it has been the scene of many stirrring locel political events. It is capable of holding from 16,000 to 20,000 people, and probably it was never bet- ter filled than it was on Saturday, and certainly it can on no previous occasion have presented a more animated appear- ance. Not only was the squire fully occupied, but every window overlooking it was crowded with spectators. There were two platform., the first being presided over by Mr R N Phillips, M P, and the other by Mr W Hoyle, and among the speakers were Mr W C Borlase, MP, Mr R Leake, MP, and Mr W Agnew, MP. Several letters of apology for non-attendance were read, among them one from Sir Henry James, the Liberal candidate for the borough, and another from Mr Trevelyan, M P. Mr Phillips described the action of Lord Salisbury and his followers as an attempt to snub the people and the House of Commons, and de- clared that the object the Tories had in view was to displace the Liberals and govern the nation themselves. The Lords, he urged, had no right to dictate when an appeal to the country should be made' and he was convinced that some change was needed in the constitution of the House of Peers. A resolution expressing confluence in the Government, and approving of the Franchise Bill, was carried with acclama- tion. A second resolution, protesting against the insulting action of the House of Lords, and expressing the opinion that the best interests of the nation demand that the power of vetoing just meatnres ought to be controlled, was submit- ted, but was negatived by an amendment calling for the ' abolition of the House of Lords.

LIBERAL MEETING AT BLACEBURN.—On Tuesday even- ing a demonstration was held in the Exchange Hall, Black- burn, for the purpose of expressing approval of the policy of the Government and condemning the action of the House of Lords on the Franchise Bill. The principal speakers were Mr Briggs, M.P. for Blackburn, and Mr P Rylands, M.P. for Burnley. The following resolutions were sub- mitted to the meeting and carried with enthusiasm : "That this meeting condemns the action of the House of Lords in refusing to pass the just and moderate measure of enfranchisement introduced by the Government and passed by enormous majorities of the House of Commons, and also expressed its emphatic approval of the decision of the Go- vernment to hold an autumn session in order to secure the passing of the Franchise Bill during the present Parlia- ment, and assures the Government of its hearty support in whatever measures it may adopt for the accomplishment of that purpose." " That the frequent disregard of the national will manifested by the House of Lords in delaying, mutilating, and rejecting bills passed by the House of Com- mons is an intolerable anomaly, and renders needful such reforms as shall limit or abolish its power."

INTERESTING COMPARISONS.—Tbe Pall Mall Gazette publishes a list of the meetings held since July 2nd "for and against the House of Lords," and says:--" From this list it will be seen that 78 meetings and picnics were held in support of the action of the House of Lords, as against 239 meetings in condemnation of the House of Lords and in support of the Government. The meetings held under Con- servative auspices generally called for an appeal to the country, as well as fr a measure of Redistribu- tion as a companion measure to the Franchise Bill. The meetings which met for the expression of their condemna- tion of the conduct of the Upper House rarely stopped with the declaration of their desire that the Government will per- sistently return the Franchise Bill to their Lordships' House until it is passed ; as a rule, they indignantly demanded either the reform or the abolition of the House of Lords, its hereditary and irresponsible character being chiefly em- phasised." Only three of the Tory meetings have been large. At Newport, in South Wales, they mustered about 25,000, at Pomona Gardens about 20,000, and at Nostell Priory, out of the 80,000 or 90,000 who, it is said, entered the park, about 25,000 attended the Con- servative meeting. During the same period 239 meetings have condemned the Lords, amongst these being Durham miners 60,000, Edinburgh 60,000. Bristol 20,000, Clerkenwell 20,000, Moseley 25,000, Leicester 30,000, Man chester 25.000, Bolton 20,000, Wakefield 30,000, Dunferm- line 30,003, and Crewe 20.000, besides a large number of meetings at which from 10,000 to 20,000 persons were pre: sent. Whether as to the number of meetings or the attend- ance, the Tories are thus in a miserable minority, without taking into account the unparalelled demonstration in Hyde Park.—The Leeds Mercury says: We ourselves formed the most liberal estimate possible of the numbers when we gave the attendance at Nostell Priory at 50,000. The data since collected seem to show that this calculation was over the mark; and some correspondents insist that not more than 30,000 persons at the outside were present in the perk, of whom not more than one half took part in the meeting. It is really a matter of small amount whether the number was 30,000 or 50,000. In either case the demonstration, in pro- moting which so many efforts had been put forth, was not of such a character as to startle the public of Yorkshire, or to give politicians reason to believe that there had been any change in the prevailing opinion of the people. Although no great effort has yet been put forth by the Liberals of Yorkshire, the balance of public demonstrations in the county is enormously in their favour. OTHER LIBERAL DEMONSTRATIONS in favour Of the Reform Bill and to protest against the action of the House of Lords were held on Saturday. At Bromley, Kent, many contin- gente, with their bands and banners, from Bromley, Becken- ham, Farnborough, St. Mary's Cray, Chislehurst, Footscray, Sevenoaks, Lewisham and Lee, Orpington, Otford, and other places, met shortly after 4.30 at the London, Chat- ham, and Dover Railway Station, and from thence marched through the town to College Field, where some excellent speeches were delivered. There were about 4,000 persons present. At Crewe the streets were filled with processions, and a large open-air meeting was held subsequently in the Alexandra Cricket Ground, under the preeidency of the 'Rev W Mellor. There were about 13,000 persons present. A magnificent demonstration took place of the artisans and railway employee of Stratford and the surrounding district in support of the Government policy on the franchise ques- tion, and in opposition to that of the House of Lords.—A demonstration of Liberals was held at Crosshills, Yolleshire, to protest against the action of the House of Lords.—A de- monstration in support of the Franchise Bill was held at Dunfermline, at which about 33,000 persons were estimated to It present. A largely attended reform demonetration took place at Great Wigston, near Leicester. Under the auspices of the Ilkley Liberal Club, a public meeting of electors and non- electors was held, at the Assembly Rooms, Weston-road, on Saturday evening, when there was a very enthusiastic gathering.—A demonstration of the unenfranchised in the Audenshaw polling district was held on Monday evening at Hooley Hill, near Guide Bridge. The Premier, in a letter acknowledging an address from the Reformers of 1832 who took part in the recent Franchise demonstration at Aberdeen. observes "It must appear strange and sad to them that a renewal conflict on this question seems to be imminent after the lapse of over half a century, and that now, as on the foemer occasion, it is the House of Peers and the Tory party who bar the progress of Reform, notwithstanding the lesson which the previous struggle ought to have conveyed." A meeting in support of the Franchise Bill was held on a I plot of land adjoining Manchester-road on Saturday, and I was moderately well attended. The chair was occupied by Mr J G Dean, who was supported on the platform by the Revs C Williams and M C Crofton (curate at St Peter's Church, Accrington), G T Bailey, J T Moore, Messrs J Hoyle, J Holt, J Schofield, D Chew, J Barlow, J Frank- lin, Hindle, E Cowpe, J Ii Chew, Sze. A very large meeting in support of the Franchise Bill was held at Zion Chanel, Llanelly, on Tuesday night. Resolu- tions calling for the extension of tha franchise and reform of the House of Lords were proposed and spoken to by Sir J. Jones Jenkins, M.P. Mr. O'Connor Power, M.P., iu sup- porting the resolution and referring to the proposal of creat- ing more peers to bear down the Conservative majority, said he was one of those who believed there were already too many peers. (Cheers.)—The resolutions were carried unani- mously and enthusiastically. In an address issued by the People's League for the Aboli- ition of the Hereditary Legislative Chamber on Tuesday night, the committee state that the reasons for their actiont need no enumeration; they are obvious to every reflecting mind. Oftener than once has obstruction by privilege brough the country to the brink of a bloody revolution, Mr. Chamberlain, who is at present on the Continent, will shortly after his return address a great meeting, to be held in the Potteries, on the question of the Franchise Bill and the House of Lords. The meeting will be held at Hanley on the 7th of October.

The Princess of Wales on Thursday presented new colours to the Gordon Highlanders, stationed at Aberdeen. The Heir Apparent, with the Royal Princes and Princesses were also present. BRITISH AssocuTrox.—The opening meeting of the British Association was held in Montreal on Wednesday night, when Lord Rayleigh delivered the presidential ad- dress, in which he dealt with the progress of physical science. He remarked, in opening, that whatever objections might at first have been felt to their holding the annual meeting in Canada were outweighed by the consideration of the magnificent opportunities which the hospitality of the people of the Dominion afforded of extending the sphere of the influence of the association, and of enabling the main- hers to become acquainted with a part of the Queen's dominions which was advancing daily by leaps and bounds to a position of importance such as not long ago was scarcely dreamed of. Having spoken of the death of §ir W, Siemens, Lord Rayleigh reviewed at great lengtte the'recent,progress of physics, and said that the present position and Prospects of experimental science gave them good ground for en- couragement. From the general spread of a more scientific education they were warranted in expecting impor:ant results, and great as were the triumphs of the 'resent cen- tury, they might well believe they were but a foretaste of what discovery and invention had yet in store for mankind. He should be happy if through that visit of the association a larger measure of the youthful activity of the West could be enlisted in the work.

--- 1 ANNIVERSARY SERMONS. The anniversary sermons in connection with the Lowton-rd. Primitive Methodist Chapel were preached on Sunday by the Itiv T Vaughan. Collec- tions were made on behalf of the chapel trust. SigatrUn ACCIDENT.—During the Process of charging a " Fire Extincteur " at Messrs. Brewis's New Mill, on Wed- nesday afternoon, a youth named Edward Kavannah WAS badly burnt about the legs and body owing to a bottle of sulphuric acid breaking, and the contents falling upon him. Mr. J. W. Kidd and Dr. Worsley were called in, and tempo- rarily dressed the wounds. BOWLER'S DINNER —The return match, Golborne a- EIS Helens, played at Golborne last Saturday, resulted in a nett gain for Golborne by 86 points. At the conclusion 0 the game the players and friends to the number of 40 sat down to an excellent dinner at the Legh Arms Hotel. Mr W Mitchell, the Golborne captain, presided, the vice-chair be- ing occupied by the St Helens captain. After the nsr..al loyal toasts, a selection of songs was given by Dr Mane'', J Addsbead, and the brothers Jackson. SAD ACCIDENT.—On Saturday, about noon, a sad accident befell William Layboume, aged 22, residing in Heath-street, Golborne, and employed at Messrs It Evans's Edge Greora Colliery. It appears he went to the reservoirs for a tank of water to send down the pit. When returning he rode on one of the boxes. As they proceeded some slack rope got under the line, with the result that the rails sprung at one end, , and before the engine could be stopped one rail jammed his foot so tightly that several toes were entirely crushed off, 1 He was conveyed horns on the ambulance stretcher, and at- tended to by Dr H Latham. During the afternoon he was removed to the Wigan Infirmary, when it was found neces- fiary to amputate the front part of the foot, including the remaining toes. He is now progressing as favourably as cam be expected. LEcrunE "ON BALLADS."—On Monday evening last a lecture "On Ballads" was given by the Rev. Father Byrne, in the Catholic School, Golborne, in aid of the Catholic Young Men's Society. There was a large atten- dance. The meeting was opened by the rendering on the pianoforte of a selection of Irish ballad airs by Mrs. Mapie. The Rev. Father Byrne, in the course of an eloquent and interesting lecture, said a ballad was distinguished from a song by being a short lyrical narrative. It was a narrative now of a deed of derring-do by some great man of prowess, now of some deed of wild adventure, and now et some love affair Ballads antedated history by thousands and thousands of years, and were in existenca long before Herodotus wrote his wrrk, and he was considered to be the father of history. If they looked at the different species of ballads they would find some of them regular, same of them sublime, some rippling like a little trout stream in the bright sun; some they would find to be majestic and slow, and others again reminded them of the rushing of the mighty tarrent. They might guage a nation by its ballads, for in them they saw its inner life. And if they wanted to know the true history of a nation, if they wanted to know a nation as it was, he maintained that the beet way was not to go into that aggregate of facts which was called ita his- tory, but rather to trace it to its fountainhead in the ballads, for in them they would find the true interpretation of the nation whose history they wished to study. The lecturer then pointed out in brief and vivid language the peculiari- ties of the ballads of various countries—of Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Ireland, and other countries. He also alluded to the influence which the bards possessed amongst the ancient Greeks, the Roman, the Norsemen, and other peoples in ancient times. Referring to the hardly-fought contro• verse' as to whether Homer was really a living person at all, or whether the Iliad and Odyssey were not merely names given to a collection of bardic songs, he said it might new be proved to demonstration that Homer's works were a co:- lection of ancient ballads brought together by a master mind. In the course of the lecture Father Byrne recited in an exceedingly effective manner several ballads, including the'• Battle of Fontenoy," and "The Fairies Passage." These etlarts evoked loud applauses from the audience, who seemed throughout to be deeply interested by the lecture.— The proceedings concluded with a hearty vote of thanks to Father Byrne.

T!,e annual brewster sessions for the Prescot constabuLry division was held in the Court-house, Prescot, on Thursday week, when the magistrates on the Bench were F W Earle, W L Evans, and A R Gladstone, Eqls. SUPERINTENDENT'S ANNUAL REPORT.—Superintendent Barker submitted his annual report as follows:—" County Police Offices, Prescot, 21st August, 18S4.—To the magis- trates in Brewster Sessions assembled.—Gentlemen,-1 have, tbe honour to lay before you returns of the licensed persona in the Prescot Petty Sessional division. At present there are doing business, licensed victuallers 118, beer sellers ter cot - gumption on the premises 63, do, (off) 14, other licenses 9, total 207, being a decrease of three beer sellers for consump- tion off tbe premises, the holders having ceased business. Population 44,321, being one licensed house to about every 214 persons. During the year three licensed victuallers, have been proceeded against, two convicted, and one die. missed. Beer sellers, five proceeded against, four convicted, one license endorsed, and one paid costs. The licensed per- sons have on the whole conducted their houses fairly well. Prosecutions for drunkenness have greatly increased during three years ended 31st July, the numbers being as follows —1881,546; 1882, 880, increase 334; 1883, 1,247, increase 367; 1884. 1,425, increase 178. With respect to this in- crease, I can only repeat what I stated in my report for last year, that in my opinion it is caused to a considerable ex- tent by people of the very lowest class, bofh male and female, drinking to all appearances the greatest part of any money they can get hold of, Number of apprehensions anti summonses for all offences for the p teL four years ended l")..t<: July are as follows:

div.p: Superintendent Barker stated that he had no objection to the renewal of the old licenses with the exception of those held by William Lewis, Bridge Hotel, Widnes •, Mark Wright, Commercial Inn, Widnes; Joseph Bell, Ship Inn, Widnes; John Gill, Manchester House, Widnes; Thomas Bradshaw, Church View, Widnes; and William Ince, Stonemasons' Arms, Widnes. He obj:cted to the renewal of these licenses on the ground that the holders had been con- victed during the past year.—The Bench decided to renew the whole of the licenses with the exception of those named; which they would consider at an adjourned licensing session to be held on the 25th September. "A TRAVELLING l'imtc-notsl."—The only new appli- cation (as stated in Superintendent Barker's report) was one by Thomas Edwardson, of Simms Cross, Widnes, who ap- plied for a retail license to sell beer off the premises. it seemed that the applicant already held a wholesale license, and intended to take round beer, Sze., in his mineral water cart.—The Magistrates' Clerk: And thus become a kind of moving public-house? (A laugh.)—Applicant: Well, yes sir.—The Magistrates' Clerk: You ought to have some proof here that you have a strong beer license already. What evidencd have you to show that you are one 2—The applicant said he bad a license, but had rot brought it with him.—Superintendent Barker : I object to this license being granted. This man would be simply a moving public-house, and going about the country he would require more watch- ing than any other man in the district —The Chairman We are unanimous in declining the application. This was all the public business, and the persons whose licenses had been renewed then came forward and received them. ,

DESTRUCTIVE AIWA, CHORLEY.—EarIy on Thursday morning the dye works belonging to Councillor Forreeter were discovered by Constable Rielly to be on fire. An Marra was raised, and the borough steam fire engine was soon paying on the flames, which caught the house and threat- ened the whole buildings with destruction. The fire Was subdued in about an hour. The principal part of the works is completely gutted, and the damage is large, but the estah- blishment was insured. RAILWAY FATALITY AT OLDHAM —On Thursday fore' noon a shocking railway accident occurred on the railway between the Mumps and the Central Stations, Oldham. A forem in navvy, named Jonathan Whitehead, went an errand to the former station and was coming down in the six foot-. way when he was knocked down by a Liverpool train, his bead coming in contact with the metals. His skull was smashed in. He was conveyed to the Infirmary,where he died, The deceased belonged to Middleton. FIRE AT HUYTON.—On Wednesday morning, about half-past four, a fire broke out on the premises of Thomas Birchen, builder, situated in Derby-road. An alarm was given and the Weet Derby Volunteer Fire Brigade was corn. municated with through the Salvage Office, Liverpool, anti the steam fire-engine, S. B. Grave, under Mr. Foreman Bat. ker, arrived on the scene of the fire at half-past six. Tbs fire had completely gutted the outbuildings, consisting et joiners' workshops, engine house, and stables, and also the- timber and stock in the yard. There was a plentiful supply of water, and the firemen,s efforts were directed to savlnc the dwelling-house and a newly erected house and shop aa.. jnining. The fire was got under about seven o'clock, brit not before damage to the extent of between £3OO and £4OO was done. The property destroyed was uninenred. The origin of the fire is unknown.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 30, 1884.

SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, the leader in the House of Commons of the Conservative party, has been delivering himself at a poli- tical demonstration at Nostell Priory, near Wakefield. It is the first speech of moment he has made during the present crisis, and it is natural, therefore, that what he has to say should be listened to with interest. But the deliverance is a disappointing one; the right honourable baronet does not seem to have his heart in his work, and he has a re- putation at stake which will not permit him to play fast and loose with facts, in order, like Lord SALISBURY to point a gibe, or, like Lord R. CHURCHILL, to polish an epigram. This much is to be gathered from his speech— that the Lords do not intend to give way on the Franchise Bill; and that, to quote his own words, the Conservative party are "prepared to stand together and fight this battle." Lord CARNARVON went still further in the way of pledging the patty; he said it de- pended upon them (the Lords) to "stand firm," and they had "no intention of run- ning away from their guns." It is to be hoped they will keep in this frame of mind, for then the Liberals throughout the country will be assured of a victory "all along the line." It is a matter of course that there will be an ex- tension of the franchise this year or next ; but if the Peers turn "tail in the autumn, and leave Lord SALISBURY to get out of the Slough of Despond as best he can, it is with- in the bounds of possibility that the present agitation for the reform of the House of Lords will be for a time abortive. English- men are just a little too forbearing in matters of this kind. There is a disposition to be easy with the bishops, because, contrary to their tra- ditions, the majority of them recently voted for the Franchise Bill. This one swallow, ,

following on a long "winter of discontent'''. has made quite a summer for them. But the order of the day with the Tory party generally is to fight the enemy, and there is therefore hope for one side or the other gaining "a glori- ous victory." Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE IS • almost eloquent about defending .‘ the great cause," though his observations lose force when it is found to be impossible to make out what is meant by " the great cause." It cannot, as of old, be opposition to Reform, for the cry is that the Government have not given them reform enough; and it cannot be that they are anxious alike. for an extension of the Franchise and a redistribution of seats, for, if they were, they would pass the one as a means to the other. It is not long since Sir STAFFORD spoke of " letting two millions of people loose upon the electorate." lie might, to judge from his phrase, regard them as so many beasts of prey; but now he has ad- vanced so far as to think "the time has come when one might largely extend the area of our electoral system and introduce large num- bers of capable citizens." Indeed, he grows so solicitous in "the cause of civilisation, of freedom, and of humanity," as to tell us that in the accomplishment, in the past, of these great things "the people were moved to an extent almost incredible and centainly un.. ' paralleled." Sir STAFFORD has only to open , his eyes a little wider to see that the same • thing is taking place to-day; but he will not discern it at picnics in Parks and Priories, where the chief inducements are "cheap trips" and " ample refreshments." Not to go away from home, he must see such gather- ings as we have had at Warrington, Runcorn, Widnes, St. Helens, and Earles- town, which, let the Tories sneer at them- as they will ,are utterly beyond their reach,- ' and ha because they have not the people ti with them. The Tories of St. Helens by Way, we suppose, of a ccitmtudf:monstration, met in their club roolli On Monday n!lt arl.c; expressed their cordial aolecment with tne House of Lords. What a contras; to the gathering, on Newton Common, of i 0,000 working-men, earnest, resolute, and self- sacrificing in their demand for the Reform Bill and the Reform of the House of Lords I Mr. GLADSToNE well said at Warrington raii- way station, on Wednesday, that " this is an affair which lies in the hands of the country." The country is fully realising this, and is not to be thwarted in its demand for a complete Reform Bill by those who, while they have the 111.11ra$9 em on their lip, haw; shown that ' , ' they hate it in their hearts. The opposition of. 1 the Tory party to the enfranchisement a ; working-men living outside Parliamentary boroughs is notoriously based on no better foundation than the assumption that the Go- ' vernment do not intend to follow on with a , just measure of redistribution—an assainptioa . coined in an evil imagination, and belied by . the most solemn engagements it is possible to give. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCoTE quotes . figures to expose the anomaly of the present , . distribution of votes, as between comty and.. : borough, and yet he would "appeal to the people" on a regi3ter admittedly bad—one, too, which excludes two millions of the., people from the exercise of the franchise. Mr. • GLADsToNE, on the other hand, would pass the- , , Franchise Bi;1 this year, and a Redistribution, Bill next year, in order that anomalies of re- presentation of every class may be grappled' with and.removed ; that the pledges given to• the nation may be honestly redeemed ; and: that a new Parliament may be elected, in the widest sense of the laureate's words_ Broad.based upcn the peolle'd will.

IMagistrates sitting in Brewster SessionS I have for many year:: had a somewhat try- ing time of it. The pressure of public opinion has undoubtedly gone in the di- rection of restricting the number of places licensed for the sale of intoxicatintr liquors, and the result is that, if there have not been many licenses withheld, there have been few new ones granted. At Runcorn. on Monday, the magistrates had before them, for the sixth time, an application for an extension of beer license to a full wine and spirit license. It may seem some- what hard on an applicant to refuse him when there does not appear to be any question as to the suitability of the house —when, in fact, the premises are unques- tionably superior to many other full-licen- sed houses? But what the Bench have to keep in, mind is that, as things go, it is much easier to grant a license than to get rid of one, and that the tendency of the times is to lessen rather than to in- crease the number. The Superinten- -1 dent's report shows that in the Run- Horn division there is a licensed house to every 184 of the population—including !women and children alto,,,Tether too many. we cannot but think, for the requirements of the inhabitants. In some towns during the past two years there has been a considerable reduction in the number of licenses, through the magistrates exercising their new powers as to dealing with off-licenses. The first move was made in Darwen, when about one- half of what are known as grocers' licenses were swept off at one sittin,-. There was an appeal to Quarter Sessions, and ultimately the case was carried to the Queen's Bench, with the result that in both instances the de- cision of the licensing justices was upheld. Last year the Blackburn magistrates, aft,-er a careful inquiry, withheld no less than 61 off- licenses, and other licensing justices have I moved in a similar direction. ' There is no question now as to jurisdiction, and it seems to us that there need be no hesitation in pro- ' ceeding along a line which has been found " to be safe and satisfactory. The Warrington Brewster Sessions are about to be held, and we observe that notice has been given of the presentation of memorials from various sec- tions of the temperance party in the borough. It is to be hoped that the suggestions of the memoralists in so far as they are reasonable, will be duly consideied, and that the magis- trates will do all they can in the exercise of their discretion to lessen the means of drunk- enness in the borough. They need not fear to act; vested inte:ests are strong but they will find in the end that public opinion is stronger.

France and China are fighting, although, in the language of diplomacy, they are not at war because there has been no declara- tion of war. The French say what they are doing is in the way of reprisal, and a terrible rep-!sal it is which involves such a massacre as ensued, last Saturday, in the destruction of the Chinese fleet. The Chinese have a way of speaking of the people of the outer world as " barbarians," and it would seem that the French are disposed to justify the title, if they cannot justify their conduct in this affair. We have, it must be admitted, heard part only of the story of the bombardment of Foochow, and trust that when the tale is Complete it will be less terrible to the ear. The French are undoubtedly in desperate

straits in their relations with China; they have gone so far that they must go further. We may well believe that, in the light of pre- sent experience, if the Tonquin expedition as to be begun now they would set about it in a somewhat Aifferent spirit. The game so far has not been found ' to be worth .the candle, and if ,the acquitition of Tonquin, is to be obtained at the price of war with China it cannot be other than a bad bar- gain. Indeed, Tonquin itself may have to • be re-conquered, for it is not unlikely that the Chinese, instead of attacking the French Openly will stir up revolt amongst the dis- affected people of Annam, and incite the Black Flags to further resistance. The French with the powerful fleet which they Command in Chinese waters are certainly Capable of doing a great deal of mischief; it will bean easy, if a cruel thing to go on destroy- ing defenceless towns and villages. They will not be likely to attack the Treaty Ports, knowing that that course would bring them into trouble with European Powers at a tune when they have quite enough on their hands. Looked at on any side, the, pros - Peet is a bad one both for France and China. The situation is another illustra- tion of the little wisdom with which. the world is governed.

WE are glad to find that Mr. Whitham's letter and our comments on the inadequate supply of drinking water to certain work- shops in Warrington have caused the Water works Company to put themselves in com- munication with Messrs RYLANDS BROTHERS With a view to coming to terms with them. It will be seen from the letter of Mr Ross that Messrs. RYLANDS have not acceded to the offer-made them—probably because they are asked to pay £5 for water for water closets which are already otherwise supplied. It is to be hoped that Messrs. RYLANDS will state their side of the case so that there may be no misunderstanding Councillor # LA.TT has taken the right course in placing on record an account of his own dealings with the Water- works Company. From his letter, which will be iCtlnd in another column, it will be seen that Le has been treated in a most extraordinary fashion It i 4 scarcely to be wondered at that, tmder the ci.etirastances, he is not taking water frout the Cornarky N,vorlder rather ;. 1••••••• • Aaosluu,Allave so persistently en- deavoured to come to terms, after having had his water meter removed when he was paying an advanced rate which the. Company had themselves proposed. It seems incredible that any commercial body of men should deal with their customers in this manner, and the matter is one which certainly calls for Fiotne explanation. Is it possible that other firms in Warrington have been dealt with in a similar way? If so, it may account for a condition of things which we cannot but say is a reflection upon the borough. The question is one which requires to be thoroughly ventilated, and, as it is a matter of public importance, we shall willingly keep Our columns open in order that it may be dis- cussed from every side.

The Liverpool Evening Express for Thursday states—with an utter disregard of the truth— that Mr. GLADSTONE'S brief speech at War- rington" was received by the crowd with no great manifestation of enthusiasm." It states further that as the train moved out of the station, there was an attempt •to raise a cheer, but it was a very feeble effort." This is equally false, and the proof of our charge shall be taken from The Evening Express itself. Let the reader turn to the Wednesday's issue of this same journal, and be will find that Mr. GLADSTONE'S speech is reported to have been received with "loud cheers, which were renewed enthusiastically as the hain moved of." It will thus be seen that our contemporary has been drawing one of the longest of "long bows." It has given itself" the lie as deep as to the _lungs."

A CITILD DROWNED AT PRESTON 1311008 —On Monday Mr J E Woreley, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Bed Lion Ins, Preston Brook, touching the death of Joseph loins, aged four years, whose body was found in the canal sWPreston Brook, on Suriciay last.—Bdward ivins, a boat- man, residing at Leigh, Manchester, said the deceased was We son. Witness was on a boat celled the Lyd, and last saw his child at play on some spare ground near the canal back. The child had always travelled in the boat with wit- ness and his wife, and had once before fallen into the canal, but witness had jumped in and rescued him. Witness be- lieved that on this °weapon the child meet have fallen into the canal whilst walking too near the edge of the water,— John Bradshaw, boatman, of Astiev-green. said on Sunday last about 3-30 he saw a boy's hat in the canal and was about ,to jump in, when he saw the body of the deneased near to the bank. He took the child to his boat, although two ',yang men who saw him said .he must not take the body from the water or he would get into trouble. Wanes, gave information to the police subsequently. Witness and others rubbed the body for about an hour, but were unable to restore life.—P.C. Boyle. stationed at Moore, said he had 'examined the body and found no marks of violence except a slight bruise on the forehead.—The jury returned a verdict of "Fonnd ,maned." MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL CANAL. A correspon- dent writs _There appears to be a strong movement in favour of Has construction of a canal between the Mersey docks and Manchester, for stearnme of a limited siza The plan laid down upon the liues suggested by Sir William Forwood, has teen designed by Mr liamil ton Fulton, the eminent engineer, who so long ago as 1360 originated the idea ef a steamship canal, and then clearly demonstrated its practicability. Mr Fulten'e estimate of the cost of the pre- pent proposed werks is £3,000,000. The amount of capital required by Mr Adamson and the other promoters for the comptetion of the defunct Manchester Ship Canal scheme was no less a sum than £10,500,000. How could such an extelavagant outlay ever prove remunerative to the Inves- tors? The annual income required to pay 5 per cent upon snob an ontlay would have been £1,500,000. A strong feel- ing is said to exist in Liverpool as well as Manchester that the dock authorities, as proposed by Sir William Forwood, should in the blended act be vested with the necessary powers to enable them to subscribe £500,000 towards, the undertaking, the completion of which would so largely in- masa trade facilities of the port ci.f leiverpool and Man- chester.

A WINDFALL Fa= CHANCRIST.—We take the following from the Trtgax Cbserver:—" Blessed is he that expecteth nothing, for he shall not be disappointed." Tots old saying has proved very true this week. About 80 years age, aMr Orford, a well-known doctor in Warrington, died. lea v ng by his will a life interest in his estete to each of his children, and, failing issue on their part, the estate had to be divided amongst his cousins and their descendants. On the deceaee of the last member of the family the estate was placed in Chancery, and then came what was proved no small matter, the finding out of the descendants of this Dr. Orford. The value of the estate left by the deceased was magnified to an enormous extent, and claitnants were forthcoming from all qaarters. Wigan supplied a coneiderable number, for one branch of the Orford family resided in this neighbourhood, and the descendants of this portionat the genealogical tree multiplied rapidly, and in the end totalled, we believe, up- wards of 300. There were three or font other branches, however, all having claimants, and the total number of par- ties entitled to participate in the dietribution of the estate was upwards of 700. Visions of luxury and affluence dawned before this army, as each one searched the parish register and traced the family history. With such a complicated business, it was not to he expected that the Court of Chancery would belie its, traditions and dis- play any extra amount of alacrity in getting quit of so in. teresting a suit. After the tepee of 13ye ars, h,wever, comes news of the division of the funds. With whet jeer was the news received by the "descendants," and how the long- looked-for day was anticipated! Ira some cases, we hear, the claimants could defer the hope of future pnisperity ne longer, and " portions" were mortgaged for temporary loans, which were to he repaid out of the aburalaut lichee forth- coming. At last the day was fixed, and on Tuesday the members of the Wigan branch proceeded to the offices of Messrs Harlington and Sans to receive their appointments Judea of their surprise when they learned that something less than one sovereign was the amount which the High Court of Chancery had in the nasjetity of cases awarded to them as their shire of the good old doctor's beqaest. King-street, for some hours presented a very animated ap- pearance, the numerous claimants eagerly discussidg their ill-luck, while some, as if they had not had enough of that commodity, were loud inatheir expreseions of a deterruina- lion to have "more law" on the subject. INTERESTING WEDDING AT RUNCORN.—That age is no j shield to the arrows of the God of Love has loner been ad- mitted, and on Thured ay morning the nuptial knot was tied at Runcorn.; under circumstances which place the subject still further from doubt. In the presence of a large assembly of people at the Parish Church, Mr. Levi Knowles, a "gay Lothario," over whose head the blasts of sixty-two winters have passed, was united in the holy bonds" to Mrs. Ann Capper, whose flowing locks have been fanned in the gentle breezes of 67 summers. Twice previously had the bride- groom taken unto himself a wife, and once pleviously had the happy bride anchored in the haven of matrimony. In Trinity-street, where the parties reside, the liveliest interest was displayed in the alliance, and the newly-married couple as they left the church were showered with rice and slip. pert and the carriage which conveyed them to the railway station was followed by large numbers of women and children. The" honeymoon was spent at Chester, and on the happy pair returning to Trinity-street in the evening, the neighbours celebrated the suspicions event with every sign of rejoicing. THE MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL. —At the recent public meetiag,s in the Free-trade Halt Mr. Adamson stated that the Corporation of Manchester would be asked to contlibute £15,000 towards the expenses of the next application to Parliament for power to construct a ship canal connecting this city with the sea. The General Pur- poses Committee of the City Council met on Thursday, and received a report from the Parliamentary Sub-committee, who recommended that steps should be taken to 'place the Corporation in a position legally to contribute to the extent that may hereafter be determined towards the cost of tbe next application to Parliament. At an interview with the committee Mr. Adammon stated on behalf of the promoters that the voluntary subscribers, including him- self, were riot disposed to continue their exertionsasuother session without the assistance and support of the Municipal Corporations, and he proposed that the Manchester C wpm.. tion should guarantee a contribution of 2,1 in the pound towards the Parliamentary expenses. The Parliamentary Committee were advised by their legal officers that the con- tribution by municipal corporations might be legally made in case the corporations agreed to join in the petition to Parliament for leave to introduce the bill, while the amount of the contribution and the extent of liability might beeffec- tively limited by agreement. The Parliamentary Commit- tee's report was unanimously adopted by the General Par- poses Committee, and will come before the Council for con- firmation at its next meeting. ' MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.— The recent changes in the law relating to municipal elections are of such importance as to deserve the serious notice of all persons interested, whether as candidates or voters. The Municipal Elections Corrupt and Illegal Practices Act 1884, comes into Operation on the Ist of October next ; and its provisions are of great et: in- gency. No meeting of any kind in connection with a mu- nicipal election will be allowed lobe held either in a public- house or in a political club room. The employment of car- riages and horses kept for hire is strictly prohibited ; and it is held to be doubtful whether the owner of such carriages and horses could use them to promote his own election. The expenses of each candidate are restricted to £25 if the num- ber of the electors in the ward or borough be 600 or under; e but if they exceed 500, an additional amount of 3d for every elector above the number of 500 may be expended. All creditors are to send in their claims to the candidate within 14 days after the election, and if the account be not sent in within Halt time paymeat will be barred. All expenses are to be paid within twenty-one days after the dar of election, and any person who makes a pay- ment in contravention of the 21st section of the Act will be guilty of an "illegal practice." The candidate is required within 28 days to send to the Town Cletk a return properly vouched of all the expenses incurred by him in connection with the election, and also to make a declaration • before a justice of the peace tbAi the account is correct. The de- claration and return are to be open to the inspection of any person at the Town Clerk's office on payment of one shilling. "Undue influence" appears to include abduction, duress. and any fraudulent device to impede the free exercise-of the franchise. With certain exceptions the Act applies to elec- tions of Local Boards, Boards of Guardians, and School Board. The Act of Parliament extending the hours of polling applies only to Parliamentary boroughs and boroughs some portion of which include a Parliamentary area.
