EXTRAORDINIRY SUICIDE AT DITTON.—THE INQUEST. 01 Wednesday afternoon, at Theme's Inn, Wilton, Mr W T Husband, the decors, ceuuts, coroner, held an inoiest 011 the body of George Cottsworth, 71 years of age, who committed su;cl.le by banging leinyeelf Sandey„ Froth the evidence adduced it appeared that the il-c-v-ed U,13 a glass blower by trade, and resided in Staideton-mw, Hale- road, Ditton. For same time pest he had been Pulp'eyed as a night watohm en by Mr Lewin, who is su”erintending the construction of the new main sewer for Widnes Feeling unwell about A fortnight ago, the deceised stayed array from his work for several days, and failing to intimate to his master the reason for his absence, his place was tilled by another man. The fact of having no occupation seemed to prey upon his mind, ant he became a little strange in his conduct. About eleven o'clock on Sunday Isis daughter-In- law, w bo lived a few yards from the houseof the deceased, I went into his house. Loaning his elbows cm the table, he said, "Oh; Polly, Pin mad; I don't know what I will do with myself." lie then went into the pantry. In a few minutes he came out and went upstairs. As he had been in the habit of going to bed every Sand iy forenoon to have a " nap," nothing was thought of this woceeding. Dinner being ready'at one o'clock, his son Peter called to him, but he received no reply. He therefore went upstairs, arid found his father suspended by a rope attached to a beam in the clothes closet. Dr Mac Donnell happened to be in the neigh, bourhood at the time, and he was called in, but it was found that life was extinct. The unfortnnate old man bad carried out his tragic act in a most determined marer. The beam to which the rope was attached was about feet 3 inches from the floor, and the cleansed was a man 5 feet 6 inches in height. Tha rope was one of lois grand children's skipping ropes, and the deceased had fennel a noose in true hung- man style, having placed the knot under tbe left ear. There being no room foe the deceased to drop, and in order to put an end to his existence he had ti push out his legs in a horizontal position and strangle hirnself.—Peter Coatsworth, son of the deceased, deposed to finding the body suspended In a sitting pesition.—The Clroner you cut him down? Witness: No. I ran for a witness first. —The Coroner: That was a strange thing to do. You should never do that. I trisst you will never coma across a dead body again in the same way; but if you do you should try to save life in the first iostanca if you cen.—Witness: I thought I should not be doing right to cut him down before some one else sew him.—The Coroner: If you found that a person had tumbled into a pool of water, would you not try to get him out before going for anyone ?Witness: I would.—P.S. Coutts said when he got to the house the body of the deceased was warm. Dr. MacDonnel was taking the rope off the neck, and he said the man had not been dead over a minute when he came There was a case at Halewood where a man went two miles for a polictinao, and left the men hanging all the limo. When the policeman reached lialewool the body was then warm and possessed life. The excuse the fellow made for his coaduct was that he was afraid to do anything at the body until someone cams as a witness.—The Coroner remarked that Coatsworth could not 11 eve been dead when found by his son. It was a great pity people should possess such au ercontaus iti,a that they onset not cut down a body except in the presence of a withess. It was one of the most nonsensical ideas he ever know.— PS. Coutts added that he knew the family of the deceastd very sell, and on Sunday, when he went into the house at the time of the suicide, the deceased's 80113 Ephraim and John were drunk. Oa Monday he bad to send a policemen to the house to quell a disturbance that was taking place between the a ms.—The Coroner remarked that with that he bad nothing to do. All be had to inquire into was what took place prior to death —The witness Peter was recalled, and said there had been n 7 quarrel between himself, his brothers, and his father. There had been a quarrel between his brothers a week ago, which seemed to have affected his father somewhat. —The Coroner said if this had been a well conducted family the fact of 'such disturbances might have caused the deceased to commit the rash act ; but it seemed to be a most unfortunate one, and he thought they could not put down the death to any family quarrel. It was an unhappy state of affairs that the sons should be drunk in the house while the father was taking away his own life; and, so far as he could see, the evidence would lead the jury to believe that doe man committed suicide whilst tempo- rarily insane. He characterised the condoct of the son-as disgracetui.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect thaw the deceased committed suicide while temporarily insane.

Mr. Bradlaugh's plans for the autumn session are in- dicated in a letter which be has just written. TLe October session, be says, is a special franchise and war-to-the• Lords session, and possibly if he does stand aside for that his con- stituents will forgive him. But theirs is the right to com- mand, and his the duty to obey. THE FIERY Caoss.—Tne principal cartoon in Panc:i this week is one of striking artistic merit, and tnßy rarely be de- scribed as amongst the most powerful that Mr Tenniel has yet produced. Our leading comic journal has strongly taken the side of the proletariat against the House of Lords, and the cartoon in which Mr Gladstone is represented as raising the fiery cross in Midlothian is thoroughly in har- mony with the spirit of the people. The execution's highly dramatic, and the conomtion ii an accurate in- dication of the current of events. - -

When five years ago Mr. Gladstone departed on tha historical Midlothian campaign it was regarded as a physical fe:t that vet uld evErtax his strength. I happened to accem- pany him throethont the campaign, heard all his speeches end witnessed all his jeurneyings, and I do not remember to have seen at any time the slighteet trace of fatigue. He is five years older now, and in entering upon a new campaign with an object as definite as that with which be went to Mid:othian in 1879, he has observed the precaution of securing two days rest after his railway journey. On the other hand, haring originally limited his appearance to two meetings, he has extended the number, and will now make three spaeches. There is little fear that he will not be equal to the leek he has assigned himself, though it is sufficient to ' tax the strength of a younger man. Few things are more remarkable in connection with Mr. Gladstone's career than his powers of recuperation. I have seen him in the House of Commons on a Ft iday night looking pale and worried, and even feverish. On the Monday, having in the meanwhile taken 21 hours rest in . some quiet couutry It use, he has come back looking as fresh as if he had not done a day's work for a month. As far as common experience goes there has been no year in which Mr Gladstone has done better work or in fuller quantity than during the last seeshon. He made several speeches which will rank with the highest efforts of his mature years. The battery of questions was opened upon him night after night, the fire being directed in circumstances that made it peculiarly difficult effectually to reply. Of late it has been the habit for all questions addressed personally to the Premier to be placed together at the end of the list. 1 They, of course, always relate to matters of the highest im- portance. Even Mr Biggar has not yet put a question to the Premier as to why tbe past cart at Bellyraggy is painted red, nor has Mr Healy demanded from him full particulars i of the retiring pension of a private in the Monaghan Con- stabulary. Having answered a question relating to affairs ' in-Egypt Mr Gladstone has to rise again, without a mo- ment's interval, to reply to another dealing with delicate matters of diplomatic negociations, and may next have to deal with a cunningly contrived question involving some controversial point in home policy. The other Ministers, without exception, prepare their replies beforehand, and nn- disguisedly read them from manuscript. Mr Gladstone speaks without note of any kind, anl with a full conscious- ness that every wora be utters will be critically weighed at home and abroad. This is no slight tax on a man. But With others it has been cheerfully met through the long ses- sion, hi 3 own share in which Mr Gladstone wound up by the tremendous onslaught on the Opposition generally, and Sir 8 Northcote in particular. What Mr. Healy is going about Ireland keeping things going, and Mr. Wggar is looming epistles in which he de- nounces Earl Spencer as a wilful murderer, and as "the head of the gait e " connected with the Dublin scandals, Mr. Parnell is quietly enjoying himself, doing a little shooting on his own grounds at Antrim; which have been secured to him chiefly. by becefactions from America. Mr. Parnell is now a welf-tc-lo man, having netted a sum of 1.29,000, which is more than some men make out of politics. Avon- d4l-. where he lives is one of those roomy loose-looking atone betties much too large for its Occupant, which one insets with about Ireland. It stands by the river Avonmore of which Moore sang. "The house is full of odds and ends, old furniture, antlers, skins, and bog-oak things adorned with green silk of hideous hue." Mr. Parnell has, I suppose, as many presents lying about at Avondale, as Mr. Gladstone has at ilewarden. Being reung, unmarried, and as some ladies declare, handsome, he has enough embroidered caps and slippers to set up a biz lar. Another more useful pre- sent is a net of carpenters tools enclosed in a polished oak chest. This was given him by the ladies of Rsthdruna, and in his rare visits to his home Mr. Parnell sometimesmakes use of the tools. A plush arm chair of a good bola crimson was aired him by the ladies of Cork. The ladies of Liverpool contributed a bright green *Win quilt with a great staring menogram in the centre. The Dublin ladies gave him a musical box which plays among other soothing tunes" The wearing of the green." From Liverpool a year or two ago there ceme to Avondale an Easter egg made in silver. When it was opened there was discovered a present of one hundred gnineas, a most useful egg desirable for hatching pu,pases. The latest addition to Mr. Parnell's miscellaneous treasure trove is an enormous Oatrich egg set on a silver pedestal. This was hr mght to him from Australia by the young Red- mends when they returned a short time age. It was a pre- sent from an Irishman living in Australia, who sent a simi- lar gift for Mrs Parnell and Miss Anna Parnell. Avondale is a beautiful place, embossed among its own trees and sung to by its own river. But the green silk quilt and the bright red plush chair are of themselves almost enough to account for the rarity of Mr. Parnell's visits. . Tee Cheater Farmers' Club, which has decreed death to the sparrows, only echoes a cry pessionately raised from the United States. An American farmer who is over here is de- lighted to discover-this evidence of awakening on the part of his British brethren. , Hitherto the English sparrow has had a strong party who have pleaded for Its life on the ground that it does more good than harm. In America it teems they 'hold the belief that sparrows are partially pro- tected fqlatheir edible emerges, 'sparrow potpie" being a kind if !Bing in which British gourmand.) fortify themselves. 81yanowtfitie.of recent importation to America, having been

lintroduced in Philadelphia in the year 1869. They rapidly spread, though many States of the Union are still free from their presence. In the neighbourhood of Philadelphia where they are said to be an insufferable nuisance, efforts are made to reduce their numbers, and if possible extinguish them by spreading poisoned wheat. At present, according to the melancholy report of my friend, there is no appreciable effect. "I reckon," he says, "that they rather like the poison and thrive on it. It maker the wheat tasty; saves them looking round for salt or pepper." The curious relations which existed between the late - Charles Heade and the lady who for many years lived as his housekeeper, and for whose tombstone be wrote a pions inscription, find odd coincidence in the case of Victor Hugo. The French novelist bad a faithful and much treasured housekeeper as the English novelist had, Label by way of completing the coincidence Madame Drouhet was, when Victor Hugo firet made her acquaintance, an actress just as Mrs Seymour was when she became known to Charles Reade. Madame Drouleet was an invaluable companion to Victor lingo, and when a short time ago she died it seemed to him also as if the light and life of Lis home were extin- guished. In addition to acting as housekeeper she copied every word he has written during the last forty years, to avoid the risk of its beisg lost or destroyed before it was printed. It is said, and generally believed by private friends of Hugo, that she left behind her a diary in which she re- corded the movements and the sayings of the great man much as Boswell did for Johnson. Victor Hugo will say nothing about this supposed manuscript, whether confirma- tory or in denial of its existebce. There is, however, a firm belief that it will be found among his manuscript. The row at the Holborn last Saturday is indicative of the state of affairs in London theatres just now. Ido not sup- pose that any one now open, including the Lyceum, is pay- ing its expenses. At the Holborn there was the misfortune to be no stockirg to fall back upon. In theatrical parlance '' . ...

• _ " the ghost wourdn't walk," so the actors did. H.ence the trouble. Tye peculiar soreness of the affair from the mana- gerial point of view, is that the House was more than half full of people with orders. These, with a baseness and in- gratitude that passes belief, were among the first to reach the pay doors demanding "their money back." In the course of a very few minutes the unfortunate manager found himself in the carious position of having returned .£2 more _ .
than be bad taken, whilst there still remained sereral hun- dred people clamouring "for their money," in default of which they " took it oat of the furniture."

SCDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN —About eleven o'clock on Thursday morning a woman named Mary Ann Nicholls, a widow. 54 yeirs of age, was found dead in bed at 2, Bylands yard, School-brew, where she cohabited with a torn named Knight, with whom she had lived for the last 30 yews. On the day previous she complained of a choking sensation in her throat, and remained in bed. Fnight ote Thursday morning went to his work as usual, and a "'nth named Adcroft, who has been brought up from childhood by the deceased, went upstairs afterwmds, and found her dead in bed, her ears and lips being very much disaloured.—Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the death at the Parade-room of the Police Station on Thursday evening, when a verdict of death from natural cautres was returned. NOTES BY THE WAY.

So little progress had been made in the match at Trent Bridge between Nottinghamshire and the Austral' Ins that on Saturday the result was I egarded as pretty certain to be a draw. Notwithstanding this fact, however, the vigour of the game never for a moment relaxed, the play being just as keen and good as though the two elevens had bad a de- finite issue before them. The match was one of the very best of the season, the all-round play being superb. Not often have the Nottingham men bowled and fielded with such consistent excellence, and the game formed a worthy finish to their brilliantly successful season. The weather was charming, and nearly 11,000 people paid at the turn- stiles. Score : Australians, 265 and 141 ; Notts, 273 and 15 for one wicket.—At Brighton, on Saturday, Sussex se- cured a well-earned victory by 19 runs with an innings to spare over Yorkshire. The Sussex elding was well up to form. Score : Sussex, 339 ; Yorkshire, 164 and 176.—F0r the greater part of the day at Cheltenham, on Saturday, it was practically certain that the match between Middlesex and Gloucestershire would end in a draw. As there was no chance of finishing the game, it was agreed to draw stumps at a Tuner to six, and the mats ended in a draw dis- tinctly in favour of Gloucestershire, who, with all their wickets to fall, required 123 runs to win. Hilt an hour's play on Wednesday morning was sufficient to finish off the match between the Australians and Cam- bridge University at Brighton, the Australians gaining a most decisive victory by 142 runs. The close of Tues- day's play left so little doubt as to the result that scarcely any interest was taken in the finish. Spofforth bowled in wonderful fine form. Score : Australians. 190 and 180 ; University, 135 and 93.—At Bradford, on Wednesday, York- shire obtained a victory over Derbyshire by ten wickets There was nothing in the play worthy of special mention. Score : Yorkshire, 231 and 16 ; Derbyshire, 126 and 117.- -The game between Glouceetershire and Surrey, at Clifton, ended in a draw on Wednesday, the weather stopping play. Some good batting was witnessed. It is worthy of remark that in the three Gloucestershire matches plavtd this year at Clifton seven individual scores of over 100 have been made. This match was the last of the Gloucestershire en- gagements, of which they have won one, lost eight, and three have been drawn.—After three days very fair cricket Kent on Wednesday succeeded in defeating Somersetshire by 159 runs. Score : Kent, 187 and 310 ; Somersetsbire, 221 and 117.

Some good all-round batting was witnessed at Gravesend, on Thursday, in the contest between the Australians and the South of England team. The Australians, who were bitting all the afternoon, scored 351 for the loss of nine wickets. For the first time in the tour the 100 was put up before the first wicket fell. No fewer that line of the first ten batsmen reached double figures.

MR. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO MID- LOTHIAN. , THE JOURNEY FROM HAWARDEN. EFEEOII AT WARAIN9T9I.I.; On Wednesday morning the I'-rim e Minister left Havearaen for Midlothian, meeting selth a British welcome all along the line. The right hole, gentleman left the castle at eight o'clock, driving to Boughton Hell Station, whence he pro- ceeded to Chester by special train. He was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, and Mr. U. Gladstone. At Chester he was respectfully ealuted by a number of people who had gathered in anticipation of his arrival, and the train was there joined by a number of Press-men. A detec- tive also accompanied the party. The saloon was joined to the 8 55 train for Warringtoo, where the Premier met with a meet vigorous reception. Here the saloon was shunted to await the arrival of the ten o'clock train to the north. At every station on the route at which Mr. Glad- stone's carriage was brought to a standstill, he was greeted with enthusiasm and good wishes sped after him. He was looking remarkable well, and it was evident that the hard strain of Parliamentary labour had not impaired his vigorous constitution. The reception of Mr. Gladstone at Warrington, where he arrived at 9-35, was noteworthy. The morning being dreary and uninviting, and the time that the Premier was expected 'o arrive not being generally known, it was impos- sible for any organised demonstration te be made. Notwith- standing, a considerable number of people assembled on the platform at Bank Quay shortly after nine o'clock, and waited patiently until the arrival of the traia, beguiling the time with conversation on political matters, the Franchise Bill coming in for particular notice. Occasionally, as the smoke of some locomotive was seen in the distance, the cry at " He is coming" was raised, and after a few such false alarms the train to which the saloon containing the Premier was attached, steamed slowly into the station. There was an eager scanning of the carriages, and when the right bon. gentleman was observed sitting near that window of the saloon which adjoined the platform, perusing a newspaper, a cheer was raised, and, as Mr. Gladstone let down the win- low of the carriage to bow his acknowledgments, the closely pressing crowd, with hats waving in uplifted hands, cheered and re-cheered. The cheering was taken up by a second enthusiastic crowd, which bad collected on the platform on the opposite side of the saloon, and the Premier again bowed his acknowledgments. The train to which the saloon was attached was then sent forward, and the saloon was shunted into a siding, about 50 yards from the end of the platform. Here apparently it was about to remain, and the assembled spectators bzgan to experience a sensation akin to disappointment. Little groups were for- med, and the situation was earnestly canvassed, whilst anxious glances were sent from the platform to the Isolated saloon. Finally, Mr Henry Roberts, the secretary of the Liberal Association, accompanied by Mr John Walker, editor of this journal, took the initiative and sought an in- terview with the stationmaster, Mr Ashuret. Shortly after- wards the three were noticed to be walking on the line to the platform, where some rcqurst was made to Mr Gladstone. The waving of hands by the advance party signalled those on the platform, who lost no time; in gathering near the saloon, when the cheering was resumed with redoubled vig- our. On its subsidence, Mr WALKER, addressing Mr Gladstone. said :—As a num- ber of Liberals of Warrington, hearing that you were passing through the tows, we felt that we could not let this opportunity go by without wishing you one word of cheer on the way to your campaign in Midlothian. (Applause.) We recognise the great efforts you have made to pace the Franchise Bill, in which we are all so deeply interested in this part of the country, especially those who up to the present time have no votes. There was an assembly on the Common in this neighbourhood, ten thousand strong, the other day, to say how earnestly they desired this Bill ; and, seeing you passing on to Mid- lothian, we feel that we are in some sense assured that steps will be taken whereby Halo Bill will be carried. We want to thank you for the noble efforts you have made to give the people this vote, and desire to say that we look upon it as an aueury of triumph that the last Midlothian campaign re- sulted so gloriously. Wean% wish to detain you longer,orask a word from you. We wish you to preserve your health and strength for the great campaign in which you are about to engage, but we cannot let you go without giving you a cheering word before leaving Warrington. (Applause ) Three hearty cheers were then given for Mr. Gladstone, and three more for Mrs. Gladstone. In reply, Mr. Gladstone said :—Sir, and gentlemen,—l thank you very much for your kind words, and I may accept the permission you gave me not to attempt to address you. I will only say this. You may rely, I think, upon the Government to do their part, and upon me, as far as I am concerued, to do my part, in a considerable national crisis. But pray recollect that this is an affair which lies in the bands of the country. (Applause.) We have not gone migrating about the country—the ministers, I mean, have not gone migrating about the country—to stir the people up. That we leave to the leaders of the Opposition, if they like to do it. (Laughter.) ,We confine ourselves to addressing those—we have confined ourselves pretty much to address- ing those—with whom we have direct political or personal relations. ~Applause.) But pray remember it does not de- pend upon us. it depends upon the country. Every man has got to ask himself what he thinks of it, and what his duty is in this emergency. (Cheers.) Mr AMU:IIIST, the stationmaster, then remarked to the gathering," Gentlemen, you hod better move on to the platform, you are in a dangerous place here." Immediately, some one jocularly responded—. Oh, we could not be in a safer place," and Mr Ashurst, seeing from the laughter that his remark might be interpreted in a different sense to thet which he intended, hastened to add," I mean as regards the line." The company then dispersed and proceeded towards the platform. The saloon was soon afterwards joined to the train for the north, and as it :passed through the station another cheer was raised. The Premier was noticed to be again reading when the train left the stttion, accompanied by a parting cheer as it sped forward with its distingnished occupants to the North. Amongst those who took part in the welcome to Mr Gladstone besides the gentlemen already named were Councillors F Monks, F Dixon, John Crostield, Messrs J H Gornall, John Greening, M Bowden, Frank Retells: the Rev J Tongs, and a large number of the I Liberals of the towfi. Wigan was reached about half-past ten, and here a large number of persons were waiting As the Premier was re• cognised a hearty cheer was given, and cheering was repea- ted at intervals while the train was being made up Dur- ing the quarter of an hour of stay, several gentlemen, in- cluding Mr Agnew, M.P.. entered into conversation with Mr Gladstone, who repeatedly bowed his acknoa ledgments to the cheers of those congregated in the station. An invi- tation to" Let us hear something" was not responded to by the right bon gentleman. The train proceeded northwards at a quarter to eleven, followed by enthusiastic cries of "Cheers for Gladstone," and "Cheers for the Midlothian campaign." At Preston station, which was reached shortly after eleven o'clock, there was a very large and enthusiastic gathering upon the platform. When the train Came in a rush was made for the carriage in which Mr Gladstone and his family were seated, and it was with considerable diffi• culty that a deputation from Southport could force its way through. With the aid of a few police officers and railway officials, however, the way was at last cleared, and the following address was presented to the Premier:— At a meeting of the members of the Southport Liberal Club, held on Tuesday evening, August 26th, 1884, it was moved by Mr W P Clarke (president of the club), secended by Mr Alderman Boothroyd (president of the Liberal Asso- ciation), and carried unanimously: That the members of the Southport Liberal Club desire to congratulate the Right Hon Wm Ewart Gladstone on the passing of the Franchise Bill through the Commons by large and increasing majori- ties, and, while regretting the action of the House of Lords In blocking this important measure for enfranchising 2,000,000 of their fellow-countrymen, trust and believe that he will conduct this struggle to an early and successful issue, and that the approaching meetings in Midlothian will still further enlighten the country, which has already proved its sympathy on this question with Her Majesty's Govern- ment.

It was thought Mr. Gladsone would hare made a speech in reply, but he contented himself with saying "Thank you," and, the train being already 13 minutes late, it was signalled out as soon as possible. So eager were some of the people to get a glimpse of the Premier that they ran round to the " off " side of the train and climbed up to the saloon, supporting themselves by the window, which under the severe pressure gave way. Cheers from all sides were given as the train left for Carnforth. Both at Carnforth and Ox- enholme, the next station, loud cheers were given for Mr. Gladstone by the people on the platform, and the right hon. gentleman responded to them with bows and smiles and cor- dial shaking of hands. Carlisle was reached at 1-45, and here there was an im- mense concourse of spectators, who made frantic efforts to get near the saloon. After many times acknowledging the heartiness of his welcome, and the people not yet being satisfied, Mr. Gladstone, in response to a call for a speech, said : Well, if you wish to hear a few words from me with regard to this question of the franchise, I will say that, so far as the Government is concerned, this is a matter which they think they ought to leave in the hands of the nation, and they therefore would confine themselves to addressing their own constituents or persons with whom they may be in special relation. But if we had gone about to one place and another speaking to the people, well, then they would have said, " That is your affair, and not ours." Now, what we desire is that it should be understood that it is your affair,and that we have nothing to do with it, except to fulfil our duty as Ministers of the Crown in Parliament and out of it, and that, we hope, gentlemen, we shall do. (Cheers.) After a few minutes' further delay, caused by the replac- ing of the broken wifulow, a fresh start was made shortly after two o'clock. At Lockerbie, the first stoppage on cross- ing the border, a great number of persons had collected on the platform, one of them carrying a banner ioscribed with the words "Reform, 1832." Enthusiastic cheers greeted the arrival of the train, which having been brought to a stand- still, Mr Brydone, chairman of the local Liberal Association, stepped forward, and addressing Mr Gladstone, said they all wished him a hearty welcome to Scotland on this the first stoppage across the border' and trusted be might be spared to finish the great work he had so well begun. Mr Glad stone, who was received with cheers, said: I thank yon very much for your kind words. Let me say—and I am sure that in saying it you will not misunderstand me—that I do not really want much assurance from the people of Scotland of

the kiadnsss and confidence with which I should be received here in connection with the principles to which you are so deeply attached. (Loud cheers.) I have explained twice on my way here—(laughter)—that I must not make speeches except to my constituents. That is not from indolence or wish. if there is to be an from' indiff armee, but or::, expression of national opinion, that it should be a sponta- neous expreesion and should not be got up by the Ministers of the Crown travelling from place to place as if it were necessary to teach the people. (Cheers.) We wish to know what the nation thinks. It i 3 the affair of the nation. and I believe it will be a genuine and hearty expression of that opinion which will suffice to gain that great and just and safe and constitutional end which we all have in view. (Cheers.)

Before the train moved onward Mrs Gladstone was presented with a bouquet, and a number of people shook hands with Mr. Gladstone. Beattock was the next station of any importance, and here there was mere cheering and hand shaking, while Mrs. Gladstone was presented with another bouquet and a bunch of heather. One of those on the platform wire welcomed the party was Mr. S. Smith, M.P. At Carstairs Junction two addresses cf welcome were presented to Mr Gladstone, one being from the electors and non-electors of Carnwath, and the other from Lanark —Mr. Gladstone, in responding, was received with loud cheers. He said: Before the train goes on I would express to you my cordial thanks for the assurances you have given me of your confidence and support. We are certainly engaged in a great cause and in the course of a day or two it will be my , duty to endeavour to set before my constituents of Midi°. thian, my kind and brave constituents of Midlothian, the view we take of that course. I share your confidence, but pray let me impress upon you that what is to be done now depends much more upon you than upon me. (Cheers.) Wken that contest has had to be waged in Parliament I have been ready, and I hope, please God, I shall be ready again. (Renewed cheers.) The question now at issue is not what is my opinion; people know that well enough— (hear, hear)—nor is it eves the opinion of the Liberal party. It is whether the Liberal party in this matter are the true re- presentatives of the nation. (Cries of "We are," and cheers.) That is the question which I believe my fellow- countrymen and my fellow-Scotchmen—(cheers)—will be ready and able to solve to the satisfaction of all reasonable men. (Loud cheers.) Another bouquet was presented to Mrs Gladstone, after which the laurney was resumed, amid hearty cheers, which were repeated at different points on the line on the way to West Princess-street Station. Edinburgh. For more than an hour previous to the time notified for the arrival of the train large crowds had assembled in the vicinity of the sta- tion. The balconies of the Scottish Liberal Club, situated immediately opposite the terminus, were gaily decorated, and a large number of ladies took advantage of the win- dows to witness the arrival of the Premier. At three o'clock the members of the Midlothian Liberal Association met in the clubroom, where an address of welcome to Mr Gladstone was decided upon. The address was handed to Mr John Cowan, chairman of the association, for presentation, and then the members of the Committee went to the railway platform to await the arrival of the train. The Earl of Roseberry had already arrived, as had Sir George Harrison, the Lord Provost of the city. After considerable delay, the train, which was 40 minutes late, entered the station amid loud cheering. Lehi Roseberry assisted Mr Gladstone from the carriage, while Mr Cowan escorted Mrs Gladstone, who was presented by Lady Torpichen with a beautiful bouquet of exotics. On emerging from the station Mr Gladstone was at once recognised and received with enthusiastic cheer- ing. Mr and Mrs Gladstone, with Miss Helen Gladstone and Lord Roseberry. having taken their seats in a carriage drawn by four horses, Mr Cowan presented the address above referred to, remarking that it was an expression of welcome to the right bon gentleman from his constituents. In a second carriage were Mr Henry Gladstone and Miss Gladstone. The party then drove off to Dalmeny House, the residence of Lord Roseberry. The streets in the city through which they had to pass were densely crowded. Thursday was spent very quietly at Dalmeny by Mr , Gladstone. In the morning the Premier remained within 'doors, transacting, it is understood, State business. During ' part of this ti-ne Lord Northbrook was closeted with Mr Gladstone, and afterwards left for Edinburgh en route for the South. After the company had been photographed at at the front entrance to the house, Mr Gladstone and Mrs Gladstone and family made an unexpected visit to the Forth Bridge works at Queensferry. On returning to the exit gate, where the party appended their signatures to the visitors' book, the 2,000 men who were then leaving work heartily cheered the distinguished visitors. Mr Gladstone, in acknowledging the compliment, said, " Success to your work, my friends." Mr Gladstone will address the first meeting to-day (Saturday).
LOCAL BREACEI OF PROMISE CASE.

At the Sheriff's Court, on Wednesday, at St. George's Hall, Mr H L Gregory and a jury sat to assess damages in an action for breach et promise brought against Joseph Henry Hay Thornthwaite, milkdealer, Neston, by Ann Houghton, of Crouton, near Prescot. The breach of pro- mise was admitted, and the defendant did not put in an appearance.

The parties in the case were in comfortable circumstances in life, the father of the plaintiff having been a farmer at Town End, near Crouton, Prescot ; and the father of the de- fendent was also a farmer in Cheshire. The courtship COM- menced in 1878, when the plaintiff was 23 and the defen- dant 28 years of age, the latter at that time being in partnership with his brother's cowkeeper at Wavertree. They continued in business to the end of 1882, when the two brothers had saved something like £1,600. The business was afterwards sold for £6OO, and the defendant afterwards went to Canada for the purpose of seeing the country with a view of settling there. As Canada did not agree with him he returned, and made inquiries with a view of setting up in businzss in Liverpool. Some time after this defendant asked plaintiff to lead his brother £3OO, and when she refused he seemed to be out of temper, and, on the plaintiff telling him that be must either break the match off or provide her with a home, he wrote to her, enclosing her photograph and de- manding back his own. From the time the plaintiff was twenty-three until she reached the age of twenty-nine she had been engaged to the defendant. There was not the slightest ground for any imputation against her. . The jury, after a brief consideration, assessed the damages at £2OO, with costs.

The latest report of Mr. H. E. Oakeley, the senior inspec- tor of schools for the Manchester district, is of unusual in- terest. The report deals with the year 1883, during which the New Code came into force. The numbers preient on the day of inspection were 91,025, showing an increase of 8,149 as compared with 1881, the last year for which a similar " ganeral report" was made. 'the percentage of passes was —in reading 927, writing and spelling 89, arithmetic 856. Mr. Oakeley expresses a high opinion of the New Code as tending to greater thoroughness in several ways. He is a disbeliever in the charge of overpressure which is often brought against the working of the Cods. He pointedly says :—"There are neighbourhoods where even two class ts are too Muck for the ho.lf-stitYed ChildrOP Whi? an ithqn, to do home lessons. Tiiere ate average iibletbOttr• hoods where the teacher would do a good and wholesome year's work if he confined his attention to good elementary and class subjects; but here one or two specific subjects are of tea also attempted, and when towards the end of the year he finds the children cannot grasp all, he gets worried and ill, and attributes the strain to the Code. Ag Ain, the abilities of teachers differ very much indeed, and this should be duly weighed in mapping out the year's work. I have of ten found a teacher attempting to teach more than is within his power, and when his failure becomes manifest he refers it to the requirements of the Code, to anything but himself. As a neighbouring school under the same social conditions the earns subjects are creditably taught bye very much abler man." Mr. Oakeley attaches much importance to physical exer- cises, and declares that "the schools where the physical exercises are best done are unquestionably those which pass the beat examinations in other respects." "At four Board Schools," he adds, "there are excellent drum and fife bands, and at my last inspection the little musicians presented a very smart appearance, with military caps just come from Woolwich." Mr. Oakeley is a supporter of the movement, initiated in Manchester, for "Art in Schools." He remarks on this head :—'• In a report made ten years ago, I begged for greater attention to what I think a very important point —the adornment of the schoolroom by flowers, pictures, casts, &c. It is strage that some people think a schoolroom quite good enough if periodically whitewashed and fur- nished with necessary school appliances. In many parts of a densely-crowded large town, the children never see any- thing beyond four or five hideous streets surrounding their altogether unlovely dwellings. Is it not quite clear that there is a direct and powerful educational advantage in showing them beautiful things in the only place possible— their school? Where some pains have been taken to develop the love of beauty, it is touching to see the children's de- light. The Committee of the Manchester Art Museum Intend to offer to managers of elementary schools small loan collections of good pictures, casts, and pottery, includ- ing coloured pictures of common flowers ferns, trees, birds, and of such pretty places as town children may see on the rare occasion of a country trip. I wieh everyone would read an excellent pamphlet by Mr. Horafall, the originator of the scheme, entitled • Art in Large Towns,' which forcibly shows the importance, from many points of view, of encou- raging among the working classes an interest in beauty and in art, still regarded by many as a plaything for idle people. I have not space to dwell further on this good movement, but I heartily wish the committee every success, and shall be very glad to see their promised loan." Almost the only severe criticism which Mr. Oakeley has apparently felt him- self called upon to make is with regard to the management of some of the voluntary schools. He says :—There are many schools (and I ackaowledge it with gratitude) where one manager at least, usually the clergyman, studies the characters of teachers and pupil-teachers, exercises a wise superintendence, is acquainted with every child and its home circumstances, encourages all by his familiar presence and good advice. The visits of his wile, or of some other lady intergated in the school, are of inestimable good for the girls, which no man, however willing, can hope to achieve. Hero ta a means of improving the school where voluntary martage'ment may have a distinct advantage over a boara, which is apt to resemble a benevolent machine. Bat there are voluntary schools here very seldom visited at all by anyone; the teacher onward plods his weary way unaided by sympathy or advice; these are in all bat name adven- ture schools. It is somewhat strange that ladies take scarcely any part in school management in or near Man- chester; there are illustrious but very few exceptions. The Roman Catholic clergy frequently visit and take the utmost interest in their schools, and this is one reason why, not- withstanding that they have pecaliar difficulties from the atreme poverty of the parents, they hold their own, though the strain is often severe. The worst managed schools are the British and Wesleyan; their accounts are usually duly kept and the papers signed, but if any manager opears at all on the day of inspection, he uneasily looks at clock and beats a hasty retreat. These schools, how. have as a rule little difficulty in making both ends 'a the parents are fairly well off, and the school fees

div.p: HAYDOCK.

IIAYDOCK LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board offices, Haydack, on Monday afternoon when there were present: Mr Charles Pilkington, J P (in the chair), Mr John Jackson, Mr W Cunliff?, an Mr Thomas Turnbull (clerk.) The minutes of the last meeting were confirmed. FINANCES —Accounts amounting to £6O fis 103 were ex- amined and passed for payment. TIIE S JPTIS OF WATER TO TIIE GIB COTCAGES.—At a previous meeting of the Board the clerk was instructed to write to the Newton Board of Commissioners asking what portion of expense they would bear towards supplying water to tha Gib cottages; and Mr Cunliffe asked if any reply bad been received —The Clerk said they would not corsent to bear any portion of the exoense.—Mr Cunliffe: How many cottages are there P—Mr Turnbull : Ten —The Chair- man said Messrs Evans proposed to continue their pipes to the cottages in question, and then the Board could charge the firm for the water running through the meter.—Mr Cunliffe expressed the opinion that the Board ought to lay their own pipes to the cottages, RS it would pay them in the long run.—The Clerk said the distance would be about 450 yards, and it was estimated the cost would be about £2s.—Mr Cunliffe ultimately moved that the Board lay water pipes to the Gib cottages ; and Mr Jackson seconded the motion which was adopted. HAYDOCZ LODGE ASTIMI —Dr Beaman of Haydock Lodge Asylum, wrote asking whether the Beaman, Local Board were willing to lays three-inch main from the present termination of the Board's pipes at the corner of Penny-lane, to front door of his instituton, or to a front immediately ad- joining. He also asked for details as to the charge for cer- tain matters in connection therewith. In the course of a discussion which ensued, it was stated that pipes would have to be laid a distance of over 300 yards, the Chairman remarking that the cost would be about £5O in round num- bers.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that they should have some sort of guarantee that so much water would be used or that Dr Beaman pay a portion of the expense.—Mr Cunliffe thought if Dr Beaman only used the water in case of a fire it would be a loss to the Board.—Mr John Jackson moved that the Board lay the pipes on condition that Dr Beaman pay five per cent. on the outlay.—Mr Cunliffe seconded the motion, which was passed.—The clerk and the chairman were instructed to see Dr Beaman upon the matter.

Novrom oF AUDIT.—Mr Turnbull stated that the district auditor had given notice of his intention to audit the ac- counts oE the Board for the year ended 25th March last, on the Bth September next, at the offices of the Local Board. CORHESPONDHNCE,—The Clerk read a communication from the Local Government Board on the epidemic of cholera, and pointing out certain precautions with reference to rags, &c., arriving from France. A letter was also read from the Public Works Loan Commissioners, asking to be supplied with a return showing that the amount of £4,500 for works of water supplied on the 24th November, 1882, had been expended for the purposes for which it was bor- rowed. The Clerk stated that the return bad been duly filled up and he would return it. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—The Clerk read the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, which stated that proceed. logs were ordered to ba taken against several parents who had neglected to send their children to school.—The School Attendance Officer had no report to present on account of the holidays. This was the only business.

A shock of earthquake was felt on Tuesday at Jersey. lasting 30 seconds. On Thursday Charles Blanchfield was committed for trial by the Manchester city justices for the murder of his wife on the 21st inst, at 28, Chorlton-street. DUBLIN SCANDALS : A HEAVY SENTENCE. Jakiir Pillar, who is said to be a Quaker, and was in an extensive way of business as a grocer in Dublin, was on Saturday sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude for felony in connection with the Dublin scandals, to which he pleaded guilty. Ile is GO years of age. In the case of Mr Cornwall and Captain Kirwan, the jury, after a pro- longed consideration, were unable to agree, because they could not believe the witnesses. The cases against French, Cornwall, Nitran now stand over till the next Commis- sion.

IVIFE DESERTION: A TALE OF MISERY. During the last few weeks there has been an unusual number of cases of wife desertion in Warrington, and on Tuesday a sad state of things was revealed at the Borough "furl, when a man, who was afterwards designated by the siting chairman, Councillor monkS, as a drUnhen vagabond, was charged with neglecting to maintain his two children, the prosecution being taken up by Mr Shearer, relieving officer, who said that the prisoner and his family had `proveCi a source of trouble to the Board of Guardians f-or the last 12 months. On the 22nd instant ON Of children were ad- mitted jot) the House, whlch formed the subject of the present charge.—Mr Harbourne, relieving officer, gave evi- dence to the effect that the prisoner's two children were in a neglected condition. He had frequently been to th 3 pri- soner's house, and found him drinking there. Ile was totally unfit to have the care of children—lnspector Nor- man also proved having visited the house, and said that it was almost destitute of furniture, two battens of straw forming the principle part. There were no provisions in the house, but the prisoner was partly drunk at the time. He was found work by the Corporation, but he ran away from it. Prisoner: I ran away because I had the diarrhma.—,lnspector Norman: The children were in a deplorable state. I have received a letter saying that on the 20th of this month he sold the last rag in the house to get a penny with which to buy 801118 drink.—P,imner was sentenced to a month's hard labour..—Thomas Bate was charged at the same court with leaving his wife and child chargeable to the Warring- ton Union.—Mr Harbourne said that the prisoner and his wife had been very unhappy for some time, and the latter had not been able to live with him, because of his miscon- duct. When be last visited their house he found her without food, and he sent the prisoner notice that be would be prose- cuted if he did not provide for his wife and children. When before the Guardians prisoner admitted having received as much as 293 a week, and that be did not give his wife any money for four months.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one month with hard labour.—On Monday, at the same court, a labourer named Joseph Ireland, of Winwick-street, was charged on remand with deserting his wife and three chil- dren, whilst living in Kinder's-yard, Latchford.—The case was adjourned for a fortnight to see if the prisoner would make some arrangement with his wife.—At the Borough Court on Thursday, George Arnold, a joiner, of 78, Bostock- street, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and four children.—Mr Shearer stated that on Monday week the prisoner went home drunk. His wife had supper ready, but he was not pleased with it, and abused her, threatening to murder her. On the same evening he turned her out of the house and she was admitted at the Workhouse, and pri- soner said that he was going to drown himself, but he appeared to have changed his mind.—Mr Harbourne stated that on the 25th of the present month prisoner's wife applied for relief for herself and children. He found that she was in need, and the same day served prisoner with a notice to provide for her.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with lard labour, at which he seemed greatly surprised.-- At the earns Court Peter Baguley (32), labouter, Cockhedge Lane, who made his 78th appearance for various offences, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and two children.—On the 10th July the prisoner's wife and family were admitted to the Workhouse, and he was afterwards ad- mitted. They remained until the 25th August, prisoner being indebted to the amount of £3 12s. On Sunday night prisoner obtained leave to go search for work, and took his family out, but he brought them back on Tuesday night. It was found that he had been working on Monday, and had not given his wife a penny.—The Bench sent him to prison for thres months with hard labour.

FARLESTOWN. EARLEOTOWN ASSOC/ATION FOOTBALL CLUB. —The members of the Earlestown Association Football Club met for their first practice on their new ground at Wargrave Moss, on Saturday afternoon. Notwithstanding the oppres- sively warm weather about 20 members turned up, a- d two teams played a good practice mach. CROW-LANE CATHOLIC Orterm.—The annual sermons in aid of the schools' connected with the Crow-lane Catholic Chapel were preached on Sunday; in the morning by the Rev Father Croft, of Leicester, and in the evening by the Rev Father Kavanagh, of St Helens The services were of a very enj )yable character, and there _wore large congrega- tions.

SE...MONS AT BURTON WOOD CHURCH.—The annual school sermons were preached in Burtonwood Church on Sunday, and they were of a very successful character. The morning preacher was the Rev J Birchall, cf Nottingham, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev J Carson, of Winwick. The congregations at the services were large, and the collections, in aid of the school funds realised the sum of £l9 133 10,11 ODDFELLOWS' SUPPER AT EARLESTOWN.—The mem- bers of the Loyal Prosperity Lodge of Oddfellows, Earles- town, entertained to an excellent supper at the Ram's Head Hotel, a number of their brethren connected with the Odd- fellows' societies of Warrington. All: present thoroughly enjoyed the capital repast which was provided, and at the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr J Hands, M.N.G., of Warrington. The usual toasts were duly honoured, the meeting being enlivened by several songs. NawroN Cnuacu CHOIR Pronc.—The choir of St. Peter's Church, Newton, held their annual picnic on Satur- day afternoon, the selected spot for the day's outing bzing the city of Chester. The choir and a few friends, along with their leader, Mr Peter Fairclough, left Newton Bridge early in the day, and thoroughly enjoyed themselves in Chester and its neighbourhood. The beautifully tine weather added much to the pleasure attending the out; and everyone evi- dently enjoyed themselves to their hearts' content. Mu. GLADSTONE AND THE EARLESTOWN DEMONSTRA- TION.—The following .reply has been received from the eremier to the resolutions passed at the recent great demon- stration of South-West Lancashire Liberals at Earlestown : 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, August 26, 1884.—Dear Mr Powell,—l am directed by Mr Gladstone to thank you for your letter of the 14th iust. lie is much gratified to observe what healty support is bAng given by South-West Lancashire to the cause of reform.—Believe me, faithfully yours, G. LETESON-GOWER.—G. H. Crowden Powell, Esq."

IRE CONSERVATIVES AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.—The enthusiastic and successful demonstration in support of the Government and to protest against the rejection of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords held at Earles•own a fortnight ago has created a very jubilant feeling amongst the local Liberals, whilst it has had a correspoodin;ly de• pressing effect upon the "opposition." There have been many rumours to the effect that the Tories meant to hold a counter demonstration at Earlestown.after the style of the Pomona Palace affair, but we cannot learn that any dednite arrangements in relation to the matter have vet been come to.

ELBLEsTOwst GOOD Taltrume.—A. meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tern- piers was held in the lodge room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance, and Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. After the discussion of one or two items of business it was stated that the quarterly ses- sion of the district lodge was to be held at Widnes next week, the lodge representatives being Brothers Georga Clarke and George Warburton, sen. The programme for the night was headed "Titbits of facts and scraps," and a number of in- teresting selectiens were read by Brothers Georga Warbur- ton, John Warbut ton, John Taylor, G Clarke, J Barnard, J Thompson, Sister C E Barnard, and others. The meeting was an enjoyable one. THE VULCAN WESLEYAN'S CLOSING OF THE ECHOOL —A few weeks ago a paragraph appeared in this paper stat- ing that a " difference ' had arisen with respect to the ser- vices and conduct of the school at the Vulcan, belonging to the Vulcan Irontoundry Company, and which was rented by the Wesleyan Methodists of the district. Since then the "dispute" has not been satisfactorily settled, and we un- derstand that the Wesleyans have decided to definitely give up the building. This was decided upon last week, and on Sunday the building was closed for the first time—neither any Divine service or Sunday school being held therein. It is stated that though the Wealeyans have given up their school in that building they are not disposed to allow the scholars to become scattered about the district, as arrange- ments are being made to get the classes together in two dwelling-houses in the immediate vicinity. The greatest difficulty, however, is in relation to the congregation ; and it is hoped that steps will be taken to secure another meeting room for divine worship, in order to keen the friends to- gether. We are informed that the ctuse of the dieagree- ment has been the fact that the owners wished to use the building as a day school, which would require certain altera- tions and additions as would unfit it, in the minds of the Wesleyans, for use as a chapel and Sunday school on the Sunday. Consequently, rather than submit to the inconveniences which the proposal would entail, they decided to give up possession of the building and this course has been followed as stated.

A DISGRACEFUL SATURDAY NIGHT Row.—Whother or not the oppressively hot weather last Saturday had any- thing to do with the large number of intoxicated people pedestrians met with in the evening we will not positively say, but certain it is if reports are to be believed, the amount of drunkenness and the consequent disorderly behaviour on the part of the" am cted" individuals greatly exceeded the average so far as Saturday nights are concerned. A corres- pondent has stated that rows and disturbances throughout the town were almost innumerable, and instanced a fight in Legh-street, while in Queen-street in the afternoon, a man employed at the Sugar Works had a quarrel with two or three Irishmen, and as a result got knocked down and " well kicked in the bargain." The cry of "police," it is stated, only drew off the assailants. But the most alarming dis- turbance occurred nen. Bridge-street about half-past eleven at night. It appears that a well-known visitor at the police court, whose name is synonymous with "Stone," had some words with a fellow-lodger in the house where they resided. At the hour mentioned the inhabitants of the neighbourhood were startled by hearing shouts and screams, and many rushed to the doors of their houses. An eye-witness of the affair states that "Stone" was knocked to the ground by his opponent, and as he lay there the latter violently kicked him on the head with his boot. "Stone" was momentarily stunned, and tke kick caused a deep gash from which blood flowed profusely. One or two men then interfered and pul- led "Stone's" opponent away, immediately after which a police sergeant and two constables appeared on the scene. " Stone " was pic'md up and carried into a neighbour's house, where it was seen that he Lad received an ugly wound. His head, face, neck, and a part of his body were covered with blood, but no sooner had be been washed and otherwise attended to than the poor fellow again expressed his willingness to fight anybody or anything. He would not enter his lodgings, and four men at last seized him and carried him into the house. On the following day " Stone " bore full evidence of the treatment he had received on the previous evening.

CANAL BOAT Paoszarnos. Messrs Charles Perks and Son, Burton-on-Trent, were summoned a second time, the case having previously been dismissed, for being the owners of a canal boat which had not been registered. Mr Browne, Warrington, said he appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority. On the 12th July, Mr Farrington, inspector for the Sanitary Authority, saw the canal beat named "Hawk" near Preston Brook, and seeing that it had not been registered he asked the man in charge of it, named Thomas Ashley, to whom it belonged. To this Ashley replied that it belonged to Charles Perks and Son.—lnspector Farrington gave evidence to this effect, and it was stated by Luke Jones, a clerk on the Bridgewater Canal, at Preston Brook, that he had also been informed by Ashley that the boat belonged to the defendants.—George Shipley, a partner in the defendants' firm, said that they ware not the owners of the boat at all and knew nothing about it. Their agents in different parts of the country were in the habit of hiring persons to convey goods by boat, but they had nothing to do with the boats themselves —The Bench were of opinion that there was no evidence, whatever to show that he defendants were at all responsi- ble for the boat, and the Chairman, addressing Inspector Farrington, said he could not expect that they were going to simply take his word. They must have proof. All that confusion had been caused by the bad way in which he had got. up the case. He (the chairman) had seen some most impertinent and uncalled for remarks which the in- spector had made to the Sanitary Authority with regard to that case. He hoped the press would take notice of these remarks. The case was then dismissed, and, on the appli- c Won of Mr Shipley be was allowed 10s as expenses. UNLAWFUL REMOVAL OF A. He told him that he had better take it biciE again or he would be summoned, but Wirrall replied that Mr Mackey had told him to take the pig to Wilderspool and take it he would —Mr Mackey mentioned that he had not been aware that the declaration was necessary, and hesadded that he had not known that Wirrall was warned by a police- man to take the animal back or be should have been very angry with him for not doing so.—Mr Mackey' was fined IS and ordered to pay the costs of the summonses. RUNCORN v. WooLrox.—Played at Woolton on Saturday. Winning the toss, the home team elected to bat, on a hard wicket, to the bowling of Wood and Gatley. The first three wickets fell rapidly for six runs, but 28 were put on beforo the fall of the fourth, and that was further increased to 81 for the sixth. Tsm WAY TO NV/CALM—The way to wealth hi Al plail as the way to market. It depends chiefly on two words. industry and frugality—that is waste neither time not money, but make the best use of both. Without industry veith them (reryttet notning tse, r... • . , -- Ika-rrma.—There is one sin which, it soma to nuf; is everywhere and by everybody under-estimateds tolerated with undue tolerance, and quite too much ovqrlooked in our valuation of character. It is the sin of fretting. He who frets is never the one who mends. And Vk hen the fretter is one who is beloved, whose nearness of relation to us makes his fretting at the weather seem almost like a personal reproach to us, then the misery of it becomes indeed insupportable. Most men call fretting a minor fault—a foible, and not e. vice. There is hardly any vice except drunkenness, which can so utterly destroy the peace, the happiness of a home.—H. H.

THE GREAT LESSON OF HU3fAN LlFE.—When the body and mind are properly fed and kept in working order, and recreation is adjusted to work and food to effort, day by day, little need is found for a dry dock into which, at the returning voyage of each year, the shattered hulk roust be hauled for repairs. This is really the great lesson of human life, so far as our physical natures are concerned—day by day our 'daily bread and day by day our daily care. The maintenance of health is the adjustment of every part of one's self to every other part—an adjustment in which we have marvel- lously the help of nature, if only we come to understand ourselves, and have our bodies under the control of oun wills and conscience.

CHTLDREN'S QUESTIONS.—It is well to answer these troublesome little questions, even if they do try the patience a little. Chilchen hunger after new things and new ideas. They will learn with pleasure facts of history, or of science from the lips of parents or teachers, which would seem like drudgery if learned by rote from books, and they take great delight in listening to the conversa- tion of intelligent people; therefore they should be allowed to remain in the drawing-room or the library, if they will not interrupt the conversation, and have been taught to conduct themselves properly. Many a man owes his success in life to the conversations he has listened to in his father's home, when his parents had not the least idea lie was old enough to take any interest in what interested them; but his young mind was drink- ing in draughts of wisdom which were of incalculable benefit to him.

KNOWLEDGE WORTH HAVING.—The knowledge which we crave and work for, which we look for and fine, which we think out and dig out for ourselves, which we rejoice in as in a newly-found treasure—that is the know- ledge, be it small or great, that is worth having. It is like the food for which we hunger—it gives us fresh power and fuller life. It matters far less even what this knowledge is than the way in which it was gained. The most systematic and well-prepared course of study worried through by a student whose only care is that he may get his diploma is of far less value to him or to the world than the vital thought of the young mechanic who, anxious to master the secrets of his trade, patiently studies its details, discovers its principles, and infuses into it his own fresh and living force, perhaps in the form of some new invention, or perhaps in a more skilful tench or a more delicate finish than it has yet received..

FORETITOUGHT.—How many times in the year the mis- tress of the house needs to be reminded of the admoni- tion of a wise woman : "Drive your work, but do not let your work drive you !" That is, plan it all out, so that each day's work will clear something from your way. Do not let work accumulute until you live under a weight of uneasiness and of hurry which is destructive of comfort. Deliberate and calm thought will help you. A strong belief in a future will help you—that is on a cold day do not allow yourelf to believe that the boys will nut need cotton bhmses in July and August, or that you can get along without any summer clothes. And, on the other hand, cherish the thought that it is of consequence that the wo.)llen stockings and wrappers are laid away clean and whole for use in a coming December. There are women who need to be reminded that to-day is not all of time.--Now York Evaning Post.

WIFE AND MornEa.—Keeping her house well, and making the little world over which she rules happy, faithful, beautiful, the womanly woman has neither time nor inclination of the life out-of-door glaring publicity which many of the sect affect. What ambition she has goes to the fame and well-being of her husband and to the future success of her sons. She feels that it is a far more blessed thing to be the wife and mother of her6es than a "personage" on her own account, and that the glory cast by the man whose name she bears is bi*.zliter aud more sufficing than any with which she is able to elllround her own name. She does not want to make speeches on platforms, to see her name in the newspapers, to be a leader of movements, to talk arrant nonsense on difficult subjects; but she helps her husband in his study, in his laboratory; and many a man has owed as much of his fame and success to his w ife's quiet and silent aid as he has owed to his own native power.

A GOOD Fiturr-liousE.—An Illinois horticulturist last year constructed a fruit-house which proved so successful that it is now being taken as a model throughout the country. It is designed on the simplest scientific princi- ples, and costs very little. The walls are double, being composed of two rows of wooden posts boarded within and without. The intervening space, two and a half feet wide, is packed as closely as possible with straw. Above are two sets . of rafters three feet apart, with boards on their upper sides and with straw completely filling the space between them. Over all is a cheap beard roof. Inside, we are told, the temperature remains approximately the same the whole year round. When the thermometer ia "perspiring " at 98deg, in the shade, the fruit-house appears by contrast like an ice-cellar. In the depth of winter the spirited proprietor wades through the snow to select fruit for tlie market, and finds the fragrant atmos- phere inside "agreeably warm " and his app4s "as sound as when taken off the trees months before."

USING LONG AND SHORT WORDS.—The grandest thoughts in any literature are expre sed in few and well- chosen words, and, as a rule, the wan of ideas i more simple in his language than he who has no originality, and relies on others for thoughts, which I e then proceeds to put into his own expressions. The 'man of ideas which are capable of standing alone is usually careless about the „appearance his ideas may make, just as the rich man is content to dress more plainly than his poorer neighbours, lecause he and everybody else knows he is rich; his wealth speaks for itself, and he has no need to put any considerab!e part of it on his back, 'while his poor neighbour is sometimes obliged .to dress better than he can afford to do, for fear acme one may think him poorer than he realiy is. It is also often noticed that men of ideas hesitate in their speech more than do those who have few ideas and few words to easpress them in. The reason is evident. Men of a large vocabulary will pick and choose in their words in order to get the word that will best do the work expected of it. If this one will not answer, it will be taken out and another substituted, while the man of a limited vocabu- lary and few ideas will never be at a loss, for the simple reason that he has but the one set of ideas and the one set of words to express them. The words are easily fitted to the ideas and the work is done.
YOU OR If we could know Which of us, darling, would be first to go, Who would be first to breast the swelling tide, And step alone upon the other side— If we could know

If it were you, Should I walk softly, keeping death in view Should I my love to you more oft express? Or should I grieve you, darling, any less— If it were you? If it were I, Should I improve the moments slipping by? Should I more closeiy follow God's great plan, Be filled with sweeter charity to mil— li it were I? • If we could know! We cannot, darling; and better so. I -hould forget, just as I do to-day. And walk along the samo old stumbling way— If I could know. I would not know Which of us, darling, will•be the first to go. only wish the space may not be long Between the parting and the greeting song • But when, or where, or how we're called to go- I would not know.

OLD-FASHIONED MOTHERS. ' Thank God, some ot us have had old-fashioned mothers. Not a woman of the period, .enamelled and painted, with her great chignon, her culls and bustle, whose white, jewelled hands never felt the clasp of baby-fingers, but a dear old-fashioned, sweet-voiced mother, with eyes in whose clear depths the love-light shone, and brown bait just threaded with silver, lying smooth upon her faded cheek. Those dear bands, worn with toit,' gently guided our tottering stops in child- hood, and smoothed our pillow in sickness, ever reaching outto us in yearning tendernesss. Blessed is the memory of an old-fashioned mother. It floats now to us like the beautiful perfume from some wooded blossoms. The music of other voices may be lost, but the entrancing memory of hers will echo in our souls for ever. Other faces may fade away and be forgotten, but hers will shine on. When in the fitful pauses of business life our feet wander back to the old homestead and, crossing the well-worn threshold, stand once more in the room so hallowed by her presence, how the feeling of childhood, innocence, and dependence comes over us, and we kneel down in the molten sunshine streaming through the open window—just where, long years ago, we knelt by our mother's knee, lisping "Our Father." How many times when the tempter lured us on has the memory of those sacred hours, that mother's words, her faith and prayers saved us from plunging into the deep abyss of sin. Years have tilled great drifts between her and us, but they have bidden from our sight the ilerY of bee pure, unselfish Itivo•
