Ha EXPRRIMEMID.—He was a bashful wooer, but there was a certain manliness about him which indicated that he only needed a little encouragement to let himself out. She saw this and she resolved on a policy of encouragement. "Do you believe these stories in the fanny papers," she asked, "about the willingness of young ladies to be kissed ?" " I—l—really can't say,' he replied. "They may bo tree." Then, gathering courage, he added: "I hope they are tree," and he drew closer to her. "It seems to me," she said, "that there is only one way in which a young man can dis- cover whether they are true or not." "And what way is that ?" he asked. There was a brief pause. Then with a far-away look in her eyes, she answered: "By experiment- ing when he has the opportunity." He experimented. ESIENTIFIC EXPERIMENT. "HOW IT'S DONE." "And now, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, I will show you a curious experiment. I carefully exhaust the air in the right-hand chamber of this vessel, and then you will see these two suspended weights exactly counterbalance each other, although the one is twice as heavy as the other, thus reversing the ordinary laws of gravitation!' lint something went wrong; and, while the small weight flew upwards, the big one came down with a crash, and an audible titter went round the hall as the assemblage dispersed. The young lec- turer turned to a white-haired sage who had been seated 'close to the table—" Professor, you know the theory is true, for you taught it me, and you have seen me successfully perform that exptriment in your own laboratory. Then how do you account for this mishap ?" "My dear boy," replied the scientific stir, "when you have had my experience, you will know that experiments are not to be trusted. The best behaved in the laboratory seem to take a pleasure in going wrong before an audience." "But I have seen you do that particular one in public at the Royal Institution and other places a dozen times without the slightest hitch," said the youth. " Yes," admitted the old gentleman, with a curious twinkle in his eye; "but then, you see, I invariably took a little precaution against accidents. I used always to tie up the heavy weight with a little bit of string." SHOOTING A EIIRGLAR.—Pott's clock got out of order one day I cot winter and began to strike wrong. That was the cause of the fearful excitement at his house on a certain night. They were all in bed sound asleep at midnight, when the clock suddenly struck five. The new hired girl, hap- pening to wake just as it began, heard it, and bounced out of bed under the impression that morning had come. And as it is dark at 5 a.m. just at that season, she did not perceive her mistake, but went down into the kitchen and began to get breakfast. While she was bustling about in a pretty lively manner, Potts happened to wake, and he heard the noise. He opened his room door cautiously and crept softly to the head of the stairs to listen. He could distinctly hear some one moving about the kitchen and dining-room and apparently packing up the china. Accordingly, he went back to his room and woke Mrs. Potts, and gave her orders to spring the rattle out of the front window the moment she heard his gun go off. Then Potts seized his fowlingpiece ; and going down to the dining-room door, where he could hear the burgulars at work, he cocked his gun, aimed it, pushed the door open with the muzzle and fired. Instantly Mrs. Potts sprang the rattle, and before Potts could pick up the lacerated hired girl the front door was burst open by two policemen, who came into the dining-room Seeing Potts with a gun, and a bleeding woman on the floor, they imagined that murder had been committed, and one of them trotted Potts off to the station-house, while the ether re. mained to investigate things. Just then the clock struck six. An explanation ensued from the girl, who only had a few bird-shot in her leg, and the policeman left to bring Potts home. He arrived at about three in the morning, just as the clock was striking eight. When the situation was unfolded to him, his first action was to jam the butt of his gun through the clock, whereupon it immediately struck two hundred and forty-three, and then Potts pitched it over tate feline. He has a new cloak now, and things are working better,--Elbow Boom. STIMSON.— the Rev. Mr. Stimson, an aged Kansas parson, owned a good horse, but the keeping of the beast was a drain on his pocket; and he PHU in the habit of dropping a hint to his parishioners once in a while that a little hay would be acceptable. One day a church member asked him to bring Mrs. Stimson to dinner. "Certainly," said Sampson; "and, as it's haying-time, I guess I'll put souse hay on the waggon when Igo back home." "All right," replied the church member, "but bring a one-horse waggon." Stimson took his wife to dinner in. a waggon with an ample arrangement at the back, that would hold a haystack. "See here," said the parishioner, as he'helped Mrs. Stimson out of the waggon, "you said you were going to bring a one-horse waggon, and now you've appeired with the most capacious hay apparatus I ever saw." Oh, I've brought the one-horse waggon," said Samson ; "but that's a twodmrse hay apparatus!' He drove away after dinner with twenty-two hundred pounds of hay. Mr. -timson was the first to use gospel tents in the West. He put them up himself. A man who passed him 005 morning as he was hard at work on his tent called to

him in a loud voice, " Halloa there! Are you going to have a circus ?" "Yes," said the parson, continuing his work without looking up; "and I'm looking for a baboon. Don't you want to hire yourself to me ?" The parson was chap- lain in the Ninth New York Cavalry during the war- The colonel was fond of leading the soldiers through deep puddles at the regular drill, and the chaplain one day rode around a puddle, and thereby fell out of the regular order. The colonel noticed it, and at the close of the drill, when the officers came together, said, with a sneer, "If Chaplain Stimson is afraid to ride through muddy water for fear of soiling his clothing, I will carry him across the puddles my- self." "Thank you," the chaplain said ; " out, as the Go- vernment provides horses, I don't see any reason why I should ride on a jackass."

div.head: VIOLENT ASSAULTSA_WARRINGTON
div.p: VIOLENT ASSAULTSA_WARRINGTON
POLICEMEN.

-----.. Several cases of assaults on policemen were heard at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Munelay.—James Loftus, a labourer, of Percival's-fold, was charged with be- ing drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Johustone and P.S. Jones, in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday evening. The prisoner kicked Johnstone twice on the leg and once on the thigh, and was taken into custody with great difficulty. It was his 21st appearance, and he was fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness and 20s and costs for the assault, or a month.--Michael Callaghan (19),a labourer, of Dohnan's lane, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in But- termarket-street, on the same evening, and with assaulting P.C. Smith by striking him on the head with a half-gallon stone bottle. As the constable was taking a prisoner into custody Callaghan followed and attempted to incite the crowd to violence. The constable was obliged to let his pri- soner go and secure Callaghan, who then " smashed" the bottle by striking Smith on the head with it. The latter would no doubt have been seriously injured but for the pro- tection afforded by his helmet.—Prisoner, who made his 11th appearance, was sent to goal for two months' with hard labour --Martin Griffin was charged with disorderly con- duct on Saturday in Winwick-street, and with assaulting P.C.'s Cheney and Smith. Cheney saw the prisoner kicking a "handful of a man," who was on the ground and inter- fered. Prisoner then knocked him down and kicked him. Smith, who came to the assistance of his comrade, was also assaulted.—Pr leaner was committed for two months, and the same punishment was meted to John Kearns, a compaeion of the last prisoner, who was seen to kick Smith when he and Cheney were taking Griffin to the police station.--The Borough Magistrates, on Tuesday, investigated another serious case of assault.—Two brothers named William and Michael Connor, one a fish hawker and the other a labourer,l living in Cockhedge-lane, were brought up on various charges. William was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of Thomas Halton, the Carriers Arms, Buttermarket street, and with refusing to quit, with being drunk in the street and breaking windows, and also with violently assaulting P.C.'s Hennessey and Smith whilst in the execution of their duty. Michael was charged with as- saulting P.C.'s Hennessey and Smith, Inspector Berry, and a civilian named John McEvoy, who was assist- ing the police.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the pri- soners.—P.C. Hennessey stated that at 10-30 on Monday morning he was called to the Corriere' Arms to eject the two defendants. At the request of the manager witness asked them to leave the house, but they refused and he had to put them into the street forcibly. He cautioned William Connor to go away several times and at last had to take him into custody. He (William) then assaulted witness with his hands and feet and the other prisoner also assaulted him, topping" him with his head and kicking him. At the call of witness a man named McEvoy came to his assistance and received a blow on the nose that knocked him down. PC. Smith then came on the scene. Witness was elm- pelled to draw his staff and use it freely. It took seven or eight persons to take the prisoners to the station. When there one of them kicked and severely assaulted Inspector Berry. Witness bad been off duty since the assault and felt very unwell. Cross-examined: We were a long time en- gaged before there was a staff used. Michael was trying to get his brother away. Michael was sober, but William was drunk.—During the cross-examination Mr Davies, apparently referring to a sotto voce remark of the Chief Constable (Mr Hunt), said be came there as a solicilor to do his duty and would not have it said that he was taking advantage. He asked Mr Hunt to say publicly in what way he was taking advantage. He bad never heard of such a thing —Coun- cillor Monies said that the Bench had nothing to do with what had passed privately. They were there to try the case.—Mr Davies: You have no right to sit there without taking notice of your own officer. I want to know in what way I have taken advantage. I shall be glad to throw up the brief if I have vexed you or anyone else. If the magistrates will not take notice of it it is hard lines for a solicitor.—Councillor Monks: We know nothing about it.— Mr Davies: Because you will not take any notice. It is a court of justice and it should have your consideration.— Evidence was then continued, and George Henderson, the manager, deposed to obtaining the assistance of the police to get the prisoners out of the house.—William Rogers, an ex-P.C., said that be was going down Buttermarket-street with P.C. Phillips when he saw Henneeey holding ens of the prisoners.. Michael Connor struck Hennessey and Wil- liam struck him (Hennessey) and knocked his head through a shop window.—Joseph Waterhouse said that he saw Michael kick and strike Hennessey severely and that he also saw William strike the officer.—P.C. Phillips also proved witnessing the assault. Inspector Berry said that when at the police station Michael Connor made a rush at him and he (witness) struck him across the arm with his cane. They then put William on the ground, and Michael came to close quarters and struck witness a violent blow in front of the left ear, which had been very painful since. A severe up-and-down strug- gle on the floor followed, and the wrestling continued for about five minutes. The necktie of one of the prisoners be- came so tightened that it had to be cut off afterwards.— P.C.Smith said that he received several kicks from the pri- soner William. They had to fight all the way to the police station.—John McEvoy deposed to being knocked down and kicked on going to the assistance of the police.—Mr. Davies, before calling witnesses for the defence, said that if he bad done anything that was wrong be must apologise, although he did not know that he had taken any advantage at all. He had told Mr. Hunt that if it was obnoxious to his feelings three he should take the case he would give it up.—Councillor Monks: We have not said you have taken advantage —Mr. Hunt: What I said to you I said to you, and not to the Court.—Councillor Broadbent: There have been no remarks derogatory to you that have come within our hearing.—Mr. Hunt: I was very near saying something. —Mr. Davies: I will not have these insinuations. You have to keep Mr. Hunt in order, and he to keep'all the borough in order. Continuing, Mr. Davies addressed the Bench for the defence. The history of the case was that the two brothers went to the Corriere' Arms, and William, whom he admitted was drunk, asked for liquor, which was refused. Michael tried to persuade his brother to leave before the police came on the scene at all, and, as he was instructed, the two did go out before the police arrived, and in that case they should have been allowed to go home. He then called witnesses for the defence, one of whom, Ann Jordan, said that Hennessey struck the first blow with his staff —Coun- cillor Monks said that after properly considering the case they were of opinion it was clearly proved. The prisoners would go to prison for six months with hard labour.—The Bench complimented the men who had given assistance to the borough police, viz., P.C. Phillips, Lancashire County Police, ex-Constable Rogers, late of the County Police, and John Mavoy.—Councillor Broadbent remarked that if the police were liable to that kind of desperate resistance they would require an army of a hundred constables.--At the Borough Court, on Thursday, a man named Samuel Crosby was brought up charged with being drunk and disorderly in Market-street on the previous evening and with assaulting P.C. Pennington, who stated that he was in the Market- place when he noticed the prisoner, who was drunk, using bad language to a stall-keeper. Witness took him into custody, whereupon prisoner kicked him in the stomach and on the legs. Mr. Place, market inspector, rendered assis- tance, and prisoner was taken to the station.—He was now sent to prison for fourteen days for each offence.

GUILD DINNER AT PEARLRY Cu°Ss.—The members of the Guild of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Joseph, held their annual dinner at the Fleece Hotel, on Saturday. About 60 persons sat down to an excellent repast, after which the Rev Father Byrne, chaplain of the guild, presided. The statement of accounts showed a balance of £54 3s 6,1 in band after the year's expenditure; the total worth of the guild being £306 7s SI. The toasts of " His Holiness Lee XIII," "The Queen and the Royal Family," were given by the chairman and duly honoured ; after which Mr Robin (vice-president), gave the toast of the evening,. The health of the president, officers, and members of the guild." In doing so he remarked that the officers had done their duty 30 well as to prevent a single murmer, and be appealed to the members to attend more regularly the meetings of the guild as well as the services of their church.—Mr T Chisnell (president) responded. Mr Prescott gave "The Bishop and Clergy of the diocese" and the rev chairman duly acknow- ledged the compliment. The proceedings were interspersed with songs by klees-s Hobin, James Clare, Joseph Barton, J H Barton, die; and the meeting, which was very enjoy- able, concluded with thanks to the host and hostess for the I excellent dinner.

THE ROYAL NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. A special general meeting of the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was held on Thursday at the show ground, Stock- port, to receive the judges' awards of prizes for the best cul- tivated farms, and for clover and grass crops. Mr G C Hale, agent to Lord Derby, presided, and there were present amongst others the secretary, Mr T Rigby (Liberal candi- date for Mid-Cheshire), Messrs John White, Warrington ; James Warburton, Dallam ; and Win. Darbyshire, Warring- ton Mr J W Kimber, in his report to the council on the best cultivated farms, said that the claimants to the farm prizes were much fewer than in the last two years. This might be attributed to some extent to the exceptional dry- ness of the season, which in eome districts had seriously in- terfered with theplanting of spring crops and their after- growth. The competition had been exceedingly close in several cases. There was no entry in the first class, which was for a farm of 150 acres and upwards. The following were the results in regard to other classes :—Best arable farm above 80 acres and under 150, Mr James Boardman, Kenyon Hall, Croft, near Warrington ; best arable farm above 40 and less than 80 acres, Mr Gilbert Marsh, Croft. Best managed dairy or stock farm of 150 acres and upwards, where the management was most successfully directed to the production of milk, butter, or cheese, or of butchers' meat, Mr Joseph Robinson, Lee Green Hall, near Warring- ton. Best managed stock breeding farm of 100 acres and upwards, where the management is principally and most successfully directed to the breeding and rear- ing of farm stock, cattle, sheep, horses, and pigs, Mr George Ashburner, Low-hill, Kirby. Best managed farm of 150 acres and upwards: Mr Alfred Alderley, Barlow-hall, Choriton-cum Hardy, Manchester. Beat managed farm above SO acres and under 150: Mr Joseph Boardman, Croft. Best ditto, not less than 40 and not above 80 acres: Mr Gil- bert Marsh, Croft. As to the clover and grass seeds compe- tition, Mr Forrester reported that the following were the awards :—Best clover for grass seeds of thesecond year's lay, most suitable for making into hay, Mr W Johnson, Hale- bank; for the best of the third year's lay for mowing or pas- ture, Mr K J Owen, Halewood; for the best pasture of the fourth, fifth, or sixth years' growth after laying down with permanent grass seeds, Mr Richard Hockton, Ashley, Altrin- diem ; for the best old pasture of not less than seven years' lay and upwards, Mr Thomas Parton, Chorlton, Nantwich. Mr Rigby, the secretary, referring to the show next week, stated that the entries were large in every class but that of sheep. Dairy cattle were especially numerous. and he an- ticipated that the mulch cows would be of a very high class. A luncheon was subsequently partaken of, at which the chair was again occupied by Mr. Hale. The Chairman pro- posed the toast, "Mayor of Stockport and Local Committee," and paid a high compliment to those gentlemen and their admirable arrangements. The toast of the "Railway Com- panies," who, it is understood, are making every arrange- ment for the convenience of the show, was also drunk. Mr R Lansdale having proposed "The Secretary," a toast which was cordially honoured, Mr Rigby, in responding, said that the society came to a town like Stockport not simply to gain the admission money, though that was a mat- ter of some importance if they were to continue their efforts successfully, but also to disseminate information and to stimulate and to interest, and, if possible, to affect an im- provement in the sate of agriculture in the district. Other toast followed.

SUDDEN DEATIIS OF WOMEN.—On Friday Mr Brig- house held an inquest at the Ship Hotel, St Helens, respect- ing the death of Ann Cullen, single woman, twenty-eight years of age, who lived with her mother at 15, Canal Bank East. Deceased had been subject to fits, the last occurring twelve months before her death. On Wednesday morning ' ahe complained of pain in the stomach, and her mother gave her some hot water and ginger. She then went to work, leaving deceased in bed. On reaching home at half-past six she found the lifeless body of her daughter in the kitchen— half on the floor and half on a chair. Her hands were clenched, and her face black. Deceased was seen by a Mrs Pickavance about half-past three in the afternoon, and she then said she was ill.—The Coroner said it seemed hard that the deceased should be left in the house, ill as she was, and nobody to do anything for her.—Police-constable Mas- sey said deceased was given to drink and a woman of lobse habits, and had been committed.—Tbe Coroner said be understood the police had made inquiries, and there was no suspicion of foul play.—The jury returned a verdict that death was the result of n ttural causes.--An inquest was held at the Lingholme Hotel, on Thursday night, on the body of Barbara Varley, seventy-four years of age, of 12, Boundary-road, St Helens. Deceased was found dead at the toot of the stairs at a quaiter past eleven on Monday night. It was stated in evidence that she was subject to giddiness, and had probably fallen downstairs, although her son, who was in bed at the time, heard nothing of the occurreoce.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was re- • turned.

THE REV. E. C. E. CARLETON AND FAIR TRADE. Sir,—Sorne months ace, I, along with several others, re- vival a note from the Rev E C E Carleton in which he put ssveral luestions respecting Fair Trade and Free Trade. The note also contained an intimation that the rev gentle- man would, as so,n as possible, arrange for a small informal meeting at which this question coald be talked over. I have heard no more about the matter, at which I am sur- p.ised. The rev gentleman, was, lam su-e, in earnest to do a naricnal good. If he thought that the term' Fair Trade" c-mtainecl something that Free Traders were overlooking all *mom to him for bringing it forward. But if since tkat time he has become convinced that he was making a mlstake, who there is still the same reason to r.cknowledge 21q r n '2. Possibly he is still labouring under the Fair T ade delusion. If so, I wish to direct his attention to an article that appears in the North American Review upon the 'evils of the tariff system," in which these words occur: With double the producing power of England we have net half her opportunity to use our wealth. We are merely provincial, our commerce is dwarfed, and our great merchants have disappeared." Perhaps Mr Carleton will 'kindly give the public the benefit of his opinion on these 'important words. Mr Wells, tl.:e writer referred to, is ef opinion that unless these tariffs are cleared out of the American merchant's way he can never enter the mukets of the world. I ask, when this is done, what becomes of the jglish merchants' market ?—Yours, &c, WHITIIAM.

BENEFIT SOCIETIES AND THE RELIEF OF THE POOR. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space in your valuable paper for the following, which may be of use to members of frield!r ocieties in this district? With regard to the with- drawal.of Jchn Southward's outdoor relief which I brought before the l'rescot Board of Guardians some weeks ago, I base recently received a communicalon from the Local G wernmmt Board contaieing these woids—" The Beard are precluded from interfering with the discretion of the Guardians of the Prescot Union as regards the withho:ding of relief in any particular ; " and also a printed circular, data January sth, 1870, in which occurs the f,llowing paragra.ph:—" In the opinion of the Board it would not be expedient to administer poor rates which are levied from all classes down to those on the very verge of destitution, in such a manner as to cause them to be recognised by the work- ing c'asses of the country as a provision substituted by the law of the land for that which, in absence of such a system, they would be willing to provide for themselves and their families, through the medium of b..nefit societies. The Board regard the prosperity and extension of these Benefit Societies as a matter of extreme import:lnes., and would be anxious to encourage their estab- lishment by all legitimate means. But the board as at pre- sent advised, believe that this encouragement could not safcly be given by allowing the Poor Rate to be treated as a subeidiary fund. The board cannot shut their eyes to the Let that the only safe basis on which the system of Benefit Societies can rest, under Vas present system of the legal right to relief, it is, that they afford the means of providing, in times of distress or disability, a more eligible, respectable, and liberal maintenance than that supplied under the Poor Law, and they should still be regarded as a mode of avoid- ing the degradation of parish support, rather than as con- ferring a title by which a claim to such support may be en- tab! lobed even beyond the line of actual destitution." If the Guardians, then. are determined to act on the lines of of the foregoing it will be impossible to administer our Be- nevolent Funds, as in many instances, nay I may say, all the applicants for asaistace are already in receipt of on!•.-dsor relief. As in the above else no out-door relief can be granted, because Southward lain rec ipt of the magnificent income of fourpeace per day, and one penny per week ; pocket money, as reduced sick pay for his lodge. It seems strange that at one time this old man was considered eligible for, or rather worthy of receiving parochial relief (3s per week), but because the Oddfellows of this district, MU, made him a grant of £lO, to purchase bed clothing,..E e, he is, now in his 82ed year, not entitled to even that small pittance. Anyone, then, who has led a peripatetic life, prey- ing on Society, becoming old and dependant, " settle)" in a Union and claims and obtains his relief without a murmur ; but another who has been prudent and thr;fty and has paid his poor rates during a respectable manhood has no claim to any such assistance.—l am, 8:e, EDWARD FIDLER, ri(11, (IS, M U. Boundary-road, St. Helens, August 28th, 1884.

Sr. HELENS TRAMWAYS COMPANY.—SUaGESTED I USE 017 STEAM. The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the St II -lens and District Tramways Company woo held at the Riven Hotel, Raven-street, on Thursday. The chairman of the company, Mr. William Busby. oi ii.a7ton Park, near Liverpool, occupied the chair.—The fol- lovring report of the directors for the half - year ending 30th June last was submitted : " The balance of revenue account for the half year is £2OO 134 lOil. and the amount brought for yard from last half year £285 2s 73, making £485 16s sd, out of which the directors have paid the interest on the mortgage debentures amounting to £428 93 23, leaving a balance of .£57 7s 31 to be carried forward to next half year. The directors reg et that they have not itatter results to present to the shareholders, and they are strengthened in their opinion that in order to make the company a dividend earning one, it is necess ry that steam be substituted for horse power; they are quite satisfied that such an alteration would be of immense advanta!,,e, more especially as the traffic is of such a fluctuating character."— The Chairman remarked that the rolliny stock of the com- pany as well an the permanent way were in good order, but unfortunately they had lost four horses during the half year. The horses on the whole, however, were in good trim. As regardA the receipts, there was an increase of £59 Ils fld, while as far as the expmdittare went there was also a slight increase, but he thought the exnenditure had been conducted on favourable conditiona. With regard to the fact of there being no dividend, they v.muld of course be disappointed. Ile (the chairman) thought the only mods to be adapted in order to make the company a dividend-paying company was to adopt the use of steam, especially on those lines where the gradients were very steep. The lines were so constructed as to be quite capable of bearing the wear and tear of steam traction. He had areat ploasure in moving the adoption of the renort and balance sheet.—Mr C 'Spencely (t'rescot) seconded the motion.—Mr Bowden expressed the opinion that the wreking exweases of the company wero too high. He alluded to the items for wages, directors' fees, secretary's salary, and auditors' fees, and said be thought there might be a redue.tion in that respect. —The Chair- man Said he did not think the wages were excessive. —The motion th it th 3 repot and balance sheet be adopted was then carried unanimously. A discussion subsequently arose on the proposed substitution of steam, and the their- min stated a definite decesion upon the queeion rested with the annual meeting It remained with the shareholders to say whether or not they would raise the money wanted—A. Shareholder asked what was the cost per mile in working expenses 2—The Secretary replied about 83.—The Share- holder : How does that compare with steam ?—The Secre- tary said the engine makers professed the working expenses would he reduced to 31 and even to 211 per mile.—A hearty -vote of thanks was afterwards passed to the Chairman, and the latter in responding said he would take steps to ascer- tain the feeling of the shareholders upon the question they had been discussing at that meeting.-Thu meeting then concluded.

TEIE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. Sir,—As the Manchester Ship Canal Bill is again thrown ont, and public meetings are being held and different locali- ties surveyed for the promotion of another scheme more suitable, and one that will not interfere with the estuary of the Mersey so much as the other schemes have done, it might not ha out of place to make a few remarks On the schemes now being talked about, that is, one starting in at Gaston. and coming out again at Ditton Iron Works; then taking the Lancashire side and through the Runcorn B:idge ; and the other scheme following the Cheshire side. I do not aspire to be a professional in such an undertaking, but simply to alittle personal knowledge of the river from Weston Paint. to Stanley House, and the Frodsham Score and marsh. I don't think it requires much engineering skill Co point out that the Cheshire side of the river is preferable to the Lancaebire side for several reasons. It appears to me that the cost of cutting a canal from Garston to Ditton Iron Works would be very great. In the first place the land it would have to pass through is valuable and would require a large amount of capital. The next thing would be the cutting, which, I believe, at the Garston end would be something like 85 to 90 feet deep before a sufficient depth of water could be got Into the canal. Such a cutting would re- quire an enormous amount of labour, and, of coarse, ex- pense. These two points must make a heavy item for con- sit oration of the Lancashire scheme' besides the roads and other rights that must be considered. Now to look at the Cheshire side, which also has its dis- advantage, that of being a long way round ; otherwise the expenso must be trifling in comparison with the Lancashire scheme, as there is neither a railway nor a high road on the whole route. Suppose the canal was started so as to empty itself below Eastham into deep water, where large ships might go in or out at any state of the tide? It might be opposed by those having interests on the Cheshire side. I should say by giving those so interested the Use of the canal at any time (whereas now they can only work by tt • tide), it would be of great advantage to them to have tie anal made. Then following up the Cheshire side by Elles- more Port, through Stanley Point, and under Ince (where formerly there was a good deep which is now tilled up; then striking across for the powder magazine on Ince Marsh and coming along behind Frodsham Score Cop for some distance towards the month of the Weaver. Here it might not be out of place to make a dock, on what is now called the big bank, for the salt trade, and Also for the conveyance of produce from Frodsham and dis- trict, for Manchester and other places, a matter in which tl e railway company have now the monopoly of the entire dis- trict. From thence to Weston Point, and so on to Runcorn bridge. The greatest disadvantage as before stated is the distance ; but the advantages seem to be far prefe.able. For instance, the land canal would go through en the Cheshire side is of little value in comparison to that on the Lanca- shire side, and again the cutting instead of being 80 to 90ft deep, would, I should think, on the Cheshire side, nowhere exceed 20 feet, and in some places not that, to obtain a sufficient supply of water, which must save an enormous amount of labour. Then again the water which empties it- self into the river in various places and in small quanti- ties on the Cheshire side, when collected together in one -volume, must have a benelcial effect upon the bar outside Liverpool by the scour that must consequently

be going on by the outfhw of water collected by the canal in its course, and also by the greater amount of water that must flow in and out of the canal each tide. Now there is little water and consequently no sewer, so that I should think a canal so made would be an advan- tage instead of an injury to Liverpool, by helping to keep open its water course and interfering little or none with the estuary of the river itself. In conclusion I may say that I hope the promoters will not b 3 long before they have a thoroughly good scheme in hand, and that we shall scon have the pleasure of seeing large ships passing up the canal to Warrington and Manchester. —Yours, &c, A FROD3IIAMITE. Main-street, August 21st, 1884.

TttE WARRING/TON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Sir,—After reading your repott of the Guardians' meet- ing at Warrington, on the 20th instant, I am completely shocked at the inconsistency of ono of our Newton Guar- dians. The gentleman in question so mimes and rolls up the particulars of what ha been done and said with re- ference to the tilling up of a vacancy at the Board for the Newton district, that a large number of us ratepayers can mike neither head nor tail of him. At the Board he put on airs of such complacency and self-confidence—assuming that he perfectly understands the entire situation, when at the same time he is wholly at sea—that I am quite sure he is very misleading to his fellow-Guardians, who take it for granted that his erratic wanderings represent the true situa- tion. A short time ago, upon the said Guardian's own Bone'. tion, a requisition was got up asking him to nominate a certain gentleman for the vacant seat on the Board, and then when he goes to the next Board meeting, instead of bringing the affair before the notice of the meeting (as I un- derstand it) he simply hands it to the Clerk to be put in the waste paper basket. When the matter is casually men- tioned by the Clerk (who by-the-bye has more manlines3 than our Guardian) at a subsequent meeting the latter makes it out, in his own way, that the requisitionists are simply offering fact ima opposition. I could very soon un- told the whole tite of the transaction with reference to the said requisition, wh'ch would not reflect very creditably on this pseudological gentlem al, but I forbear, though at the same time this much I must say, he is one of those kind of persons who run with the hare and rA hold with the hounds. I see also in the aoovemaentioned report one of the Guardians makes Mr Sutton say there is no power to make them fill up the vacarcy unless they themselves write to the Local Government Board. Well, we shall ace. Some- body else can write the letter besides the Board. It's all very well for the Guardians to imagine that the wisdom of the late two Guardians his been concentrated in the num- ber that is 1, ft. In my humble opinion, if Newton must be sufficiently represented, we ought to have two more mem- b-rs on the Board instead of one, as one of our Guardians is hardly ever at his past, an those two who do attend are so efficient that they can let the simple question of medicine supplied to our district exceed the cut of same suppled to Warrington township by about 53 6d, or in other words, where Warrington costs one shilling per thousand, Newton costs six shillings per thousand. In conclusion. Mr Editor, it is to be hoped the Guardian above alluded to will in future, when he has occasion to present a petition from the ratepayers to the Board, give facts in connection with the LIMO instead of fiction —I re- main, dear sir, yours, atc. PRO BONO PUB lICO

Sir,—l see that you gave. a rather lengthy report of last, week's meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, and especially of that part referring to the vacancies on the Board. Much was said in favour of the filling up of the vacancies, and but little (in substance) to the contrary. I was glad the chairman looked at it in a sensible light, as did also the clerk, who plainly told them that they were doing a thing which the Local Government Board might possibly I undo. The Board has a life of three years, and why should we be without our proper represent aim], at a time, too, when fair representation is PO much the cry of the people ? It would be altogether another thing if elections took place every twelve naruths and half the time had elapsed. Mr. Appleton, our repres,ntative, seems to me to be like a chameleon—able to change his colour whenever he pleases. Anyhow, without doubt, he says a thing in Earlestown, yet when he gets five miles away he Ir.COMeS a Most strenuous opponent of his own proplsa!s.- He ought honourably to I have told the Board that he kMr. Appleton) proposed to a number of persons in Earlestown that the vacancy ought to be filled up, promised to 11:10,74 in the matter, and asked for a requisition (not necessarily large, he said) just to strengthen his hands. If the names on the requisition—which, by- the-bye, no one seems to have seen save the clerk—were not numerous, they included some of the mat ialuential tradesmen of Earlestown. Without a doubt he put the affair in a wrong light. He attempted to play on two fiddles at once, and when the Guardians and the people know bow , Pac!fl really stocd thy will consider, lam sure, that he failed ignominiouily to play either satisfactorilv.—Yours, dic , WATCHMAN.

DRINKING WATER FOR WORKPEOPLR. Sir,—As the supply of drinking water for noikpeniak seems to b 3 attracting some measure of public attention, you will perhaps allow me the use of your columns to give the result of my experience in the matter. Before the present secretary of the Warrington Water- winks Company came into effice I paid £2 per annum for the supply of water, for all purposes, for the workahop in me. After Mr Ross was appointed secretary, the Water Compsny found that this sum was not large enough, and proceeded to put down a water meter. I had then to pay £2 12s per annum, being the minitimm charge for water taken by meter. By-and-love it was found that the minimum quantity of water was never need, and that, consequently, nothing further was to be got on that basis of charge, so the Water Company proceeded, notwithstanding my remon- strance, to remove the meter and decided to charge on the basis of so much per head for the workpeople. Thus there had been three distinct ways of charging for the water:— first, a lump sum; second, by met(r ; third, so much per head. And as I could not foresee what the next mote would be I declined to take the water any longer, and put up tanks to secure a sufficient supply of water for trade purposes. However, on March 20th, lam, 1 wrote to the Water Company offering to pay £5 per annum for supply of water, for drinking purposes only, for this one workshop. The secretary replied that my offer would be laid before the , directors. home time elapsed and I received no further I answer, and on inquiry as to the reason I was given to under- stand that my offer was not worth consideration, and so no reply bad been sent me. On August Bth last I went again to the office of the Water Company and offered to pay, for drinking water only, the maximum charge of six per cent, on the total assessment of the workshops, offices, warehouse, kc , which would have amounted to over £8 per annum for Lythgoe's-lane work- shop. This was declined, and I was told the charge was sixpence per heed for workpeople. I agreed to this, and proceeded to fill up a form of agreement provided by the Water Company. Before I had quite completed filhielg it I up, the secretary asked me if there wee a water closet on the premises. I replied that there arSs, but that it was hardly ! ever used, and was supplied from a large tank (this tank holds 1,300 gallons), and that I did not require a supply for it. I was informed that before drinking water was supplied , for the h Juts I must agree to pay an extra charge for this chow t, whether supplied by the Water Conipany or not, and that there would also be an extra charge for the offices, ; which are also already supplied. I remarked that it seemed to me to be quite useless attempting to come to any agree- ment on the subject, and left the office. No sooner, sir, is oae demand conceded than a fresh one is made. There the matter stands :—the Water Company refusing to supply drinking water at their own price, unless I agree to take water for other purposes, or else to pay for it whether I take it or not. I have no doubt other manufacturers are similarly treated ; and now the Water Company gets up an agitation, the object of which is to compel employers to sub- mit to their exmrtionate demands. But there is more in the question than appears on the surface. The purchase of the Water Works by the Corpora- tion must come sooner or later. Meanwhile the Water 'Company Fs making every effort, just or unjust, to increase ' the I esEnue,knowing that for every £1 perannum wrung from . the ratepayers the town will have to pay in purchase money I perhaps £25, perhaps £3O, or even more. I think it is the duty of all consumers of water to keep this in view, and to resist to the utmost all unjust and extortionate demands and charges made upon them by the Water Works Company.— Yours truly, JOHN PLATT. Lythgoe's-lane, Warrington, August 28tb, 1884.

THE WARRINGTON WATERWORK9 COMPANY ANT) THE SUPPLY OF WATER TO WORKS FOR DRINKING PURPOSES. Sir,—My attention has been directed to a letter signed " H. Whitham," inserted in your issue of the lilth met, and also to a leading article on the same subject which appears in last Saturday's issue. I shall be glad if you will, in fairness, give publication•to the following letter which, under instructions from my direc- tors, I wrote to Messrs. Rylands Brothers on the 21st Met, and I think that, after reading it, you will consider that the blame is not with either the cotnnany or myself. I may add that Messrs. Rylands have declined the pro- position contained in my letter, so there the matter rests at present.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, JOHN ROSS, Secretary.

Warrington, August 29, 1884. [coPY Waterworks Offices, Warrington, August 21st, 1884. WARRINGTON WATER —Mcsmi. Rylanda Brothers. —Urentle- rnen,—l am instructed to inform you that at the monthly meeting of the Board of Directors, held yesterday, your ap- plication for a supply of water for drinking purposes at your works was considered. The Board are most wishful that your requirements in respect of water supply should be fully satisfied, and would not seek to itnposs upon you, in respect of such supply, any terms which are not fair and rea- sonable. But having fully considered the matter, they are of opinion that the terms proposed to you in my letter of the 11th instant, viz , 61. per head for drinking and £5 per annum for water close's, washing offices, dm , are most moderate, and they do not feel able to reduce them further. With a view, however, to satisfy you of their wish to meet you in the fairest possible mincer, I an instructed to say that if you maintain your objection to the terms stated, the water may, nevertheless, be laid on at once, and the question of price and terms of supply be referred to the Local Government Board, and whose decision as to same shall be binding as well upon yourselves as upon the com- pany. Please to let me know whether I am to lay on the water, and whether you accept the terms fixed by the company;

ANTI-CONSTITU fIONAL GUARDIANS. Sir,--I should think the constituents of the Warrington Board of Guardians will have been considerably surprised by _ . . . . .

the sudden display of dialectical skill made by their repre- sentatives. at their last meeting. Theseietaid and respectable gentlemen who are appointed to look after the interests of the poor in this neighbourhood appear, if occasion requires, to be able to deyelope resources in making the worse appear the better she which might be enoied by a synod of casuists. The cause of this unexpected display of latent abilities was a question of filling up the !SCAM places on the Board, it appears there are two vacancies on the Board, one for Wareington and the other for Newton, and as it will be about 1$ months before there will be a reeular election, it would seem to ordinary people the plainest of duties to have these vacarteries filled up at once. But not so to the majority of the Wartington Board of Guardians; and in support of what is apparently an unprecedented course they put forward some very ingenious arguments, and aome other arguments which.ceu hardly be called ingenious. One gentle-man with an artless simplicity which makes us think of the "days of innocency,' says, in elect, "We don't want any eleotion or any more members; look how nicely we get on together, and there is always a querum." How irresistible, in its simplicity, must this argument appear—especial/7 to those who, like Mr. Justice Shallow. would be "se the quorum." But surely "getting on nicely together," or the presence of a quorum, is not all that is required in a representative body: If that were so the argument might be applied in a way which shows its absurdity. For instance, if the liriusc ci Cgmmons were to be depleted by death or by FOMEI other means—or, it might be, "purged" by a company GP soldiers after the Cromwellian fashion—in the Liberal in- terest, how nicely those who were left would get on together! What a rapil succession of Reform Bills ve, should have! Or, say, the same process was gone through in the Tory interest—how quickly would the "suspended" animation be strangled out of that bete noir the Fianchise Bill. And we might be sure there would not be wanting a quorum for that purpose. This application of the "getting- on-uic,ly " argument would no doubt be very pleasamt to the party favoured by it, but it would hardly be constitu- tional. Yet the Rowe of Commons, like the Beard at Guardians, is a representative body, and what is applied to one might just as fairly be applied.to the other. Another argument was that Warrington and Newton are already sufficiently represented on the Board, the one having nine members and the other three. This may be flattering to the " nine," but it seems to me to be apart from the question. The whole of the ratepayers are supposed to be represented on the Board, hut that is not so at present. The large number who voted for Major Cartwright and looked upon him as their special representative are now in fact disfran- chised.

00..,_. But there is another consideration which ought 1 to have some weight. "Getting on nicely " does I not always mean getting on well, or in such a way as I the ratepayers desire. It too often simply means making it ! pleasant for each other, and it is a matter of common ex- perience that when people all look at things from the same side, the conclusions they come to are not always very sound. Therefore even a single representative who has an individuality of his own is a great loss to a public body, seeing that many a question which is settled in a perfunc- tory manner might have had a different complexion put upon it had he been present. Let us take an illustration from this very same meeting of the Board of Guardians. An apptication was there made by one of the memb-rs for the Board to supply—by means of its school band— caeap music for a Mayoral "At Horne," and this application was at once granted. That may be cal eel "getting on nicely," but was it getting on well? If such a member as I referred to had been present he might bare looked on this application in a way which none of the present attenuated Bt rd appear to have looked on it. He might have said that an " At Home " was, to say the least, only a semi-public affair, and alto- gether different from a Band of Hope festival or a Walking, Day; and that, therefore, the granting of this application might in:cadges a vicious precedent. If one guircliato; he might boy gam') on. Vra t. 9 l'avC for that purpo.§e Atlanta` might want it or a gatdeu party or something of that kind and how could they refuse , one if thy granted to another? I give this illustration I only to show the Mischief that may come of turning a rt- presentat vs body into a kind of Close corporation. A third argument was as to the cat of an election, and this seems to have had a great deal of weight with several of the guardi ans. But [must confess I cannot see whet bearing .it has on the question whether the hard ought to go months Of years without its full number of m'onl.)ers. To my mind it appears to he an excellent at gument for devi- sing some method or reducing the cost of el tCtios, but not at all far keeping the Board in an imperfectly constituted. state. If we are to tare local self government with all its ad- vantages we must p ly for keeping the 132C33SAry in ;chiaery in order. In conclusion I must express the hope that the Board of IGoy:retains will reconsider their d, cision as to this matter. These are not days for disfrarchising voters, no matter upon ) what ingenious pretexts, but rather for enfranchising them I —I am, sir, A 13, ITEPA.YER.

THE TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT AT WIDNES. HARI Eir FESTIVAL AND FRUIT BANQUET.

On Saturday, the quarterly meeting of the District Juvenile Council of Good Tempters was held at Widnes, under the presidency of Brother Preston. There was a good attendance of delegates and offlcials.—The Chairman stated that last quarter 20 temples reported a fnembership of 518 boys and 8-10 girls, mrking a total of 1,158. This quarter there were 22 temples with a membership of 555 boys and 714 girls ; total, 1.2. There had bees 2113 members initi- ated, 70 suspended, 48 withdrawn' 15 had entered a sub- lodge, 4 had been expelled, and B bad died. The average weekly attendance of members was 740. There were 174 honorary members, or an increase of 57. Two new temples had been opened since the het meeting. The report was adopted and the ordinary business proceeded with. Subse- quently the delegates and friends had tea at (be Public Hall, Hutchinson-street. In the evening a harvest festival was held. In had been arranged biz-the Star of Widnes Lodge of Good Template, and the Blueltibben Gospel Armr, and was very' successful. The room, which usually presents a by no means inviting aspect, bad been metamorphised by decorations of flags and flowers and foliage, and mottoes in various designs graced the walls Particular attention had been paid to the platform, which was laden with fruit. &twerp, and vegetables, arranged with good effect. The decarations had been carried out under the superintendence of Messrs T. 13 Ball, C A Leech, Grurten, Mrs Turton Mrs Birkhall, and Mrs Steadman. Assistance was els° rendered by the committee, which consisted of Messrs Pierce, Poole, Bullivant, and Andrews. Previous to the proceedings cora- mencing,in the hall, an open-air meeting was held, after vitatch there was a procession headed by the Star of Tem- perance Brass Band to the Public Hall. . Mr. Preston, district superintendent of the Juvenile Tempters, occupied the chair, and he was supported by Mr U Tarte', Mrs Bowles (ciptain), and Miss Mitchell (lieutenant) of the local branch of the Blue Ribbon Army. A number of children belonging to the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple occupied seats on the platform.—The Chairman delivered a brief address, in-- which he expressed "hie gratification in pre- siding over a meeting arranged by two different bodies working together in the interests of a common cause. He referred to the importance of training up children to habits of sobriety, so that they might fill their stations in life with clear heads and to the glory and honour of God, and he hearttly advised that chil- dren should enter the juvenile lodges and the adults the Good Templar Order.—Mr Bebbington alluded to the Licensing Laws, and said many magistrates seemed to think that a public-house in a certain neighbourhood was an abso- lute necessity, and 'they ruled that one should be placed where a person wanted witboat tonsalting the people. Public-houses were planted right in the midst of working- men, and they had preyed the greatest bane to the moral and religious welfare of the town of Widnes. He-pointed with encouragement to the fact that the temperance advo- cates were now on the winning side. (Applause.)—Mr Kirkus, of Liverpool, also delivered a short address. The proceedings were enlivened with an entertainment in which the following children took part :—D Johnson, Hague, Stocker Dodd, F Price, Turton. Broderick, Wilkinson, and P and L Bradburn. The members of the Juvenile Temple sang several melodies, Mr A Ogden being at the harmo- nium.

On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held in the same building; and a good audience assembled. At intervals during the evening fruit and vegetables Fere distributed amongst those present. The following ladies and gentlemen contributed the articles named r—Wheat and oats: Mr J Prescott, Hough Green; Mr Tarton, Hale; Mrs Joseph Long- ton, Didefield ;Mr Swaine, Four-top Toke Farm. Flowers: Messrs Beswiek and Hunt, Penketh ; Mrs Horrabin, Mr Joseph Rocker. Vegetables: Mrs Longton, Hough Green; Mrs Joseph Longton, DidsSeld ;Mrs Horrobin. Fruit: Mrs Hill and Mrs Taylor, Old Marsh. The chair was occupied by Mr William Clarke, of the Hollies, Ditton, who, in open- ing the proceedings, referred to the bountiful harvest the farmers were reaping, and went on to say that he was not a pledged teetotaller nor a blue ribbonite, but he seas neverthe- less a total abstainer in every sense of the term. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry he had not been a total abstainer longer than he had, and if he were speaking to anyone who had experienced the different feel. logs caused by the use of drink, let them take his advice and from that night become total abstainers. He was glad to be able to do what he did for the cause of temperance. They were at work at Ditton, and last winter about 70 pledges were taken; and they would try to get another seventy during the coming winter. The cause was making rapid progess in all parts of the country, and he was convinced that the question of total abstinence would soon be the great question of the day. (Applause.) —Mr. Eelick, of Liverpool, depicted the evils which the liquor traffic brought upon all classes of the community, but especially upon the working' men, and Mr. Andrew Poulson pointed out that while there was a decrease in the amount spent in intoxicating liquor, there was an increase in the deposits at the Post Office Savings Bank.—During the evening the band-bell ringers and the band gave several selections of music, and the choir rendered " Bring in tke

div.head: IMPORTANT LIGE, DECISION.
div.p: IMPORTANT LIGE, DECISION.

At the Warrington Boroueh Police Court, yesterday morning, before Captain Reynolds and Mr John White, a case that was of Beall immaterial proved of considerable importance. A woman named Ellen Howley, the wife of a shoemaker, summoned Anne Spendelow, of 201, Orford- avenue, the wife of a colour-sergeant in the 3rd Liverpool Regiment, for using provoking language to her on the 21st August, calling her a reptile a cat, and other opprobrious epithets.—Mr Davies appeared for the complainant, and Mr Cottingham, barrister, instructed 13! Mr .1 Field, solicitor, Manchester, defended.—Evidence as to the language havin; been called, Mr Cottingham informed the &Ai that the case did net come within their jurisdiction, as it had been decided by a superior court that unless it were sworn by the complainant that such complainant went in bodily fear, or an actual assault had been committed, the Bench could not bind over the,defendant to keep the peach..—Mr Davies wished to ask complainant the question whether she were not in bodily fear, but Mr Cottingham objected, as Mr Davies had had the opportunity of questioning his witnesses before. I After the complainant had- heard the point she would be ready to swear anything. Mr Cottingham then read the f, !lowing extract from the "Law Times," July 19th, 3879, viz Personal insults not accompanied by any act which can be construed into an assault cannot, it seems, be pre- vented by any legal means. This point was decided last week in the case of Philips v. Justices of Gateshead, which came before Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and Mr .FuetMe I Field, sitting as the Divisional Court for hearing motions , from all the &visions. The facts of the caso were these. A I policeman at Gateshead bad been dismissed from the force, and in order to be revenged on the police-constable, who; it is to be presume I, was the cause of his dismissal, the dis- charged officer took every opportunity of using insulting laoguage about and towards hie late chief. The chief put up with the annoyance for a considerable time, but hie patience becoming exhausted, and not knowing what else to do to put a stop to the nuisance, he ap- plied to the justices to bind over the ex-police- man to be of good behaviour on the ground that be, the chief-constable, would otherwise be provoked to commit a beeaeh of the peace. Tied justices, with a natural desire to support the dignity of so important a person as the head of the polite, at once acceded to theapplicrion, and ordered defendant to find sureties for his good behaviour for six months, subsequently committing him to prison for that period in default of finding the sureties re- quired. Thereupon a rale for a writ of certi- orari to bring up a warrant to compel the pro- ceedings to be quashed was ob'ainecl, and in making it ab- solute, it was pointed out by the Court that a condition pre- cedent to the granting an order calling on a parson to enter recognieances to keep the peace or be of good behaviour, was an oath by the applicant that he went in bodily fear of . .

the person to tie boui& over. What would inevitably be the result of a case like the one in point must be obvious, but at the 'same time it brings to view a state of things by no means satisfactory. It simply comes to this, . .

that it one man _ chooses to insult and annoys another, he may continue to do so as long and sit often as he pleases provided he does not commit an assiult, or make use of slanderous or obscene language. The person annoyed has no remedy ; he has no right of action; there is no criminal procedure which will relieve or protect him, and if he takes the law into his own hands and avenges the insults by persona: chastisement he renders himself liable to a prosecntion for assault." He also quoted other authorities in support of his contention.—The Magistratee Clerk (Mr H B White), said that he had not before heard the case in point. After hear- ing what had been advanced by Mr Cottingbarn he must advise the magistrates that in future the ordinary cases of using rovoking language must ba dispensed with.—The Bench were of opinion that that would not be a matter of regret to the magistrates, as there were so many trivial cases of that description came before the court.—The case was then dismissed as not coming within the jurisdiction of the Court, and the Bench declined to accede to the application of Mr Davies that a Case for appeal should be granted.

ANOTHER LONDON MYSTERY.—A shocking discovery Was made on Tuesday by a servant girl named Edith Poole, re- siding at 32, Clarendon-gardens, Maida-vale, London. The Voting woman had occasion to go down the front garden to answer the bell, wheq she noticed what appeared to be a bundle of paper, the end of which was protruding from under some bushes in the garden. The parcel was taken from its hiding place and conveyed into the house, when, on its being opened, it was founi to contain the body of a girl, supposed to be about ten or eleven years of age. The police were at once communicated with, and Police-constable Hampton re- moved the parcel to the Carlton-terrace Police Station, where it was examined by the divisional surgeon. The body was in a fearfully decomposed condition, and until a post- mortem examination is made it is impossible to state the precise cause of death. It is, however, feared that the child had been criminally assaulted and then murdered, and sub- sequently— probably during Monday night—conveyed to Clarendon Gardens, which is a very quiet and secluded road. The body was entirely nude, and was wrapped in a piece of brown paper, securely fastened by- a string. With the object of reducing the size of the bundle, the child's legs were drawn up from the knee into the body, and its head pressed down on to its chest. The child was of fair complexion, about four feet in height, and had long brown hair.

RUNCORN S PAEMBOWKETT BUILDING 800.43 TY. The annual :meeting of the members of this society was held in Bethesda School-room, last evening. Mr S C Beckett, one of the trustees, presided; and there was a good attend- auco.—Mr W Handley, the secretary, read the minutes of the last annual meeting, which were passed on the motion of Mr Booth, seconded by Mr J Frith.—The Chairman baid be was very pleased indeed to take the chair at this the third annual meeting,.especially considering that they had so favourable a report. He bad no hesitation in saying that that it was one of the best reports of a Starr-Bowkett Society within twenty or thirty miles around. The society had made during the year, which, of course, represented three years, a profit of £5O 9s Od, which he thought spoke well for the management of the society. The chairman concluded with moving the adoption of the report, which has appeared in this journal.—Nir Haerop asked far an explanation of the item £l5 5s 2d, repayment of subscriptions to widows of deceased members. The chairman replied that the rules provided that if a member died, the directors could repay to his widow the whole of his subscriptions without deducting the Is 31 per share per year for working expenses. (Applause.) There bad been several deaths amongst members during the year.—The report being seconded was adopted unanimously.—The elec- tion of four directors was the next business, and there were seven nominations for four places. Mr C Dut- ton and Mr T Handley were appointed scrutineers. The result was declared as follows : Messrs WAt Booth, 58 votes;: A Riley, 48; W Armstrong, 41' • R Foulkes 34, J Poole 32, J R Digges 17, Robert Hoyle 8. The first four gentlemen were declared elected. Mr W Brookes was re-appointed auditor, on the motion-of Mr J R Frith. On the motion of Mr Booth, Mr Joseph Cunnab, of Frodsham, was also appointed aadi:or. Mr W Brookes and Mr J•Poyah, the auditors for the past year, were voted £2 each for their services on the motion of Mr Harrop, seconded by Mr Thomas Nan. The Chairman moved that the secre- tary's salary of £45 per year as per rule be confirmed. The motion was seconded and carried. The Chairman announced that as the present society had obtained its fall number of members, it had been decided to open a second society in Runcorn. (Applause.) A provisional board of directors had been selected, and Mr W Handley had been appointed secretary. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. .1. R. Frith, seconded by Mr. James Ball, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the directors and the secretary for past services.—Mr. J. Poole responded on behalf of the directors.—The 18th appropriation then took place. Mr. John Lunt and Mr. C. Dutton were appointed scrutineers, and a boy named Little was selected to draw the ballot balls. Ilumiser 170 was brought to light, and a refer- ence to the books showed that Mr. Win. Brearley, of 9. Cawdor-street, was entitled to MOO free at interest for 12i years. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.'

The appointment of Mr Petherton, Q.C., to be Chief Justice for the Western Provinces in India is gazette& A telegram from Philadelphia states that the Orion. from Wilmington for Liverposl, has put into Lewes in distress, with crew down with fever.

Cmcarr.--The Australian innings closed yesterday for 358. The South made only 178 in the first innings, and consequently followed on. •The second inning ended for 73, the a ustraliaas thus winning by one innings and 107 runs. 'SUICIDE OH THE RAILRUC.—An inquest was held on Pliday on a man named Bryant, who was killed by jumping from a train iq which he Nils being conveyed to I.4lwes poi on a charge of robbery. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased deliberately committed sui- cide. _ _

Sanaa; A Corr Ann ON Firm—Jane Jones, of Pontes- bury, was on Friday committed for trial by the Shrews- bury magistrates on the charge of arson. The prisoner, it is alleged, set fire to the thatch of a cottage occupied by a widow named Morgan, who was unable to pay the rent de- manded by Mrs Jones. THE ALLEGED POISMING AT BACDP.-01 Fri lay morn- iSg, at Bocup, a hawker named Dunn was remanded for assaulting his sweetheart. It is alleged that he tiled to poison her a week ago because she refused to live with him as his wife. The prisoner, it is stated, asked her to drink of some beer into which ha had dropped a powder—the con- stituents of which are not known, as the liquid has not yet been analysed—and when she.refuEd struck her. Tan GRAVESEND COLLISION.—The Board of Trade in- quiry into the collision between the steamships Dion a and Camden, off Gravesend, concluded on Friday. The court found that the couse of the collisioh was the excessive rate of speed of the Dione, and suspended the certificate of her master for six months, allowing him, however, a chief mate's certificate. The master and second officer of the Camden were not to blame, and Mr Rothery did not think the pilot could have avoided the collision.

THE KHARTOUM EXPEDITIOIII—LORD WOLSELEY'S DEPARTURE The Central News says the personal staff of Lord Wolee- ley will comprise Lieutenant• Colonel L. V. Swaine, who hal been appointed military secretary to his lord- ship, and no following aides•cle-camps :—Major Wardrop (3rd Dtagoon Guards), Major Creagh, BA., Lieutenant Childers, RE ,and Lieutenant Adye, R.A. Lord Wolseley, accompanied by some of him personal staff, will leave Lon- don on S'undiy evening, and travel direct overland to Trieste, where he will embark on board the his for Alex- andria. It is not, however, certain that his staff will accompany him in the Iris, the accommodation of the vessel being somewhat limited. The officills at the War Office are still busy with the labours entailed by the arrangements for the expedition, and are working till a late hoes. _ . .

The Duke of Cambridge visited the War Office to-day, and was in consultation with the heads of the departments at both this office and at tee Admiralty. The officials are working in the most indefatigable manner to Dealt on preparations, so that everything shall be in readinese when required. The following steamers have, the Central News learns, been taken up by the Government to convey four hundred of the boats for the expedition, and will sail at various dates between the third and fifteenth September :—The Pelletn, President Garfield. Aston Hall, and Naranga to sail from London and Portsmouth; the Pelle th also takes about four hundred tons of stores and provisions. The hiagdala to sail from Liverpool, and the Frutera to sail from Glasgow. The British India Navigation Company's Steamer Rewa has been substituted for the Malwa, and will sail on September third with the first division of the telegraph and Field Park Royal- Engineers, who- will embark at Gravesend. The strength of the Engineers will be increased by one company:. Messra Glovers fine steamer Spelley, 2,000 tons, will leave England Sept. 4th for Sierra-Leone, and will afterwards embark the 300 Kromen who are to join the ex- pedition. She will then sail direct for Egypt. The only officer accompanying Lord Northbrook will be Captain L A Beaumon, R.N., but he will probably have on his staff In Egypt Major Marriott, and Moulin Mahomed Samiulla Khan, who is coming from Bombay. Lord North- brook will meet Sir, E Baring at Gratz, and travel with him to Cairo. LETTER FROM GENERA!: GORDON. CAIRO, FRIDAY (Central News telegram).—General Gor- don's letter has arrived at Old Dongola. It states that Khartoum is quiet. THE FReNCO-lIIIINESE WAR. REPORTED DESIRE FOR A SETTLEMENT. SetAncrear, FRIDAY, 1140 AM—The 'Viceroy of Canton has ordered all French subjects in.Liang Knang to leave im- mediately. It is reported that the Chinese Government shownan in- clination to come to terms with France.' The French Consul here has received a telegram from Admiral Conrbet announcing that he made an attack upon Kinpai, which bad been completely puccessful. Pants, FRIDAY.—A telegram from Shanghai, dated Aug. 29, 11-30 a.m.' states: Perfect tranquilitt prevails among the European inhabitants, but the Chinese are leaving the town and concessions in alarm. Proclamations have been lamed by the consular body and the Taotai of Shanghai, in- viting the natives to remain and to fear nothing, as the French do not intend to operate against Shanghai or Woo- sung for the present. The Chinese authorities at Shanghai have received a very important telegram from Pekin' and rumours are again current that China wishes to coins to an arrangement with the French Government. THE CHOLERA. • MArtermuzs, FRIDAY, 9-30 Am.—Two deaths from cholera occurred here last night. Tonsom. FRlMY.—There were five 'deaths from cholera here last night, one of which occurred in the city, three in the suburbs, and one in the Bon Rencontre Hospital.

Wittuneorrox Muslim SOCIRTY.— The annual general meeting of this seciety is advertised to be held on Thurs. day evening next at the schoolroom in Cairo-street. Mr. John lands, President, is expected to take the chair. The Medical Press an 4 Circular, commenting on the figures read at the Salford Brewster Sessions, said they nom; psi the reflection that a terrible agent in the production of disease and crime is practically encouraged in the midst of the people by the reckless increase of the 'number of drink- ing houses, for which the licensing magistrates are mainly responsible. MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A BARMAID.— Considerable ex- citement was occasioned in Bolton on Wednesday conse- quent upon the mysterious death of a barmaid named Annie Day. For some time the girl had been receiving the atten- tions of an old farmer, William Kay, of Ainsworth, near Bury. On Tuesday evening the pair left town by train, and were seen to proceed along an unfrequented lane, where two hours afterwards the girl was found dead in Kay's arms by an expoliceman named Eastbam, who bad been attracted thither by hearing cries of distress. The police have the matter in hand.
